full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This appeal by the plaintiff directed against judgment and decree dated 14-10-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong dismissing Other Class Suit No. 90 of 1991 renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 163 of 1998.

2. Appellant as plaintiff filed the suit praying for following reliefs:-

(ক) ১/২ নং  বিবাদীর নামীয় প্রচারিত বি, এস ৬৩ নং খতিয়ানে নিম্নতপশীলভুক্ত দাগ অর্ন্তভুক্ত করা যোগ সাজসী, ফেরবী,ভুল,অশুদ্ধ, বেআইনী অকর্মন্য ও তঞ্চকতা পূর্ণ হওয়া এবং তদ্বারা বাদী কোম্পানী বাদ্য নহেন এবং বাদী কোম্পানীর নামীয় নিম্ন তপসীলভুক্ত সম্পত্তি ৬৪ নং বি,এস খতিয়ানের অর্ন্তভুক্ত ও তাহা বাদী কোম্পানী স্বত্ব দখল কার মালিক হওয়া মর্মে উচ্চারণ বা ঘোষনার ডিগ্রী হয়:

(খ) নালিশী তপশীলোক্ত সস্পত্তিতে বাদী কোম্পানীর শান্তি পূর্ণদখলে বিঘ্ন সৃষ্টি না করার জন্য এবং তাহাতে জোর পূর্বক প্রবেশ না করার জন্য বারন করিয়া ১/২ নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞা ডিক্রী হয়।

3. The suit land mentuined as:-

তপসীল

জিলা- চট্রগ্রাম, থানা-কোতয়ালী, মৌজা-কলিম বাজার প্রকাশ বিছমত কাশিম বাজার, সি,এস, খতিয়ান নং- ৮,সি,এস ১৪২ দাগাদীর আন্দর আর,এস,খতিয়ান ৬৪ আর, এস ১৩০ দাগাদীর আন্দর বি,এস খতিয়ান নং-৫৪, বি,এস,দাগ নং- ১৬ জমির পরিমান ৭১৮৭ একর বা/(১৬৯১ কানী/ষোল গন্ডা) অবস্থিত স্ট্রাকচারসহ।

4. In the suit defendant No.1, defendant Nos. 4 to 8 and defendant Nos. 9 and 10 contested by filing 3 separate written statements. In the appeal, Mohammad Iqbal, son of late Mohammad Ismail, Md Shawkat Ali Chowdhury, son of late Alhaj Mohammad Ali Chowdhury, Hosseinul Arefin, son of Alhaj Kamal Uddin Ahmed and Shameem Akter, daughter of Maulvi Nurul Islam added themselves as respondent Nos. 11-14 by this Court's order dated 5-7-2000 and 24-3-2010. These respondents are purchasers for value from plaintiff appellate when the suit was pending before the Lower Court having claim title and possession and no stay order was operating from the lower Court as to the sale of the land/property.

5. Although it is not so necessary, but it may be referred to as, defendant No.1, in his written statement denied the case of the plaintiff and also in his written statement stated that he did not sell the land to anybody, even to defendant Nos. 4-8 but defendant Nos. 4-8 and defendant Nos. 9 and 10 in their written statement empathetically claimed that they purchased the land from defendant No.1. Defendant Nos. 9 and 10 in their written statement stated that they also purchased land from defendant No.1. Defendant Nos. 4-8 claimed that no land was sold by defendant No.1 to anybody else except them. On the other hand, defendant Nos. 9 to 10 also claimed that no land was sold by defendant No.1 to anybody else except them. Defendant No.4-8 and defendant No.9 and 10 made contradictory statements as to the sale of land. It is further found from record that defendant No. 1 sold an over 0.8800 acres of instead of 0.7187 acres to defendant Nos. 4-8 and defendant Nos. 9-10 making sale of non-existing property.

6. Plaintiff's case in nutshell is that the suit land was originally belonged to Pakistan Tobacco Company Ltd. After liberation of Bangladesh as per provision of President Order No. 16 of 1972 suit land vested in the Government. Government sold the suit land to the plaintiff by registered deed, Exhibit-1. Government sold to plaintiff 0.3550 acres of land from PS plot No. 17, 0.2287 acres of land from PS plot No. 18 and 0.2200 acres of land from PS Plot No. 19 of PS Khatian No.5 of J/L No.4 of mouza Kashim Bazar, PS Kotwali, District Chittagong. On behalf of Government Hon'ble President of Bangladesh executed the deed and after purchase plaintiff mutated its name, paying rents and maintaining possession.

7. Mrs Sigma Huda, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, filed application under Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for withdrawal of the suit stating that the suit is running with some formal defects and further submits that suit was filed on wrong recording of BS Khatian No. 63 and 64 but submits that, by this, authority has corrected the Khatian in favour of plaintiff appellant and further submits that while drafting the plaint it was mistake of the learned Advocate who did not include the land of PS plot No. 19 containing 0.2200 acres of land and learned Judge dismissed the suit holding that plaintiff claimed excess land than acquired by exhibit-1. Learned Advocate further submits that the genially of acquiring title by the plaintiff title by the plaintiff has not been properly described in the plaint, also the cause of action and schedule of the property have not been mentioned properly as there is no boundary of the schedule given in the plaint, as such, learned Advocate, further submits that if the suit running with this plaint the suit must fail as such prayed for withdrawal of the suit.

8. Mr Suvash Chandra Saha, learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant No.1, submits that, learned Judge on finding that the schedule of the property and cause of action having not reflected property dismissed the suit and on the facts of the given case learned Judge committed no illegality in dismissing the suit.

9. Mr Mahbubey Alam, Mr Omar Sadat, Mr Md Aminul Islam and respondent Nos. 11-14 on the other hand submits that, they have purchased the suit land from plaintiff appellant with value and they are possessing the suit land and if the suit be withdraw then their purchase should be protected. Mr Omar Sadat, learned Advocate and Mr Md Aminul Islam, learned Advocate and Mr Md Ramzan Ali, submit that plaintiff's title has been perfected by the fact that the suit land was vested in the Government as per provision of President Order No. 16 of 1972 and from purchase from plaintiff added respondent acquired indefeasible title and such purchase should be protected while allowing plaintiff's prayer for withdrawal of the suit. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Advocate on behalf of respondent No. 11-14 also submits that section 14 of the aforesaid President Order stand a bar for instituting any legal proceeding against property vested in the Government as per President Order No. 16 of 1972 and so far-said vesting has not been challenged by any parties, purchase of respondent Nos. 11-14 from plaintiff appellant shall stand acquiring good title to them and possession, of respondent Nos. 11-14 under such purchase cannot be questioned by anyone.

10. On considering the entire material before us as regard title of the plaintiff appellant as well as purchase from plaintiff appellant by added respondent Nos. 11-14 it is our considered vies that such purchase cannot be questioned as they acquired good title as per provision of President Order No.16 of 1972 because when the property vested in the Government it vested with its entirety free from any encumbrances as such, title of added respondent Nos. 11-14 is perfect title. It appears that plaintiff appellant sold the suit land to respondents Nos. 11-14 then delivered possession to respondents Nos. 11-14 who possessed the suit land unless the possession of the respondent Nos. 11-14 be in danger, a suit for permanent injunction by the seller plaintiff against defendant No. 1 without properly constituted the suit, without describing the schedule property and without describing properly cause of action is running with formal defect. It appears that defendant Nos. 4-8 claimed purchase from defendant No.1 whom authority found while correcting record of right of BS Khatian to be a fictitious person, did not admit that he sold land defendant Nos. 4-8 and also to defendant Nos. 9 and 10, as such, defendant Nos. 4-8 and 9 and 10 acquired no good title save and except dispute, as such, they should, at first, perfected their legal status before dispute possession of plaintiff to that effect, of respondent Nos. 11-14. It appears that plaintiff appellant sold the suit land to respondent Nos. 11-14 who has been delivered possession to respondent Nos. 11-14 and possessed the suit land, as such, unless the possession of the respondent Nos. 11-14 be in danger, a suit for permanent injunction by the seller plaintiff without any properly constituted and without describing properly cause of action is running, with formal defect.

11. We have already mentioned herein above about the formal defect identified by Mrs Sigma Huda, learned Advocate.

12. Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure is as follows:- "At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim.

2. Where the Court is satisfied-

(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of claim. It may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim.

3.	 Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from institution any fresh sit in respect of such subject-matter or such party of the claim."

13. Let us see what is meant by formal defect. There is no defamation of formal defect. It has to be settled from pleadings. Formal defect includes every kind of defect which is in no way affect the merits of the case i.e. a defect of form not a defect in the merits of the case. In the full Bench decision of Ramras vs Appanna, AIR 1940 Bom. 121 (FB) it is held that expression formal defect must be given a wide and liberal meaning and must be deemed to connote every kind of defect which does not affect the merit of the case, whether the defect be fatal to the suit or not, rejection of a material document for not having a proper stamp and the erroneous valuation of the subject matter of the suit. In the case of Atul Krishna Roy vs Raykishore Mohonty, AIR 1956 Orissa 77, in the case of Brajamohan Saberfo vs Sarojini Panigrahi and others AIR 1975 Orissa 39 it is held that failure of the plaintiff's counsel to incorporate a Prayer in the plaint was a defect constitutes 'sufficient ground' for permitting the plaintiff to withdraw his suit with liberty to file a fresh suit. In the case of Balide Kamayya vs Pragada Papayya AIR 1918 Mad 1287 it is held that the expression other sufficient grounds' occurring in clause (b) of Order XXIII, rule 1 (2) CPC is not necessary restricted to defects of a formal character but is wide enough to embrace other defects as well. In the case of Robert Waton and Co vs The Collector of Rajshaye and others, 13 Moor S Indian Appeals 160, Saidur Rahman Malia and another vs Abdur Rahman and others 13 DLR 160, Madan Mohan vs Abdus Samad, 32 DLR 176 similar view have been taken i.e. formal defect must be given a liberal meaning to include every kind of defect which does not affect the merit of the suit.

14. It appears that in drafting the plaint the learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant did not notice the schedule of the deed and drafted plaint as if there is no defect in the cause of action; no prayer was made to challenge the deeds of the defendants claiming title proper genealogy of driving title by plaintiff was not made, there is defect in the genealogy of acquiring title by the plaintiff and there is defect in the schedule of the property which constitute formal defect; by which if the suit and appeal, it is settled law that appeal is continuation of the suit, be run it must fail as such we are of the view that, plaintiff appellant rightly invoke Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

15. Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that if there be any formal defects and suit for the formal defects shall fail and if the Court is satisfied that no effective purpose would be served in prosecuting the suit, court can pass necessary order allowing plaintiff to withdraw the. Suit along with judgments and decree permission to sue afresh if it is not barred by limitation.

<u>16. Learned Advocate for the appellant referred to a Single Bench decision of Mustafa Kabir Uddin Ahmed vs Badrun Nessa Chowdhury, 54 DLR 416, where it has been held that 'There is no legal bar in granting an application for withdrawal of a suit with liberty to file a suit afresh on the self same matter even at the revisional stage provided the other requirements of the law are complied with.. In the case of Abdur Rahman vs Kheru Malitha and others 50 DLR (AD) 71, AZM Khalilur Rahman vs Md Syed Hossain and others, 25 DLR 485, Mir Golam Kibria vs Rayn Promatha Deb Ray, 39 DLR 586, Kanta and another vs Goya Proshad, AIR 1972 All 143 similar views have been taken.</u>

17. In an unreported decision, (in CWN 1st issue, January, 24 and 25, 1897 where it has been noted as Court of law described unreported case as pocket pistol), the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Khawaja Neamatulah and another vs Khurshidi Begum and others, Civil Petition for Special Leave Appeal (CPLA) No. 40 of 1974 which was dismissed on 12-6-1974 where it has been held that 'It occurs to us that .there is no force in the contention that the High Court Division did not notice that the trial Court while allowing the plaintiff prayer did not assign by reason. Of course, the trial Court did not, in clear terms, state that it was satisfied that there was formal defect or other sufficient cause but it must be presumed from the order itself that the trial Court having been satisfied about the formal defect and other sufficient cause as required under Rule 1, Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure passed the order in question."

<u>18. In the case of Shyamal Chandra Roy vs Probhat Chandra Roy, 51 DLR 504 it has been held as "The plaintiff is at liberty to withdraw his suit at any stage without any permission from the Court and he needs permission for withdrawal only when he wants to sue afresh on the same cause of action." In the case of Shahabuddin Ahmed vs Upazila Education Officer, Bakerganj and others, 41 DLR 168, on the question of applying provisions of Order XXIII Rule 1(2) for withdrawal of suit, it is held Court to decide whether there is any formal defect or sufficient ground if there is none, duty of the Court is to reject the application- But if it allows withdrawal, leave to bring a fresh suit cannot be refuse." In the case of Jaban Ali and others vs Tazir Muhammad and others 59 DLR 584 it has been held that "The Court cannot withhold permission to bring fresh suit while allowing withdrawal of the existing suit in which the prayer is made.</u>

19. It appears that from the aforesaid facts of the case discussed and on consideration of the materials before us, we find that this suit runs with formal defect and if the suit be withdrawn then nobody will be prejudiced as title a defendant Nos. 4-8 and 9-10 is defective as there vendor disowned them and defendant No. 1 has been found to be a fictitious person in addition to the fact that CS plot No. 142 is a hill situated to the East side of a road and whereas PS Plot Nos. 17,18 and 19 and BS Plot No. 16 is a plain land situated to the west side of a road, as such, they are required to settle their identity to challenge the title of the plaintiff. Respondent Nos. 11-14 who are added during continuation of the appeal, also should have no grievances as their purchase by withdrawal of the suit is not going to affect their clean title and rightful possession which by all means is perfected as there is no suit pending at present, as such, their purchase is not hit provision of its pendency under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and consequently their possession also cannot be threatened by anybody.

20. Plaintiff's Other Suit No. 90 of 1991 renumbered as Other Suit No. 163 of 1998 pending in the Court of learned Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Chittagong is withdrawn with the plaint, written statement, depositions and also judgment and decree is hereby withdrawn and cancelled the plaintiff is allowed to sue afresh if it feel necessary.

21.	In the result, this appeal is disposed of.

22.	 Send down the lower Court record. Communicate this order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This rule by the plaintiff, directed against judgment and Order No. 209 dated 17-6-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Comilla in Arbitration Suit No. 01 of 1995 of that Court rejecting the application of the plaintiff dated 23-1-2006 under section 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 as amended/ added by Ordinance No. 49 of 1978 published in the Extra Ordinary Dhaka Gazette dated 5-12-1978 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for' rejecting the objection petition dated 9-10-2005 and 14-11-2005 filed by the defendant No. 5 against award and to pass a decree in terms of award dated 20-8-2005 filed by the learned Arbitrator.

2. The short facts relating for disposal of the rule, is that, the opposite party, Bangladesh Water Development Board, floated Tender Notice No. T-3 of 1987-88 issued from the Office of the Executive Engineer, Gomati Water Development Division, Bangladesh Water Development Board, Comilla; (here we tempted to note that whenever our national poet, Kazi Nazrul Islam went to Comilla, his father-in-law's house, he spent time on the bank of river Gomati and in some of his eternal songs river Gomati occupy considerable place) petitioner submitted tender on 10-4-1988 for construction for Flood Control Embankment in Reach No. K-1(A) at length of 32.00 chainage both sides of Gomati River from Eliotgonj to Kushiara under sub-project of Gomati first phase during the year 1987-88; original tender amount was Taka 21,04,600; total work at length 0.00-32.00 chainage; during progress of the work, opposite party No.4 Change alignment of the respective design and for that, quantum of work was enhanced; from 30-4-1988 plaintiff started his work according to the aforesaid work Order being No. 834 dated 24-3-1988 and completed 9% of work which is evident by the progress report dated 26-3-1989 prepared by Sub-Divisional Engineer, Gomati Water Development Board, Comilla. After one year, vide certificate dated 2-10-1989 issued by the Executive Engineer, plaintiff came to know that the alignment and design of the aforesaid work has been again changed and re-fixed from country side to deep river side and duration of the said work extended up to 1989-90; subsequently, duration of the aforesaid work was extended up to June, 1991, which is evident from certificate dated 29-5-1990 issued by Executive Engineer, Gomati Water Development Board, Comilla. Thereafter, plaintiff completed the work i.e. the north side of Kala dumuria River from Eliotgonj to Kushiara and able to complete the entire work within 30-6-1991. Plaintiff was entitled to get Taka 98,84,098 but he was paid Taka 16,29,436 only. Plaintiff on 2-9-1992 submitted bill and requested defendant opposite party No. 1 to pay the bill. Subsequently, plaintiff petitioner on 2-9-1992 submitted representation and asked for settlement of the bill through Arbitration. Since the defendant opposite parties failed to start Arbitration proceedings, plaintiff-petitioner by issuing legal notice dated 1-4-1995 upon the opposite parties, appoint an Arbitrator under the Arbitration Act of 1940 to settle the dispute.

3. After several bouts of legal proceedings for appointment of arbitrator, lastly, Mr Justice MA Wahab (Retired) was appointed as arbitrator who gave the disputed award.

4. Opposite party No.4 contested the case by filing written objection denying the material allegations made in the plaint.

5. It is admitted fact the arbitrator did not submit the award of his own but as per direction of the Court, submitted award to Court on 20-8-2005.Defendant-opposite party objection on 9-10-2005. Here start the litigation between the parties afresh and ultimately this revision was filed. Plaintiff filed application for rejecting the written objection on the ground that it was filed beyond time and also no security accompanied with written objection. Learned Judge accepted the written objection on the ground that since the award was filed not by the arbitrator on his own motion, but as per direction of the Court, as such, it was an illegality and objection having been filed in Court, although after period of limitation, but when the arbitration itself suffers from many illegalities, the delay can be condoned. On the question of furnishing security submitted as claimed by the opposite party, the learned judge observed that he find security with the record, as such, since security has been filed, all the requirements of law having been complied with, the objection as filed can be accepted.

6. Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner referred to the Limitation Act particularly Article 158 and 175 and submits that Arbitration Act being special law, the time limit provided ,in the sections shall be construed as mandatory and section 5 of Limitation Act has no manner of application in this matter. Learned Advocate further submits that the security as filed by the opposite party is nothing but personal bond and if the plaintiff be given decree then it will take 100s of litigation's to get the decreetal money from the opposite party. Learned Advocate further submits that opposite party being a government functionaries, the security ought to be submitted in bank guarantee or pay order so that decree if passed, the decreetal amount can be realized without further litigation. Learned Advocate mainly submits that written objection having filed out of time without security is liable to be rejected outright.

7. In support of his submission, learned Advocate relied on the case of Abul Bashar vs Investment Corporation of Bangladesh, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 178; Nilkantha Sidramappa Ningas her pellant vs Kashinath Somanna Ningabo, reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 666; Sh Mahboob Alam vs SH Mumtaz Ahmed, reported in 1960 PLD (WP) Lahore 601; Adamjee Sons Limited vs Jiban Bima Corporation reported in 45 DLR 89; Masud Ahmed vs Khushnehara Begum, reported in 46 DLR 665; Sonali Bank vs Md Al-Akram (Badal), reported in 46 DLR 122; Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Progati Prakaushali, reported in 49 DLR 335; Haji Amir Bux vs Sono Khan, reported in PLD 1979 Karachi 45; Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim and Brother, reported in 1988 BLD 369; Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 7 BLT 26; Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 4 BLC 407, 18 BLT (AD) 380, 1 BLC 81 and also referred to some decisions of Indian jurisdictions. Learned Advocate prays that the rule may be made absolute.

8. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate along with Mr Mir Joynal Abedin, learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite parties, submits that, since the arbitrator did not submit the report to the Court himself as such question of limitation does not arise in this case as, as soon as the opposite party came to know of filing of the award in Court, defendant No.1 appeared and filed written objection. Learned Advocate further submits that date of Knowledge cannot be construed to be the date of notice, there is difference in between knowledge and notice and when the opposite party gathered knowledge he filed written objection and also security as such opposite party cannot be thrown out of Court on the ground of limitation. Learned Advocate further submits that the security as submitted was submitted in accordance with the provision of law and this security is a legal one and was accepted by the Court as such filing of security cannot be challenged.

9. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate, referred to the decision of Sonali Bank vs Hare Krishna Das, reported in 49 DLR 282 where their lordships observed that-

"The liability of the principle debtor is co-extensive with that of the guarantor. A creditor is at liberty to pursue either the principal debtor or the guarantor according to his sweet will for realisation of his dues or he can proceed against both of them simultaneously.

"Learned Advocate also referred to decision of Gangaram Chhaplia vs Chief Engineer (Projects), Orissa, reported in AIR 1983 (Ori) 262; Chokolinga Chittar vs Dandayuthapani Chettiar, reported in AIR 1928 (Mad) 1262; MR Sikder vs Bangladesh Water Development Board, reported in 49 DLR 113; Dhaka Leather Complex Ltd vs Sikder Construction Ltd, reported in 8 LG (AD) 75; Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK) vs MN A lam and Associates Ltd, reported in 54 DLR 161. He lastly prays that the rule should be discharged.

10. We will refer to the decisions cited by the parties if required.

11. Points formulated on the pleadings of the parties are (i) whether the written objection can be accepted when it is filed beyond the period of limitation as prescribed under section 30 of the Arbitration Act and secondly, whether the security as deposited in the Court can be said to be filed as per section 33 of the Arbitration Act.

12. Let us take up first point first for consideration. From the order sheet of the case it appears that award was filed in Court on 20-8-2005. From order dated 27-8-2005, it appears that the learned Advocate for the Water Development Board in the margin of the order put his signature by signing. Thereafter, it appears that the learned Advocate for the Water Development Board took adjournment on 3-9-2005, 6-9-2005, 21-9-2005 for filing written objection and on 9-10-2005 written objection was filed Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, learned Advocate, submits, this is actually beyond the period of limitation as prescribed under section 30 of the Arbitration. Act. Let us quote section 30 of the Act, section 30 speaks,

"Grounds for setting aside award-An award shall not be set aside except on one or more of the following grounds namely:-

a)	that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings;

b)	that an award has been made after the issue of an order by the Court superseding the arbitration or after arbitration proceedings have become invalid under section 35;

c)	 that an award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid."

13. If any party wants to set aside an award he must come within these three categories otherwise award shall remain valid.

14. Limitation filing written objection is 30 days as prescribed in Article 158 of the Limitation Act which is:-

Description of application 	Period of limitation	Time from which period begins to run.

158 Under the Arbitration Act, 1940. (X of 1940) set aside

an award or to get an award remitted for reconsideration. 	Thirty days	The date of service of the notice of filing of the award.

15. For disposal of this rule, relevant sections of Arbitration Act as well as Limitation Act are required to be referred to. We have already referred section 30 and 33 before. Now, we refer section 37 and 42. Section 37 runs as :-

"(1) All the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1908 (IX of 1908) shall apply to arbitrations as they apply to proceedings in Court. By this section, Arbitration Act given entry of Limitation Act in the proceeding of arbitration subject to the provision of Arbitration Act i.e. where the Arbitration Act itself provide for limitation then the period mentioned in the Limitation Act shall have no applicability as Arbitration Act being a special law its provisions shall have the effect over the period mentioned in the Limitation Act. When provision of Limitation Act made applicable to special law it applies specially and in applying the provision of Limitation Act Court must guard itself so that by applying the provision of Limitation Act the provision of special Act would not be given a meaning by which the special feature of special law would stand as nugatory .According to Black's Law Dictionary special law defamed as 'a law that pertains to and affects a particular case, person, place, or thing as oppose to the general public. But it is a paramount law as it continue in force with its special identity for an indefinite period i.e. a provision of law, which is no applicable generally, but which applies to a particular or specified subject or class of subject. Since provision of Arbitration Act applies to a certain class of person with its provision, is a special law, as such, when it made provision of applicability of Limitation Act, the provision of Limitation Act should be applied specifically, strictly and specially.

16. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, made his submission that since no notice was served by the Arbitrator, this opposite party filed the written objection within time of his knowledge with adequate security. From the papers produced, it appears that opposite party appears in the suit on 3-9-2005 and filed application for adjournment for filing written objection and court allowed time and fixed on 6-9-2005, when it again adjourned at the instant of opposite party and fixed on 21-9-2005, when it again adjourned at the instance of the opposite party and fixed on 9-10- 2005 when written objection was filed. From 3-9- 2005 up to 9-10-2005 is 36 days i.e. more than 30 days as provided under Article 158 of the Limitation Act. It is argued that notice of filing of the award was not served but when opposite party appeared on 3-9-2005 at that time this point may be taken, but on subsequent dates, till filing of written objection, opposite party continue with definite knowledge of filing of award as such, each day opposite party spend with definite knowledge of award in court and opposite himself allowed time to run out as opposite party filed the written objection on the 36th day.

17. Let us refer to the decisions on this subject. In the case of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha Vs NM Alam and Associates Ltd, 54 DLR 161 where a division Bench of the High Court Division held, "It appears from the record that the defendant-petitioner appeared in court on 3-2-1999 and after taking several adjournments filed the written objection on 28-3-2000 which is, in our opinion, not at all time barred. It also appears from the impugned Order dated 7-5-2000 of the Court below that the Court not only rejected the written objection on the ground that the same was barred under Article 158 of the Limitation Act, but also for want of security deposit relating to the award. The Order of the learned Court below is quoted is a clear bar against taking such a plea.

18. This decision did not find support from other decisions of this sub-continent.

19. Next, the case of Dhaka Leather Complex Ltd BCIC vs Sikder Construction Ltd, 55 DLR 578, where it is observed and held as "M Samad read Order dated 20-3-2002 and submitted that by the order the written statement filed was accepted and after such acceptance, the delay, if any, in filing the written objection must be held to be condoned.

20. We are unable to accept such submission. Receipt of the written objection by the Court cannot be termed as condo nation of the delay in making the objections. The defendant never sought for condonation of the delay by making any application. Limitation under Article 158 of the Limitation Act goes to the root of the right to set aside or get the award remitted for reconsideration. In the circumstances, there is no escape from the conclusion that the objection filed was out of time by more than a year and such objection did not deserve any consideration, and was, therefore, liable to be rejected out-right upon such ground of limitation alone. It was however, rejected on merit."

21. Next, the case Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Progati Prakanshali, 49 DLR 335, it is observed and held as it appears from the Order sheet that he appeared before the court on 15-5-1994 and ultimately filed the written objection/application under section 33 of the Arbitration Act on 20-7- 1994 which is beyond the period of limitation and there is nothing on record to dislodge the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge on that point. It is further admitted that at the time of filing of the written objection/application under section 33 of the Arbitration Act the second party appellant did not make any deposit as was required under section 33 of the Arbitration Act and that rendered the application under section 33 of the Arbitration Act a nullity in the eye of law for non-compliance of the provision to section 33 of the said Act and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly took, the view that non- compliance of the proviso to section 33 of the Arbitration Act rendered the said written objection/application under section 33 of the arbitration Act nonexistent in the eye of law.

22. In the case of Hazi Mir Bux vs Sonokhau, PLD 1979 Kar 45, it is observed and held as "Mr Zafar submitted that the trial court has no power to extend and in support of this submission he referred me to judgment of a Single Judge of the West Pakistan High Court as Thai Development Authority vs Nisar Ahmed Qureshi (PLD 1962 Lah 830). The learned Single judge held in that case section 5 of the Limitation Act was not available to extend time under Article 158 of the Limitation Act, no Judgment to the contrary has been cited. I would therefore, follow this Lahore case, and the result is that the trial Court's order permitting the respondent to file objections after 30 days as illegal. As the objections were thus time-barred, the First Appellate Court erred in setting aside the award on the basis of this time-barred application. And by so doing it committed an error affecting its jurisdiction, there- fore, the Revision should be allowed."

23. In the case of Mol Enterprises Inc )IS Bangladesh, 1999 (VII) BLT 265, it is held as 'The application challenging the validity of the Award having been filed beyond limitation, the same could not be entertained and section 5 of the Limitation Act was not at all applicable for condo nation of delay: Similarly, the Court also got no jurisdiction to decide the proceeding under section 14 of the Act. Support for this proposition of law is sought to be drawn from authorities placed before us on behalf of the appellant which are Mohamed Esoof vs Vr Subramanyam AIR, 1957 Mysore 78, Ganesh Chandra Misra vs Artatrana Misra, AIR 1965 Orissa 17, Hastimal Dalichand Bora, AIR 1965 Orissa 17 Hastimal Balichand Bora vs Hiralal Motichand Mutha, AIR 1954 Bomiya 243, Divi Dilla vs Babu Ram, AIR 1927 Lahore 273, wherein it is laid down that a Court has no jurisdiction to entertain any application for setting aside an award if it is filed after the period of limitation of 30 days as erihanced in Article 158 of the Limitation Act and the Court also got no jurisdiction to condone the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act which got no manner of application in this regard. In the unreported case Civil Appeal No. 1 of 1984. Khurshid Anwar, appellant vs Jamil Akther, respondent, arising out of Civil Revision No. 149(c) of 1982, judgment dated Tanuary 14, 1985 their Lordships of the Applet (Division considered the question whether the-inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was attracted in condoning the delay in entertaining an objection to the Award given by the Arbitrator which was filed beyond 30 days as prescribed in Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The Appellate Division answered the question in the negative. The Observations of the Appellate Division is couched in the following language;

"This clearly shows that the respondent got knowledge of the flaring of the award in Court and as such, even if limitation starts from the dated still the objection is found to have been filed beyond 30 days as prescribed in Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The provision for exercising Court's inherent power under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code is not attracted. to a case specifically governed by statute."

24. In the decision of 52 DLR (AD) 178 it is held Arbitration Act is a special law, no application for extension of period of time limit can be entertained after the period prescribed as, learned Advocate submits, Article 158 of Limitation Act prescribe 30 days limitation from the date of service of the notice or filing of the award in Court.

In 8 LG (AD) 75 in paragraph 17 it is held as,

"In the instant case the appeal was filed under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 which amongst other provides that no appeal shall lie from such decree except on the ground that it is in excess of or not otherwise in accordance with the award. In the Instant case the High Court Division observed that after an award is given under the Arbitration Act, various remedies are provided for under the Arbitration act by way of modification under section 15, correction under section 16 and set- ting aside the award on any of the grounds under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. But section 17 empowers the Court to remit the award or any of the matters referred to arbitration for reconsideration or to set aside the award. According to section 17 of the Arbitration Act after the time for making an application for setting aside an award has expired or such an application having been refused, the court shall pronounce judgment according to the award and upon such judgment a decree shall follow and that no appeal shall lie against such decree except in a case where the decree was passed in excess of the award or not in accordance with the award. In the case of Abdus Salam vs Osman Gani and another reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 346 the Appellate Division held that a decree is to 'follow upon the pronouncement of the judgment according to the award. No appeal lies from such decree except on the ground that it is in excess of or not otherwise in accordance with the award. In this case objection filed out of time was rejected on the ground of limitation under Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The Appellate Division held that the Courts decreeing the suit in accordance with the arbitration award is justified and the appeal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 before the High Court Division was not competent as the suit was decreed in accordance with the award."

25. Admittedly, the defendant-petitioner of this revisional application appeared before the Court on 3-2-1999 and after taking several adjournment filed written objection on 28-3-2000 which, according to Mr M A Samad is beyond the period of 30 days and governed by Article 158 of the Limitation Act and the learned Subordinate Judge, according to him, rightly rejected the written objection of the defendant-petitioner being barred.

26. After appearance in Court the question of serving of notice does not arise as from that date, opposite party got definite knowledge of filing of the award in Court and time was running out from that date for filing written objection and if the time runs out then filing of written objection does not arise.

27. As such we have no other option but to reject the written objection as it was filed long after the period of Limitation prescribed under Article 158.

28. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate relied on the decision of 8 LG (AD) 75 wherein it is held that:

"knowledge of the filing of the award acquired otherwise than in the way prescribed by section 14(1) should be distinguished from the service of notice under section 14(2) in the absence of the service of notice the application under section 14(2) for direction to cause the award to be filed in court should be made with- in three (3) years from the date when right to apply accrues according to the residuary provision of Article 181 of the Limitation Act."

29. Even we accept the submission of Mr Kamal-ul-Alam that the written objection so filed can be treated as an application for setting aside the award then also the written objection as filed cannot be accepted as opposite party is bound by the provision of section 33 of the Arbitration Act and is governed by the general principle that it shall be filed within a reasonable time with the security not after in ordinance delay.

30. There is another hurdle for the opposite party. From the impugned Order we find that learned Judge having found 'there is security' accepted the written objection as well as the security so filed. Here, Article 178 of the Limitation Act, governing limitation for filing security may be looked in to which runs as:-

Description of application 	Period of limitation 	Time from which period begins to run.

178-Under the Arbitration Act, 1940 (X of 1940) for the filing in court of an award. 	Ninety days 	The date of service of the notice of making of the award.

31. Provisio to section 33 of the Arbitration Act make it clear that unless there be any security filed no one can challenge the award as such, when an award is challenged, security must accompany with written objection or to be flied along with the written objection.

32. Provided that where the Court deems it just and expedient, it may set down the application for hearing on other evidence also, and it may pass such orders for discovery and particulars as it may do in a suit.

33. Provided that no application challenging the existence or validity of an award or for having its effect determined shall be entertained by the Court unless the applicant has deposited in the Court the amount which he is required to pay under the award or has furnished security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum or for the fulfillment of any other obligation by him under the award.

34. Provided that where the Court determine it just and expedient, it may set down the application for hearing on other evidence also and it may pass such order for discovery and particulars as it may do in a suit.

35. This proviso has been incorporated as per Law Reform Ordinance, 1978 and as per language of law, is mandatory and unless there be any security as per law, court has no jurisdiction to consider/entertain any objection either in the nature of application or written objection challenging the validity of the award.

<u>36. We have scrutinised the entire order sheet but we do not find any order giving entry of such bond or security. No application for filing this bond or security filed by the opposite party as such, it is clear that this bond or security placed in the record must be in connivance with some black under hand tries stealthily which thus cannot be accepted. Since there is no order entering this bond or security is record we are taken aback how the learned Judge work on it and accepted it when law does not permit him to do so. It may presume that bond was filed beyond the period prescribed proviso to section 33 of the Act, as such, there was no order entering the bond on records as such we can safely say that no bond has been filed. In the case of Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim & Brothers, 1988 BLD 369, it is held; in such circumstances, now we are to decide whether the letter of guarantee that was submitted long after the filing of the application under section 33 of the Act, is a valid deposit as contemplated under the law. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the lawyer did not know of the provision of law. The ignorance of law or mistake of law is no ground and the learned Advocate cannot lawfully plead that before this court. Further the language as quoted above clearly says that the application shall not be entertained if the deposit of money as required to pay under the award has not been made. Thus no application can be entertained if the deposit is not made in accordance with the law. We hold that the deposit under section 33 of the Act is a condition precedent for entertainment of the application and without the deposit it is to be construed as if there was no application in the eye of law. Thus it is correct to say that the guarantee that was filed look after is no deposit under the law and the application has been rightly rejected.</u>

37. 54 DLR 161 wherein on similar fact, the High Court Division observed that ,

"The deposit contemplated under the law is a condition precedent for entertainment of the application challenging the award. Deposit made during the pendency of the case cannot be treated a valid deposit as the language of the law is mandatory. "

38. Law is to obey and procedure is to follow if not justice being blind, cannot resent the litigant. Here we refer to the provision of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act. SAVINGS-(1) Nothing in this Act shall affect section 25 of the Contract Act, 1872 (IX of 1872.)

(2) Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefore by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefore in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, Appeal or application by any special or local law-

(a) The provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special law; and

(b) The remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply.

In the decision of Bangladesh Water Development Boardvs Progati Prokashani, 44 DLR 335 it is held-

"if any party misled by the Order of the Court filed objection to set aside the award, the mistake made by the party is nothing more than an irregularity which is not such as to entitle the Court to overlook his objection and to pray a decree in term of the award. It means in any form when an award is to be challenged that must necessarily with security."

39. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate for the opposite party referred to Article 181 of the Limitation Act i.e. relating to the application.

40. Let us quote Article 181 of the Limitation Act which is-

Time from

Description of 	Period of 	which period

application 	limitation 	begins to run.

181-Application 	Three 	When the

for which no period 	years 	right to

of limitation is provided		apply

else-where in 		accrues.

this Schedule or by

section 48 of the

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of

1908).

41. Since we find the written objection and security is list by the provisions of section 30 and 33 of the Act, provisions of Article 181 of the Limitation requires no consideration.

42. Now, the mode of submitting security. Petitioner vehemently challenge the security as it is filed on stamp paper of Taka 150 by an Executive Engineer who is not the authority but an employee and if the executant either removed from service either of his own volition or otherwise or died, then further complication would arise as such, security would be on such instrument which will not cause any hindrance in getting the decreed money on the event of success by the plaint it I. Mr. Kamal-ul- Alam submits that such type security on Taka 150 stamp paper is accepted by court and refer to the decision of NR Sikder vs Bangladesh Water Development Board, 49 DLR 113. where it is held, "A copy of this bond or security has been annexed with the petition. We have carefully gone through this and it appears that one Mr M Majidul Islam, Chairman, Bangladesh Water Development Board on behalf of the said Board undertook to pay to the plaint it a sum of Taka 4,95,29,000,00 (Taka four crore ninety five lac & twenty nine thousand) only as awarded by the learned Arbitrator Mr Justice Abdur Rahman Chowdhury by his award dated 27th November 1993 and also undertook to pay any other sum as may be adjudged by the Court to be payable thereunder and the Board (BWDB) guarantees the payment of such sum in the event of above proceedings ending in favour of the plaint it I by the Court. It appears from this document that on behalf of Bangladesh Water Development Board the Chair- man undertook to pay to the plaint it I any amount that may be allowed by the trial Court while disposing of Title Suit No. 284 of 1993 and this has been executed on behalf of the board and the Board guarantees payment of such sum. Through in this security of Guarantee of bond in which name this may be styled on properly has been included as required under Order XXV rule 1, Order XXXVIII rule 5 Order XLI rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the plaint it I in case of their success in the suit. Further, the Water Development Board has been constituted under President's Order No. 59 of 1972 which is a body corporate having its common seal and this Board is Governed by the provision of this order and it has also own properties. So far merenon including of the properties in the security the same cannot be brushed aside or rejected. The meaning of the word security that we have found out covers the bond that has been executed and filed on behalf of the Board."

43. Since a Division of this Court accepted such type of Bond as security, the security so filed can be accepted if it is filed as per law provided under section 33 of the Act.

44. Question also be whether such type of security can be said to be good enough. It is our considered view that when a government functionary is involved then the security shall be either in the form of bank draft or pay order or bank guarantee otherwise it will take time to get the money as if security given by the office i.e. the Executive Engineer on the event of either death or removal or retired from service then further such type of bond is required to be filed in Court.

45. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate for the opposite parties has submitted of section 128 of Contract Act and referred to the decision of Sonali Bank vs Hare Krishna Das, 49 DLR 282. Section 128 of Contract Act relating to liability of the surety which is co-extensive with the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. This law binds the surety to perform obligation immediately on the failure of Principal debtor to perform its part. In the cited decision it is held, "It is true that the onus is on the petitioner to prove his case and in the instant case on perusal of evidence and materials on record we find that the plaintiff have been able to prove their case against the defendants. Besides, there is another aspect of the case which has been lost sight of by the learned Subordinate Judge that is, that the liability of the principal debtor is co- extensive with the guarantor. A creditor can pursue either the principal debtor or the guarantor according to his sweet will to realize his dues or can proceed against both simultaneously. In the instant case the defendant No. 1 is the principal debtor and defendant Nos. 2-4 are guarantors. The defendant Nos. 1-3 did not contest the suit. The case of the plaintiff with regard to defendant Nos. 1-3 remains uncontested. Moreover, the plaintiffs have proved their case against them by cogent evidence. In view of that matter we do not find any reason why the learned Subordinate Judge did not decree the suit at least against defendant Nos. 1-3 and the judgment is not sustainable on that court also.

46. We have perused the materials and evidence on record and we have already found that the plaintiff have been able to prove their case against all the defendants who are jointly and severally liable to repay the loan. It appears to us that the Court below failed to appreciate the true import and tenor of the relevant provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and the learned Subordinate Judge is absolutely ignorant about the relevant provisions of the said Act. The learned Subordinate Judge on a total misconception of law and facts misconstrued and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and most illegally dismissed the suit although the plaintiffs have successfully proved their case. In the result the Appeal is allowed without cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 30-9-84 passed in Money Suit No. 11 of 1984 of the 1st Court of Additional subordinate Judge, Chittagong, are set aside. 'The suit is decreed with cost.

47. We do not understand how in applying section 128 of the Contract Act improve the case of Mr Kamal-ul-Alam improve as in the instant case the question of acceptance of written objection and security, liability of guarantor would arise it there be any dispute in payment of money so guaranteed.

48. Since we find written objection is not maintainable, such valued submission do not require to be considered, we leave it to Mr Kamal-ul-Alam to agitate it before the higher forum if required.

49. We find substances in the Rule.

50. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and Order No. 209 dated 17-6-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Comilla in Arbitration Suit No. 01 of1995 is hereby set aside.

51. The order of stay at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated.

Let a copy of the judgment be sent to the court below at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 17-1-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur, in Title Suit Nos. of 2007, should not be set aside.

2. The relevant fact for disposal of the Rule, in short, is that one Siddiq Ullah instituted Title Suit NO.5 of 2007 in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Lakshmipur, for a declaration that the Heba deed dated 13-5-2007 shown to have been executed by him in favour of the defendants, is fraudulent, inoperative, without consideration and for setting aside the said deed alleging that the plaintiff was the owner of the land as described in the schedule of the plaint. He was an old man of 90 years and he was suffering from various diseases. His sons Abdur Rahim, the petitioner and Abdul Mannan, the defendant No.5 had been serving in Saudi Arabia. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the daughters of the plaintiff. Their husbands are clever men. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 made attempts several times to grab the property of the plaintiff fraudulently. The plaintiff executed a power of attorney on 31-8-2004 in favour of defendant No.4. On the basis of that power of attorney the defendant No.4 transferred some portion of land to defendant No.5. In the first part of May, 2007, at the instance of the husband of the defendant No.1, she brought the plaintiff in her father-in-law's house. On 13-5-2007 the defendant No.1 and her husband gave proposal to the plaintiff to go to Chandraganj to give him treatment by a doctor. The plaintiff agreed to that proposal and went to Chandraganj. Thereafter the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and their respective husbands managed to get some signatures of the plaintiff in some papers and using the same created the impugned deed fraudulently. Hence, is the suit.

3. During pendency of the suit the sole plaintiff died on 7-9-2007. On 12-10-2009 the defendant No.4 filed an application under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for transposition of his name in the category of the plaintiff. On the other hand, on 2-6-2008 the defendant Nos. 1,2,6 and 7 filed an application for noting the order of abatement of the suit. The trial Court rejected the defendant No.4 petitioner's application and allowed the prayer for noting the abatement of the suit in respect of defendant Nos. 1, 2,6 and 7 by his order dated 17-1-2010. Challenging the said order the defendant No.4 filed this revisional application before this Court and obtained the instant Rule.

4. Mr Abul Kamal Chowdhury with Mr Md Osman Ghani, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioner.

5. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Joint District Judge has committed an error of law in rejecting the application of the petitioner for transposition of his name from the category of defendant to plaintiff in as much as the interest of the defendant No.4 and the plaintiff are identical. In this written statement the defendant No.4 himself, in fact, supported the plaint case and stated that he would not have any objection if the suit is decreed. He further submits that the learned Trial Court has committed an error in noting the order of abatement inasmuch as the heirs of deceased plaintiff are already on record. He lastly submits that, in fact, the second application for transposition was a review application to review the order passed on the basis of first application as filed by the petitioner earlier which is maintainable.

6. Mr Khair Ejaj Masud along with Mr Sarder Abul Hossain, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-6.

7. Mr Khair, the learned Advocate, submits that after expiry of 90 days as per provision of the Limitation Act, in fact, the instant suit has been abated. Without prayer for setting aside the abatement the application for transposition of the name of the defendant No.4 in the category of plaintiff was not maintainable. He submits that the second application for transposition was also not maintainable. He finally submits that if the defendant No.4 is found to be aggrieved by the impugned deed he can file a fresh suit. The learned Trial Court rightly rejected the application for transposition.

8. We have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties, perused the application and other materials on record.

9. The plaintiff Siddik Ullah was the father of defendant Nos. 1-2 and 4-6 and husband of the defendant No.3. It appears that he instituted the instant suit for declaration that the Heba deed dated 13-5-2007 in respect of the land as described in the schedule 1 of the plaint is fraudulent and the same has been obtained by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 collusively and for setting aside the said deed.

10. It appears from the written statement as filed by the defendant-petitioner, Annexure-H to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner, that he, inter alia, stated-

বাদী নালিশী দলিল লিপি লিপি করা জন্যে কথিত লেখককে বলে নাই কথিত লেখককে বলে নাই অথবা সাক্ষীগণ কেহই স্বেচ্ছায় স্বজ্ঞানে দলিল সম্পাদন কিভাবে লিপি করা হইয়াছে মাত্র। Lastly it has been stated, উল্লেখিত অবস্থাধীনে বাদীর মোকদ্দমা ডিক্রি হইতে এই বিবাদীর কোন আপত্তি নাই বা রহিল না”।

11. This is, he unconditionally supported the plaint case.

12. The contesting defendant opposite party No.1, in the written statement, stated that the impugned deed is valid one and the plaintiff knowing fully well about the contents of the deed executed the same. That is, the case of the other defendants, particularly the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 6 and 7 is hostile to the defendant petitioner. On the other hand, it appears from the plaint and written statement filed by the defendant No.4 petitioner that their pleading and interest are identical. When a defendant takes hostile stairs against the interest of the other defendants and he supports the plaint case filing written statement stating that he would not have any objection if the suit is decreed, we are of the view that he may be transposed in the category of the plaintiff.

13. The objection of Mr Khair Ejaj Masud is that earlier the defendant No.4 filed similar application which was rejected by the learned Joint District Judge but challenging the said order) the defendant No.4 did not take any step in the higher forum. Annexure- "C' to the revisional application is the certified copy of the application filed by the defendant No.4 for his transposition. The learned Joint District Judge by the order dated 30-6-2008 rejected the said application holding,

" lt appears from the record that defendant No.4 is already impleaded as party. Therefore, I do not find any reasons to transpose his name as .plaintiff from defendant on the death of the plaintiff. The heirs of the plaintiff can be substituted as plaintiff, if not already substituted and the defendant No.4 can protect his interest by contesting the suit as defendant. Therefore the petition be rejected."

14. From the said order it appears to us that the learned Joint District Judge, at the time of passing the said order, miserably failed to apply his mind in view of the fact that the sole plaintiff instituted the suit for setting aside the deed on the ground of fraud. Except the defendant No.4, the other defendants in their written statement stated that the impugned deed is genuine one and knowing full well about the contents of the same the plaintiff executed the same and only the defendant No.4 in his written statement stated that he would not have any objection if the suit is decreed i.e. he supported the plaint case. In such situation, we do not know how the suit would proceed and the interest of the defendant No.4 will be protected as all the heirs of the plaintiff are on record in the category of defendants.

15. From the second application the defendant No.4 narrating the entire facts and circumstances of the case lastly stated,

প্রকাশ থাকে যে এই দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষে ইতোপূর্বে বাদী শ্রেণীভুক্তির অপর একটি দরখাস্ত দাখিল করা হইয়াছিল। কিন্তু বিজ্ঞ আদালতের সম্মুখে সঠিক উপস্থাপন করিতে না পারায় বিজ্ঞ আদালত এই মর্মে মন্তব্য করেন যে, এই দরখাস্তকারী বিবাদী শ্রেনীতে থাকিয়াও স্বার্থ সংক্ষণ করিতে পারেন। মূলতঃ এই দরখাস্তকারীকে বাদী শ্রেণীভুক্ত করিলে অত্র মোকদ্দমার ন্যায় বিচার সুনিশ্চিত হইবে।

16. Mr Abul Kamal Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that, in fact, the second application for transposition was prayer for review of the earlier order. In Support of his submission he cited the case of Nizamuddowla vs Nurul Islam, reported in 22 DLR 277, wherein it has been held.

"--------- Subsequently application being in the nature of a prayer for reviewing earlier order, discretion exercised by trial Court in accepting the prayer need not call for interference."

17. We have already held that at the time of considering his first application the learned Trial Court totally failed to apply its judicial mind holding that the interest of the defendant No.4 will be protected if he contests the suit as defendant in the suit. It appears to us that since the learned Joint District Judge committed gross illegality in rejecting the earlier application of the petitioner, we are of the view that the second application in the nature of reviewing the earlier order was maintainable.

18. The power of transposition as provided under Order 1 rule 10, sub-rule (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure should be exercised, for the ends of Justice if is required to transfer from one side to another. On the other hand the refusal to do so prejudicially affect the applicant by driving him to another suit.

19. Mr Khair Ejaj Masud, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that the defendant No.4 can easily file a fresh suit to protect his interest but since the interest of the plaintiff and the defendants No.4 are identical, we are of the view that the interest of the defendant No.4 can be protected by transposing him from the category of defendant to the plaintiff after the death of sole plaintiff. Filing of a separate suit is not at all necessary we find support the above views in the case of Ramizuddin Miah vs Jarimunnessa, reported in 15 BLD (AD) 52. In that case it appears that the plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration and cancellation of two deeds of Heba-bil-Ewaj bringing allegation that the defendants obtained her thumb impression by practicing fraud upon her. After the death of sole plaintiff two daughters of the plaintiff who were impleaded as proforma defendants filed application for transposition of their names in the category of the plaintiffs but the learned Assistant Judge rejected the said application. On revision, the High Court Division set aside the said order of the Assistant Judge and allowed the application for transposition. On appeal their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed that the right to sue has survived after the death of the sole plaintiff and the High Court Division rightly held that respondent Nos. 1 and 2, who were already proforma defendants in the suit, are entitled to proceed with the suit as heirs of the deceased plaintiff and that they made the prayer within time.

20. Mr Kbair submits that as per provisions of Article 176 of the Limitation Act the instant suit has been abated after 90 days of the death of the sole plaintiff. While assailing the submissjon of Mr Kbair, Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that since all the heirs of the deceased plaintiff are already on record and the defendant No.4 petitioner filed application for transposition of his name in the category of the plaintiff, the question of abatement in the instant suit does not arise at all. In support of his submission Mr Chowdhury at first cited the case of People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Abul Kaiser Choudhury, reported in 37 DLR (AD) 85. In the said case it has been observed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division.

"It is well settled that when a party respondent in appeal dies and one of his legal representative is already on record in another capacity the appeal does not abate even though no application is made to bring them on record."

21. The second citation of Mr Chowdhury is the case of Mahabir Prasad vs Jage Ram and others, reported in AIR 1971 (SC) 742. In the cited case the Indian Supreme Court observed,

" When a party respondent in an appeal dies and one of his legal representatives is already on record in another capacity the appeal does not abate even through no application is made to bring them on record."

22. His next citation is the case of Abu Taher Bhuiyan vs Sree Lal Mohon Mondal , reported in 10 BLT (HCD) 127. In the said case it has been observed, "Since the heirs of Lal Mohon are already on record, no question of abatement arises at all."

23. In the case of Tara Miah vs Bhovotosh Das, reported in 2 BLC (AD) 59, it has been observed by the Appellate. Division,

"It appears that although respondent 1 filed the application without any prayer for setting aside abatement and without any application of condo nation of delay he filed the applications within reasonable time of the receipt of the record by the trial Court and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division observed that "this circumstances for non-filing of application in time may also be construed as an application under Order 22 rule 9(2) of the CPC." However, relying upon two decisions of the High Court Division, the learned Judge treated both the applications under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in the facts, and circumstances of the case. We find that the learned Single Judge has committed no illegality calling for any interference by this Division."

24. Mr Chowdhury lastly relied on the decision of the case of Abdul Kader Mandai and others vs Md Shamsur Rahman alias Md Shamsur Rahman Saha, reported in 19 BLD (AD) 183. In the above cited case their Lordships observed,

"It has been held by almost all the superior Courts of this sub-continent that the provisions of Order 22, Rule 9(2) (3) of the Code should be liberally construed. The reasons for such approach are not far to seek. In the first place, abatement of a suit precludes fresh suit on the same cause of action, although there is no trial on merit of the case. An order of abatement never goes to the merit of a dispute between the parties. If abatement is set aside the merit of the dispute can be determined. If the abatement is not set aside the applicant is deprived of the opportunity of proving his claim only on account of his culpable negligence or lack of vigilance. "

<u>25. In the instant case we have already found that the legal heirs of the sole deceased plaintiff are already on record and right to sue survives and the interests of the defendant No.4 and the plaintiff are identical and earlier within the reasonable time the defendant No.4 filed an application for transposition of his name to the category of the plaintiff from the defendant. If the legal Representative in a suit is not brought either on record under Order 22 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure then they can be brought on record under order 1 rule 10, read with section 151 of the Code because failure to bring the parties on record as legal Representative will preclude the applicant to get justice.</u>

26. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and decision as referred above our considered opinion is that in the instant case the learned Joint District Judge has committed an error of law in not allowing the application for transposition of the defendant No. 4 petitioner in the category of the plaintiff from the defendant.

27. Accordingly, we find substance in this Rule.

28. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The abatement is set aside. The order dated 17-1-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur, in Title Suit No. 5 of 2007 is hereby set aside. The application for transposition of the defendant No.4 in the category of the plaintiff is hereby allowed.

29. The Trial Court is directed to proceed with the case in accordance with law.

Communicate the order at once.

End.
