<u>14. We have heard the submissions advanced on behalf of the respective parties, perused the civil review petition, impugned judgment and order passed by this Division and other connected papers on record. At this stage we have to consider whether the points raised on behalf of the petitioner is justified in a review petition. Article 105 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh provides for review of a judgment or order passed by the Appellate Division which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"105. The Appellate Division shall have power, subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament and of any rules made by that division to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it."</u>

<u>15. From the aforesaid provrsions of Article 105 of the Constitution this Division has power to review its judgment subject to any provisions of any Act of Parliament or any Rules made by this Division. Rule making power of the Supreme Court have been provided in Article 107 whereby the Supreme Court may with the approval of the President, make Rules for regulating the practice and procedure of each Division of the Supreme Court and of any court subordinate to it. Accordingly, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988 have been framed. In Part IV of the Rules, Order XXVI envisages detailed provisions for review of judgment of the Appellate Division. Order XXVI Rule 1 provides as under:</u>

<u>"Subject to the law and the practice of the Court, the Court may, either of its own motion or on the application ofa party to a proceeding. review its judgment or order in a Civil proceeding on grounds similar to those mentioned in Order XLVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in a Criminal proceeding on the ground of an error apparent on the face of the record."</u>

<u>16. According to Rule 1 of Order XXVI the power of review may be exercised in a criminal proceeding on the ground of error apparent on the face of the record. In case of civil proceeding review may be made on the ground similar to those mentioned in Order XLVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case it appears that the writ petition has been preferred challenging the criminal case initiated against the petitioner after submission of investigation report before consideration of its acceptance by the concerned Court. In the case of Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md. Masdar Hossain reported in 21 BLD (AD) 126 = 7 BLC (AD) 92 this Division observed that-</u>

<u>"a review is by no means an appeal in disguise whereby an erroneous decision is re-heard and corrected. A review lies where an error apparent on the face of the record exists. It is not a re-hearing of the main appeal. Review is not intended to empower the Court to correct a mistaken view of law, if any, taken in the main judgment. It is only a clerical mistake or m is take apparent on the face of the record that can be corrected by the leave but it does not include the correction of any erroneous view of law taken by the Court."</u>

<u>17. While speaking on review the Appellate Division in the case of Ershad Ali Sikder (Md) vs State reported in 56 DLR (AD) 87 observed that-</u>

<u>"13. Review under Order XXVI of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988 is subject to the law and practice of the Court. The Court may of its own motion or on the application of a party to the proceeding may make review on the grounds of an error apparent on the face of the record.</u>

14. Thus a review is by no means an appeal in disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected but lies only for patent error apparent on the face of the record. Unless the impugned order shows as such merely reversing the order basing on the evidence on record would render the order in review without jurisdiction. Similarly, "an error which has to be established by a long process of reasoning on points where there may conceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be an error apparent on the face of the record."

18. The expression "the error apparent on the face of the record" has been considered by the Appellate Division in the case of Zenith Packages Limited vs Member Labour Appellate Tribunal Dhaka reported in 52 DLR (AD) 160 which is quoted as under:

"In view of the aforesaid findings the grounds upon which review of the judgment is sought have already been decided. A wrong decision on interpretation of certain provision of law or principle laid down in a decision relied upon by a court are no grounds for review 'Error apparent on the face of the record' cannot be said to be so where a lengthy argument is .advanced to explain such expressions as is argued by the Petitioner.. Therefore on the grounds urged for review of judgment by the petitioner it seems to us that we are asked to sit over our judgment by way of appeal in a circuitous way addressing a lengthy and repeated submissions which already received our due notice in the judgment sought to be reviewed".

19. Further the expression "error in the face of the record" has also been eloquently discussed by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Thungabhadra Industries Lid. vs Government of Andhra Pradesh reported in AIR 1964 SC 1372 in the following terms:

"A review is by no means an appeal in dis- guise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected, but lies only for patent error. We do not consider that this furnishes a suitable occasion for dealing with this difference exhaustively or in any great detail, but it would suffice for us to say that where without any elaborate argument one could point to the error and say here is a substantial point of law which stares one in the face, and there could reasonably be no two opinions entertained about it, a clear case of error apparent on the face of the record would be made out."

<u>20. This Division in the case of Ekushey Television Lid vs Dr. Chowdhury Mahmood Hasan reported in 55 DLR (AD) 26at page 31 paragraph 24 elaborately expressed the principle as stated below upon which a review petition lies:</u>

<u>"24. A review lies only when the alleged error in the judgment is so evident that it can be established without going into elaborate arguments and the factual matrix of the case. It may be remembered that a review in counsel's mention cannot justify review of the verdict. No doubt the court has constitutional power to review its decision but it does not undertake on the asking of the petitioners once conflicting claims have been settled by a decision of the court. The cases are reviewed strictly within the boundaries laid down by innumerable judgments of the jurisprudence, which are highly coherent in its interpretation and application."</u>

<u>21. In the said case reported in 55 DLR (AD) 26 at page 31 paragraph 25 this Division further observed as under:</u>

<u>"There are certain general principles of review whose authority is universally acknowledged that ought not to be disregarded. The fundamental is that an error is necessary to be a ground for review but it must be one, which is apparent on the face of the record, and so obvious that keeping it on the record will be legally wrong. The contention that the court has gone wrong in the application of law to the facts or the exposition of law is erroneous (unless it lays down a bad law) or that inference is drawn on appraisal and appreciation of evidence is erroneous does not constitute valid grounds for review."</u>

22. While commenting on the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioners in the review petition concerning the merits of the case this Division in the case of ETV further observed that: "They also relied on the points raised by them in the leave petitions in this respect to show that the court has committed error apparent on the face of the record. The elaborate arguments that have been advanced was done at the leave petitions but those have come to an end with the rejection of the leave petitions by the petitioners and now cannot be reopened in a review petition." [55 DLR (AD) 26 at pages 31-32 paragraph 29]

<u>23. In view of the aforesaid discussions and in the light of Article 105 read with Order XXVI of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988 and the case laws discussed above, one may conclude that in order to review a judgment there must be an error apparent on the face of the record and that this error is so apparent and manifest and clear that no court of law would permit such an error to remain on the record. We are therefore convinced to reach to the conclusion that the error must not only be apparent but must also have a material bearing on the face of the case. In the case of LI.- Col. Nawabzada Muhammad Amir Khan vs Controller of Estate Duty, Government of Pakistan. Karachi reported in PLD 1962 SC 335 = 13 DLR (SC) 105 the Supreme Court of Pakistan observed as under:</u>

<u>"To perm it a review on the ground of incorrectness would amount to granting the Court the jurisdiction to hear appeals against its own judgments or perhaps a jurisdiction to one Bench of the Court to hear appeals against other Benches; and that surely is not the scope of review jurisdiction. No mistake in a considered conclusion, whatever the extent of that mistake. can be a ground for the exercise of review jurisdiction."</u>

24. Similarly in the case of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto vs The State reported in PLD 1979 SC 741 wherein the Supreme Court of Pakistan observed as follows:

"It is also to be borne in mind that as finality attaches to the judgments delivered by this Court, which stands at the apex of the judicial hierarchy, a review proceeding is neither in the nature of a re-hearing of the whole case, nor is it an appeal against the judgment under review. It is accordingly not permissible to embark upon a reiteration of the same contentions as were advanced at the time of the hearing of the appeal, but were considered and repelled in the judgment under review, in an effort to discover errors said to be apparent on the face of the record."

25. There is no denying the fact that judgment pronounced by the Court is final and departure from that principle is justified only when circumstances of a particular case having substantial character make it necessary to do so.

<u>26. In the instant case the offence was alleged to have been committed by the accused-petitioner from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 which comes within the validity period of the Ain of 2002 which was repealed by Section 31 of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ordinance,2008 on and from 15-4-2008. Section 31 (2) of the Ordinance saved the pending cases and proceedings under the Ain of 2002 as if the said Ain had not been repealed. Similarly, this Ordinance of2008 was repealed by Section 31 (1) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2009 on and from 24-2-2009. Section 31 (2) of the Ain of 2009 saved pending cases and proceedings under the aforesaid Ordinance as if those were filed or initiated under the Ain of 2009. We have already observed in the impugned judgment that nothing has been said about those offences which were committed before the enactment of the A in of 2009 but these were either not disclosed or even if disclosed no FIR was lodged during the operation of the earlier law which was repealed subsequently. This scenario raises a question that whether those offences cease to be the same after the enactment of the repealing Act/Legislation. Answer to the said question has been elaborately enumerated under the provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.</u>

<u>27. From the above provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act it appears that Section 6 deals with the effect of repeal of any Act of Parliament by enacting a repealing Act providing certain consequences enumerated in Sub-Sections (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of the said Act. It is well established that the sole object of repealing or amending an Act is to get rid of certain provisions of obsolete matter, and replacing the same by subsequent amendment of an Act or enactment of a new legislation, thereby abrogating the earlier provisions of the law, which is the inherent power of the legislature alone. We have noticed that in the repealing Act a special saving clause has been inserted in order to deal with the effect of repeal thereby making exception to the general rule that the normal effect of repeal is to obliterate the repealed Act from the statute book as if it had never been enacted. However, Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides an exception to the rule that the normal effect of repealing Act is to obliterate the repealed Act from the statute book unless a different intention appears in the repealing Act. In this context in the impugned judgment we have considered some of the leading cases of the Apex Courts of the Subcontinent, namely, Md. Nazimuddin vs The State reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB) 70, TS Baliah vs Income-lax Officer, Madras reported in AIR 1969 SC 701, Sarju vs State reported in AIR 1964 Allahabad 6 and the case of Akhtar Hossain Khan vs State reported in 29 DLR (SC) 101, wherein it has been held that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is applicable to a simple case of repeal, as well as to a case of repeal of a statute followed by a fresh enactment on the same subject and that Section 6 would be applicable unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the section, and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new law. In the case of repeal of a statute followed by a fresh legislation on the same subject where no contrary intention appears therein repeal does not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed law.</u>

<u>28. In the case reported in AIR 1969 SC 701 the Supreme Court of India observed that the principle of Section 6 is that unless a different intention appears in the repealing Act, any legal proceeding can be instituted and continued in respect of any matter pending under the repealed Act as if that Act was in force at the time of repeal. In other words. whenever there is a repeal of a enactment the consequences laid down in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless, as the section itself says a different intention appears in the repealing statute. In the case of a simple repeal there is scarcely any room for expression of a contrary opinion. But when the repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject the Court would undoubtedly have to look to the provisions of the new Act, but only for the purpose of determining whether they indicate a different intention. The question is not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Section 6 of the General Clauses therefore will be applicable unless the "new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the section". Such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new statute and the mere absence of a saving clause is by itself not material.</u>

29. The same view has been reiterated in the case reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB) wherein the Court observed as under:

"There is hardly any controversy that the above principle of law is not applicable to both the cases where a statute has been repealed; and where the statute has been amended, or repealed and after repealing a new provision on the same subject has been re-enacted. When a repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject the court has to look to the provision of the new law to examine whether the new law indicates a different intention. The enquiry would be not to find out whether the new law expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Another test is, to find out whether the new provision manifests an intention incompatible with the provisions of the section, and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the provisions of the new law."

<u>30. In the impugned judgment and order we have already observed that firstly, the writ petition is misconceived one and not maintainable since vires of the law has not been challenged. Secondly the provision of Sub-Article (1) of Article 35 of the Constitution will not be attracted since the offence as well as it's punishment, if any would be dealt with under the Ain of 2002. Finally, on perusal of the FIR, Investigation Report and other materials on record it appears that a prima-facie case of money laundering has already been disclosed against the accused-petitioner under Section 2(ট) (আ) and (ই) and Section 13 of the Ain of 2002. The offence was alleged to have been committed by the accused-petitioner from 01-1-2003 to 3 1-5-2007 when the Ain or 2002 was in operation. Admittedly the case was instituted long after the repeal of the said Ain or 2002 and the Ordinance of 2008 and after the enactment of the A in of 2009. It has al ready been noticed that the savings clause contained in Section 31 (2) or the Ain of 2009 has no manner of application in saving the instant case which was not in existence on the date of enactment of the Ain of 2009. But in view of the above discussions Sub-Sections (b), (c), (d) and (e) of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act are applicable in the case of repeal of the Ain of 2002 followed by a fresh legislation on the same subject "unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the Section and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new law". Accordingly, the Ain of 2002 is applicable in the instant case since the new legislation does not manifest an intention contrary to the provisions of Section 6. The offence was alleged to have been committed within the validity period of the Ain of 2002 in pursuance of which the procedure in respect of lodging Complaint, holding investigation, trial and other related matters shall be initiated and continued under the ACC Act of 2004 and the Rules framed thereunder. Furthermore, we are of the view that if the actus reus of an offence is committed with necessary mens rea, it remains an offence for all time to come, even if the provisions of law creating the said very offence is repealed, without declaring the said law as ultra vires the constitution. There is no doubt that, after the repeal of the relevant provision of law, the subsequent actus reus even, if committed, ceases to be an offence. But if the offence committed during the period when the said provision of law was in force, any offence committed during the subsistence of the said law but, detected / revealed later on, even after it's repeal would still come under the mischief of the said repealed law as if the said law has not been repealed.</u>

<u>31. According to Article 35(1) of the Constitution there is a prohibition on conviction or sentence under an "ex post facto law" not trial of the offence alleged to have been committed or the procedure to be followed in the investigation, inquiry in respect of an offence alleged to have been committed. In the case reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90 this Division observed that a person accused of the commission of an offence has no fundamental right to a trial by a particular Court or by a particular procedure except insofar as any Constitutional objection by way of discrimination or violation of any other fundamental right may be involved. In other words, the prohibition under this clause does not extend to merely procedural laws and procedural law would not contravene Article 35(1) merely because retrospective effect is given to it.</u>

<u>32. In the impugned judgment passed in the Civil Petition we have observed that nowhere from the repealing Ordinance of 2008 or the subsequent Ain of 2009, one can find any indication stating the intention that repealing Act shows any different intention that such repeal has destroyed the liability or penalty incurred or investigation initiated under the repealed Ain of 2002. However, we have no hesitation in holding that the repealing Ordinance of 2008 or the Ain of 2009 has not destroyed the offence committed under the Ain of 2002. We are of the view that a prima facie case as has been dis- closed under the Ain of 2002 is found to have been saved by the provisions of Section 6(b), (c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. It is well established that a criminal offence never abates or destroyed even after the repeal of the law under which the offence is alleged to have been committed. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is applicable to a repeal of a law without any fresh enactment on the self-same subject and it is also equally applicable to a case of repeal of a law followed by fresh legislation in the same subject unless a different intention appears in the repealing law with that of the provisions of the Section and such different intention has to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the repealing law. In the impugned judgment it has been answered that inspite of repeal of the Ain of 2002 under which the offence was alleged to have been committed from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007, Section 6(b), (c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act enables the prosecution to continue with the legal proceeding or to institute any legal proceeding or to take recourse to any remedy which might have been effective before the repeal of the Act for getting remedy in respect of rights privilege, liability, penalty or punishment as the case may be. In that view of the matter in the impugned judgment we have held that the proceeding against the accused-petitioner may continue under the provisions of the Ain of 2002 as if the same Ain had not been repealed by the subsequent legislation. We have also observed that the procedure in respect of inquiry, investigation, conducting prosecution and holding of trial shall be governed under the provisions of the ACC Act, 2004 in view of the insertion of the Ain of 2002 in the schedule to the Anti- Corruption Corn mission Act, 2004. Furthermore by amending the Ain of 2002 a new Section namely. Section 3(ka) has been inserted in the Ain by Section 2 of the Ordinance No.17 of 2007. Section 3(ka) of the Ain of 2002 provides that the offences under the Ain of 2002 shall be treated as scheduled offences under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 which shall be investigated by Anti- Corruption Commission and the said offences being the scheduled offences having been included in the schedule to the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 shall be triable by the Special Judge. Accordingly, inquiry, investigation, lodging of complaint and conduct of prosecution of cases and holding of trial in respect of those cases under the Ain of 2002 shall proceed under the Provisions of ACC Act, 2004 and that in case of any conflict with the provisions of the Ain of 2002, the provision of the ACC Act, 2004 and the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 shall prevail though the Ain of 2002 was repealed by the Ordinance of 2008 keeping similar provisions as of Section 3(ka) in Section 9 of the Ordinance of 2008 and also in Section 9 of the Ain of 2009.</u>

33. We have already noticed that the consistent view of the apex courts of the sub-continent including this Court is that "review is by no means an appeal whereby an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected. A review lies where 'an error apparent on the face of the record' exists." It cannot be in any way a rehearing of the original appeal. This view has further been established in the case of Girilal Garwala vs Collector of Customs, Chittagong reported in 58 DLR (AD) 45 at page 46 paragraph 4 wherein this Division held that:

"However, the grounds taken above for review indicate that the petitioner intends rehearing of the whole Civil petition which is not permissible under Article 105 of the Constitution. The matter has been disposed of on merit and here the prayer is for rehearing of the whole matter by entering into the facts of the case which this Division cannot do in such situation."

34. The submissions advanced on behalf of the petitioner and grounds taken in the review petition were properly and extensively considered in the impugned judgment and order passed by this Court which was argued before this Court in the civil petition and in the impugned judgment there is no error apparent on the face of the record. Rather the grounds urged for review of the impugned judgment and order by the petitioner are nothing but an appeal in the guise of review against the impugned judgment and we are asked to sit over our judgment by way of appeal 'in a circuitous way addressing lengthy and repeated submissions which has already been answered by this court in the impugned judgment sought to be reviewed.

<u>35. The grounds taken for review of the impugned judgment are nothing but a device or rehearing of the whole civil petition for leave to appeal which is not permissible under Article 105 or the Constitution read with Order XXVI of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules,1988.</u>

<u>36. Moreover, It is to be noted that in the impugned judgment we have extensively answered the points raised and argued on behalf or the petitioners in the civil petition. It has been observed that the Ain of 2002 has been repealed and substituted by the Ordinance of 2008 which was also subsequently repealed and substituted by the Ain of 2009. The grounds raised and the submissions advanced on behalf of the petitioner in the review petition which went deep into the merit of the case are not permissible under Article 105 of the Constitution read with Order XXVI of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988.</u>

37. In view of the above discussions and findings we are of the view that in the instant case there is no error apparently on the face of the record to interfere in the impugned judgment and order passed by this court in the civil petition. There is no legal ground in the review petition for review of the impugned judgment and order passed by this Court in the Civil Petition which does not merit our consideration.

Accordingly, this review petition is dismissed.

End.

parties:
Aktaruzzaman alias Shahin ------ Appellant 
Vs.
Abdur Rashid Khan & others ------ Respondents
case_source:
(From the judgment and order dated 3rd November, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 614 of 1998 and Civil Revision No. 615 of 1998 with 
Civil Revision No. 524 of 1998).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Aziz J: These appeals by leave arose out of the judgment and order dated 11-3-04 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.524, 614 and 615 of 1998 making absolute the Rule obtained in Civil Revision No. 524 of 1998 and discharging the Rules obtained in Civil Revision Nos. 614 and 615 of 1998.

2. The Civil Revision No.524 of 1998 was filed by the pre-emptor and Civil Revision No.614 of 1998 and Civil Revision No.615 of 1998 were filed by the pre-emptee against the judgment and order dated 4-11-1997 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No.13 of 1987 filed by the preemptor and the Cross Objection No.31 of 1987 filed by the preemptor dismissing the both by the Court of Additional District Judge, Patuakhali and affirming the judgment and order dated 27-1-1987 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (Now joint District Judge), Patuakhali in Miscellaneous Case No.27 of 1983 allowing the same in part filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

3. These appeals involve common question of' law and identical facts and having heard analogously are being disposed of by this common judgment.

4. Facts, in short. are that the pre-emptor tiled the Miscellaneous Case. stating, inter alia, that plot No.5351 appertaining to khatian No. 1739 belonged to Rajjab Ali Khan and he was survived by two sons, one daughter and a widow, that widow of Rajjab Ali Khan gifted her share to her daughter that Ashman Ali Khan. vendor opposite-party No.2, predecessor of respondent Nos. 2- 13, being one of the sons of Rajjab Ali Khan, sold 380 sashasrangsha from plot No.5351 to the pre-emptee-opposite-party No.1 appellant by kabala dated 23-1-1983, that the pre- emptor-respondent No.2 came to know about the said transfer on 28-1- 1983 and thereupon tiled the application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act seeking preemption of the land claiming to be co-sharer by inheritance and that he is in need of the case land and the structure standing thereon, and the pre-emptee-purchaser is a stranger to the case land, etc.

5. The prayer for preemption was resisted by the pre-emptee-opposite-party No.1-appellant, stating, inter alia, that pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the case land but a contiguous land owner, that land of plot No.5351 was partitioned by a registered deed of partition amongst all the co-sharers before the impugned kabala dated 23-1-1983 and there has been separation of the holding and the parties are in enjoyment separately of their respective share by constructing different structures having separate boundaries, that father of the pre-emptee-purchaser had been in possession of the demised land with structures as a bharatia under the vendor, and he (pre-emptee) made improvements spending Taka 20,457, that application under section 24 of the NAT Act is not maintainable since the land was separated by partition, that there was no change of possession and the pre-emptee is in enjoyment of the property as per earlier possession, etc.

6. Trial Court, on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, allowed the prayer for preemption in part i.e. to the extent of 1/3 of the land transferred. As against the judgment and order of the trial Court, pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.13 of 1987 and the pre-emptee filed cross objection No.31 of 1987. the lower appellate Court dismissed the appeal as well as the cross objection.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the lower appellate Court, the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee moved the High Court Division by filing aforesaid civil revisions and obtained Rules. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute obtained in Civil Revision No.524 of 1998 by the preemptor and discharged the Rules obtained in Civil Revision Nos.614 and 615 of 1998 obtained by the pre-emptee-appellant vide impugned judgment and order dated 3-11-2004.

8. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment holding that mere existence of the partition deed ipso facto does not cease co-sharership without splitting up of the Jama within the meaning of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

9. Against the judgment and order of the high Court Division, the pre-emptee-petitioner filed civil petitions for leave to Appeal Nos.139-141 of 2005 before this Division and obtained leave to appeal ill all the petition on 3-7-2006 to consider the following grounds:

"The High Court Division failed to consider that once the properties among co-sharers arc partitioned by a registered partition deed showing possession in specific share, co-sharership under section 24 of the NAT Act ceases and separation of tenancy is not necessary. The High Court Division failed to consider Exhibit- A (partition deed), Exhibit-B (impugned kabala) and Exhibit-C (agreement for sale) wherein specific possession is shown with boundaries and also failed to reverse the finding of the appellate Court about partition. The High Court Division failed to appreciate that co-sharer ship in a non-agricultural land ceases on partition and did not consider the concurrent finding that pill No.5351 was partitioned amongst the co-sharers and did not also consider that in the partition deed the pre-emptor is a party to the document and none of the co-sharers has challenged the document incorporating the partition and thus the High Court Division committed error or law occasioning failure of justice."

Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Counsel, appearing for the appellant, argued that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that once the land is partitioned amicably and voluntarily by a registered partition deed amongst co-sharers or by a final decree passed in a partition suit showing specific share and possession to all the co-sharers, co-sharer ship in the land ceases for the purpose of preemption under section 24 of NAT Act and it does not require separation of holding or splitting up of the Jama. he argued that the learned Single Judge has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in reassessing the evidence disturbing concurrent holding of fact of the Courts below about partition between the co-sharers and also failed to consider Exhibit-A partition deed, Exhibit-B impugned kabala and exhibit-C agreement for sale and did not reverse the concurrent finding of the Courts below that plot No.5351 was partitioned amongst the co- sharers and the preemptor was a party to the partition deed and none of the co-sharers challenged the same (Exhibit-A) which incorporates both the agreement and the kabala deed showing separate possession with boundary walls consequent upon partition and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. Mr Islam also argued that the High Court Division misunderstood and misconstrued the decision of the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and in the case of Md Muzaffar Khan vs Md Yusuf Khan reported in 11 DLR (SC) 78.

10. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for appellant relied upon the case-laws in the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and Shafiuddin vs Md Abdul Karim reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41.

11. On the other hand, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan. the learned Senior Counsel appearing in support of the impugned judgment for the pre-emptor-respondent No.1, Vehemently opposed the appeals controverting the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the appellant, contending that mere existence of a registered deed of partition does not extinguish the status of co-sharer ship unless and until the Jama of the land is splited up and separated and that the partition deed in made only for the convenience of possession of the co-sharers in the case land and as such the judgment and order of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. He continues that right of preemption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is not lost with the partition and co-sharer ship in the land transferred does not cease due to registered deed of partition amongst the co-sharers when there is no splitting up of the holding and the Jama is not separated by opening a new khatian pursuant to registered deed of partition and therefore, the interpretation given by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on the right of pre-emptor under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is correct and is in consonance with law. he also argues that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act a co-sharer loses his co-sharer ship in the tenancy or holding by separation of Jama through mutation proceeding and the principle is equally applicable in both the cases of Agricultural and Non-Agricultural land and the High Court Division has thus rightly passed the impugned judgment and order. He contends that a final decree passed in a partition suit for amicable partition separates and divides the land for the purpose of possession only, but does not ipso facto terminate co-sharer ship in such land till subdivision of holding and distribution of rents takes place in accordance with law, and as such, the respondent still continues to remain as a co-sharer in the case land and is entitled to exercise his right or preemption which has rightly been held by the High Court Division correctly considering the Exhibits-A, Band C.

Mr Bhuiyan referred the cases of Md Muzaffar Khan vs Md Yusuf Khan reported in 11 DLR (SC) 78. the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury vs Rezia Begum reported in 16 DLR 77. Rokeya Begum vs Md Nurul Absar reported in 1 ADC 247.

13. We have heard the learned Counsels of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and those of the lower Courts and other materials available on record.

14. There is no dispute that the case land sought to be preempted by the preemptor-respondent was amicably partitioned among the co-sharers by the registered partition deed to which among other co-sharers both the preemptor and the vendor- opposite-party No.2 were parties and the vendor- opposite-party No.2 sold it to the pre-emptee-appellant by registered kabala after partition.

15.  The moot question in the case as argued by the learned Counsels of both the parties is whether either a registered partition deed original decree in a partition suit puts an end to the co-sharer ship in the land so partitioned or whether the co-sharer ship continuous till the same is separated and splited up by separation of Jarna through mutation.

16.  Substance of the submissions of Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-appellant is that a registered partition deed or a final decree passed in a partition suit is a complete transaction of transfer of ownership and possession of the respective shares/shaham of the land partitioned among the co-sharers and it finally determines and cease co-sharer ship and is binding on the co-sharers, who are parties to the same and separation of Jama is not necessary to cease their co- sharer ship in the land so partitioned and divided among the co-sharers. On the contrary, according to Mr Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the pre-emptor-respondent, a registered deed of partition is a document of peaceful possession in the respective land of the co-sharers and not of change of owner- ship of the land and an end to the still us of co-sharer ship unless and until Jama of the case land is spited up and separated by mutation and it does not extinguish the right of preemption of the pre-emptor under section 24 of the NAT Act.

17. The registered partition deed vide Annexure-A shows that the case land was amicably partitioned among the co-sharers and they were put to possession of the respective land allotted to them. Both the preemptor and vendor are parties to the said deed. Consequent upon such partition, the vendor vide Exhibit-B sold the case land to the appellant pursuant to an agreement vide Annexure-C. None of the co-sharers challenged the said registered deed to partition. In the said deed vide Annexure-A, the kabala vide Exhibit-B and the agreement vide Exhibit-C have been incorporated.

<u>18. On perusal of the decisions cited by Mr Islam, we find substance in his submissions that the registered deed of partition is a complete transaction of transfer of ownership and possession among the co-sharers, which put an end to co-sharer ship. The decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 was a splited judgment and the majority  view lend support to Mr Islam. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relying on the minority view of the judgment made the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No.524 of 1998 and discharged the Rules issued in Civil Revision Nos.614 and 615 of 1998 on an erroneous finding that a partition deed does not extinguish and cease co-sharer ship without splitting up of the Jama within the meaning of section 24 of Non Agricultural and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>19. In the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD, 41, their Lordships were of the view that passing of final decree in partition suit implies that all the directions in respect of distributing and separating the Saham of the parties contained in the preliminary decree was complied with the nothing remain, to be executed after the passing of the final decree and therefore it is wrong to imply that the final decree has to be executed for the separation of till Saham land. Their Lordships were also of the view that after passing of the final decree in partition suit it is effective between the admitted co-sharers and for the purpose of a pre-emption proceeding were the transfer is made by a co-sharer to a stranger in that view of the matter, the passing of the till:" decree in a partition suit finally determines the right of the co-sharers in the land. Hence, the application for the pre-emptor-respondent on the basis of co-sharership is not maintainable. Partition suit ending in a final decree or an amicable partition of the property among the admitted co-sharer through a registered deed of partition put an absolute end to co-sharer ship for all practical purpose irrespective of separation or splitting of land or Jama through mutation proceeding.</u>

20. The decisions cited by Mr Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the respondent does not apply in the instant case.

21. In consideration of the decisions reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and 52 DLR (AD) 41 as above we are of the opinion that a final decree in a partition suit for a registered deed of partition put an end to co-sharer ship extinguishing his right of pre-emption.

22. In that view of the matter, we find merit in the appeals and the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside being not sustainable in law.

The appeals are accordingly allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 11-3-2004 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division is hereby set aside.

End.

parties:
ABC Attire Ltd  ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh and others   ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: In the rule nisi dated 11-11-2010, the petitioner sought for a direction upon respondent Nos. 5-9 to consider/dispose of the petitioner's application dated 6-10-2010 and 18-10-2010 in the light of guidelines as contained in Memo No. প্রধান কার্যালয় পরিপত্র নং- ৪১ আই টি এফ ডি/রপ্তানী/গার্মেন্টস/১০৭৮ dated 22- 9-2010 (Annexure-F to the Writ Petition).

2. In the supplementary rule nisi dated 15-12-2010, the petitioner sought for a declaration that the execution and registration of Saf-Kabala deed NO.9193/2010 dated 2810-2010 (Annexure-K-I to the Writ Petition) is in violation of Memo No . প্রধান কার্যালয় পরিপত্র নং- ৪১ আই টি এফ ডি/রপ্তানী/গার্মেন্টস/১০৭৮ dated 22-9-2010 (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition) and thus unlawful and is of no legal effect.

3. Material facts necessary for disposal of the case are as follows:- The petitioner, ABC Attire Limited (hereinafter stated as the Company) is a private limited garments manufacturing company. In course of its business the Company obtained some loan for running factory from respondent No.9 i.e. Sonali Bank Limited, Dilkusha Corporate Branch, Dilkusha, Dhaka (in short, the Bank) but the Company could not repay the loan to the Bank. A good number of garment industries of the country had become sick and required to be restored. To rehabilitate such industries, the Ministry of Commerce formed a committee entitled "Committee on Restarting of Sick Garments Industries" (the Committee, in brief) through Gazette Notification dated 28-2-2005 published on 7-3-2005 in the Gazette (the Notification). The Company was listed as a sick garments industry by respondent No. 2 i.e. Secretary of Ministry of Commerce. The Committee submitted a report with certain recommendations to rehabilitate the sick garments industries for restarting (চালুকরন). The Committee registered 270 sick garments industries along with the Company for rehabilitation. Meanwhile, the Bank on 21-3-2001 instituted Title Suit No.69 of 2001 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka (hereinafter stated as the Adalat) for recovery of loan amounting to Tk. 4,59,97,042 as stood on 31-1-2000 and interest therein till realization impleading the Company and others as defendants of the suit. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on 12-9-2001 and final decree was drawn up on 13.4.2003. The judgment-debtors having failed to pay the decretal dues, the Bank filed Title Execution Case No. 160 of 2003 and the execution case was disposed of by issuing a certificate under section 33(5) of the Ain for khas possession and right to sell the mortgaged property in favour of the Bank on 24- 2-2008. Thereafter the Bank filed Title Execution Case No. 132 of 2009 for recovery of balance detrital dues and the said execution case is pending before the Adalat. Subsequently, International Commerce Finance Division of Sonali Bank (respondent No.8) issued a circular being Memo No. প্রধান কার্যালয় পরিপত্র নং- ৪১ আই টি এফ ডি/রপ্তানী/গার্মেন্টস/১০৭৮ 22-9-2010 with some guidelines (hereinafter mentioned as the Guidelines) relating to loan of 85 garments industries as per direction of the Government vide Memo No. অম/ব্যাআ প্রবি/ঋঃরুঃশি অধিশাখা/রূগ্ন শিপ্ল ১/২০১০/২৮৭ dated 17 August, 2010 issued by the Ministry of Finance. Earlier the Bank issued a letter to the Company about availing the benefit of the Guidelines and the petitioner expressed its willingness to reschedule the loan as per the guidelines by letters dated 6-10-2010 and 18-10-2010. The Bank without complying with the provision of the Guidelines accepted the auction of the mortgaged property at the valuation of Tk.70,00,000/- and it was approved by the Board of Directors of the Bank. The Bank communicated it to respondent No.11 through Memo dated 26-10- 2010. The auction sale of the mortgaged property of the Company is in clear violation of the Guidelines dated 29-9-2010. Hence, this Writ petition.

4. The petitioner subsequently filed an application for issuance of supplementary rule stating that after issuance of the rule with an order of stay, the petitioner communicated the same to the Bank and came to know that the mortgaged property as mentioned in the schedule of the application i.e. District-Dhaka. Police Station-'Mohammadpur, Mouza-Brab, JL No.238, Khatian No.CS232, SA- 173.Dag No. CS and SA 701, Mutation Khatian No. 170/9, of land 25 decimals  (hereinafter referred to as the mortgaged property/the property) has already been sold by registered saf kabala deed NO.9193/2010 dated 28-10-2010 to respondent No. 11 in auction. The said sale deed has been executed without giving any information to the petitioner and no offer was made to the petitioner for purchasing the same at the auction price and, as such, the execution and registration of the Saf kabala deed No.9193/2010 dated 28-10-2010 for the property is liable to be declared to be without lawful authority.

5. Respondent No.9, the Bank contested the case by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that the rule was issued upon the respondents on 11-11-2010 for disposal of petitioner's applications dated 6-10-2010 in compliance with the Guidelines. Subsequently, on the prayer of the petitioner, supplementary rule was issued on 15-12- 2010 for declaration that the execution and registration of the safkabala deed No.9193/2010 dated 28- 10-2010 with the Sub-registrar, Mohammadpur, Dhaka is in violation of Memo No . প্রধান কার্যালয় পরিপত্র নং- ৪১ আই টি এফ ডি/রপ্তানী/গার্মেন্টস/১০৭৮ dated 22-9-2010 and so, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Prior to issuance of original rule nisi to respondent Nos.5-9, the respondents transferred the property to respondent No. 11 in auction vide saf-kabala deed No.9193/2010 dated 28-10-2010. Initially, the auction purchaser respondent No. 11 was not made a party to this Writ Petition and he was subsequently made respondent No. 11 in this Writ Petition. Presently, respondent No. 11 the auction purchaser has been in possession of the party through his auction purchase. Moreover, the Guidelines and the Notification with recommendations cannot be enforced through Court for not having legal force of law. Long before issuance of the Guidelines the Bank instituted Title Suit No.11 of 2010 against the petitioner and others and the suit was decreed ex-parte on 12-9-2001, final decree was drawn up on 13.4.2003 but the Company (the petitioner) did not take any step whatsoever to pay the decretal dues although the petitioner had full knowledge about the aforesaid facts. Due to non-payment of the decretal dues, the Bank .filed Title Execution Case No. 160 of 2003 and in the execution case attempts were taken under sections 33(1) and 33(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the Ain, in short) for auction sale of the mortgaged property but without success. So, on an application filed by the Bank a certificate was issued on 29.3.2008 under section 33(5) of the Ain in favour of the Bank for possession and enjoyment of the property as well as to sell the property. Subsequently, Bank published auction sale notices in three daily newspapers but without result. Thereafter, the Bank again published notice for auction sale of the mortgaged property in the daily Bhorer Kagoj on 14-5-2010. Out of 4 bidders, respondent No.11 became the highest bidder offering Tk. 70 lakh for the property (mortgaged property). Respondent No. 11 had deposited 10% of the bid amount. The Bank by its letter No . SBL/Dil/Boi Ba Bi/3S17 dated 27-10-2010 informed respondent No. 11 that the bid submitted by him being the highest bid was placed in the lS9 Board Meeting of the Bank held on 19-10-2010 and the Board approved the transfer of the mortgaged property to respondent No.11 for the bid amount of Tk. 70,00,000. The Bank in the said letter requested respondent No. 11 to take necessary steps in this regard. Respondent No. 11 thereafter, paid balance auction amount after deducting Tk. 7 lakh which was deposited by respondent No. 11 at the time of bidding as earnest money. The Bank on receipt of the auction money from respondent No.11, transferred the mortgaged property to respondent No. 11 by the impugned saf- kabala deed No. 9193/2010 dated 28-10-2010. The petitioner was fully aware about the decree of the suit against it, filing of execution case to recover the decretal dues, attempts to sell the property in auction under section 33(1) and 33(4) of the Ain, issuance of certificate under section 33(5) of the Ain and auction sale of the mortgaged property to respondent No. 11 with delivery of possession. But the petitioner by suppressing all these facts has filed the Writ Petition and obtained the rule as well as the supplementary rule and, as such, those are liable to be discharged with costs.

6. Respondent No. 11 i.e. the auction purchaser also contested the rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that the Bank in order to realise the outstanding decretal dues published re-auction notice. for sale of the mortgaged property in the Daily Bhorer Kagoj on 14-5-2010. Respondent No. 11 participated in the auction for purchasing the property offering Tk.70 lakh. He also deposited 10% of the bid amount as per direction of the reaction notice through pay order enclosed with his letter dated 31-5-2010. Thereafter, the Bank vide its letter No. SBI/Dil/Boi BaBi/3517 dated 27-10- 2010 informed respondent No.11 that the bid submitted by respondent No.11 being the highest bid was placed in the 159th Board Meeting of the Bank held on 19-10-2010. The Board of Directors of the Bank considering the fact that the offer of Tk.70 lakh made by respondent No. 11 for purchasing the mortgaged property is the highest offer, approved the transfer of the mortgaged property to respondent No.11. The Bank in the said letter also requested respondent No. 11 to take necessary steps in this regard. Respondent No. 11 then deposited the remaining amount through pay order after deducting the earnest money of Tk. 7 lakh. Thereafter, respondent No.11 requested the Bank to transfer the mortgaged property to respondent No. 11 by executing and registering, a sale deed. The Bank by registered sale deed No. 9193 dated 28-10-2010 sold the mortgaged property to respondent No. 11. Thereafter, the officials of the Bank on 31-10-2010 in presence of local residents handed over the possession of the property to respondent No. 11. Since then respondent No. 11 had/has been in possession of the property free from all legal encumbrances. Respondent No.11 by his letter dated 22-12-2010 informed the Bank about his possession and requested the Bank to hand over all the necessary documents relating to the property to respondent No-11. Respondent No. 11 participated the auction complying with the terms and conditions of the auction notice and purchased the property from the Bank through registered sale deed lawfully. The Bank handed over the possession of the property to respondent No. 11 on 31-10-2010 and since then he has been enjoying peaceful possession of the property. The petitioner by suppressing all the facts, falsely informing the Court that it is in possession of the property obtained the rule and supplementary rule. Thus the rule as well as the supplementary rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

7. Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner along with Mr. Syed Khalequzzaman, has taken us through the Notification dated 28-2-2005, the Guideline dated 22-9- 2010 and advanced before us the following arguments:-

(i) the petitioner obtained loan from the Bank but failed to pay the loan and considering the fact that many garments industries were closed down, the Government decided to take steps for rehabilitation of those industries;

(ii) accordingly, Ministry of Commerce issued a Notification dated 28-2-2005 forming the Committee and the Committee submitted a report with some recommendations about sick garments industries;

(iii) the Committee identified and registered 270 garments industries along with the petitioner as sick industries for rehabilitation;

(iii) meanwhile, the Bank filed Title Suit No. 69 of 2001 before the Adalat for recovery of loan and obtained decree against the petitioner and others. Eventually, the Bank obtained a certificate from the Adalat for possession, enjoyment and right to sell of the mortgaged property of the petitioner;

(iv) subsequently, the Bank filed another Executions Case against the petitioner and others which is still pending;

(v) the respondent No. 8 issued the Guidelines and as per direction of the Government dated 17-8-2010. Thereafter, the Bank informed about the Guidelines to the petitioner and the petitioner also wrote letters dated 6-1-2010 and 18-10-2010 for reschedule of loan as per the Guidelines but without any result;

(vi) the Bank without following the Guidelines has sold the mortgaged property to respondent No. 11 and, as such, the saf-kabala deed No. 9131/2010 dated 28-10-2010 is liable to be declared to be without lawful authority and the Bank should be directed to consider and dispose of the application dated 11-10-2010 and 18-10-2010 filed by the petitioner in the light of paragraph "(ট)" of the Guidelines."

8. In reply, Ms. Hosneara Begum, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.9, the Bank for-

warded before us seven-fold arguments which are as under:-

(i) it is evident from the Writ Petition and the supplementary affidavit that the petitioner obtained the rule along with an order of stay on 11-1-2010 but prior to issuance of the original rule with an order of stay, the property has been sold to respondent No. 11 by executing and registering the impugned deed of sale dated 28-9-2010;

(ii) the petitioner was fully aware about filing of the suit, its decree, filing of execution case and publication of notices for auction sale of the mortgaged property in various newspapers in compliance with the provisions of section 33(1) and 33(4) of the A in in the execution case and finally issuance of certificate in favour of the Bank under section 33(5) of the Ain;

(iii) the Guidelines was issued by the Bank on 22-9-2010 but certificate has been issued in favour of the Bank on 24-2-2008 which is more than one 1 and 1/2 years prior to the issuance of the Guidelines by the Bank;

(iv) meanwhile, several attempts were taken by the Bank to sell the mortgaged property in auction by virtue of certificate lawfully issued by the Adalat and eventually, the auction notice was published in daily Bhorer Kagoj dated 14-5-2010 and respondent No.11 and three others participated the auction. Respondent No. 11 became the highest bidder offering Tk. 70,00,00 to purchase the mortgaged property. So , his offer was placed before the Board of Directors of the Bank and with its approval the property was lawfully sold to respondent No. 11 through registered deed dated 28-10-2011 and possession was delivered to him on 31-10-2010;

(v) the petitioner neither opposed the auction sale of the property at any stage nor took any attempt to pay the decretal dues;

(vi) the Notification is purely some recommendations without creating any legal right to anyone and it has been decided in a good number of cases that the recommendations is not binding upon the Bank and it cannot be enforced through Court.

(vii) similarly, the Guidelines was issued after issuance of the certificate under section 33(5)of the Ain in favour of the Bank and the Guideline has also no legal binding force, and, as such, the rule as well as the supplementary rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

9. In support of her submissions, Ms. Hosneara Begum has relied upon decision in the cases of Talekhal Progressive Fisherman Co-operative Society Ltd vs Bangladesh reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 103 and Chandpur Fisherman Co-operative Society vs Abdul Awal Bhuiyan, reported in 1 BCR, 8.

10. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing along with Mr. Margub Kabir on behalf of respondent No.11 the auction purchaser contends that in response to the auction notice dated 14-5- 2011 published by the Bank in the daily Bhorer Kagoj respondent No.11 submitted tender to purchase the property at Tk.70,00,000 by depositing 10% auction money. He next contends that being the highest bidder, his offer was accepted by the Board of Directors of the Bank and he was asked by the Bank to take necessary steps for transfer of the property in his favour. He also contends that he deposited the balance amount of auction money and thereafter, the property was transferred to him by saf- kabala deed NO.9193/2010 dated 28-11-2010 in accordance with law and the possession of the property was delivered to him on 31-11-2010. He also contends that the petitioner by suppressing all these facts has obtained the rule and he did not take any step to oppose auction sale. He further contends that by suppressing the fact of the execution and the registration of the deed of sale in favour of the auction purchaser and delivery of possession of the property to him on 31-10-2010 the petitioner obtained the rule. He lastly contends that once an auction sale is completed no relief is available against such auction sale but the mortgagee may proceed against the mortgagor bank for compensation, if it is proved that there was illegality in the auction sale and, as such, the rule as well as the supplementary rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

11. In support of his contentions, Mr. Huq, has referred to the decision in the case of Elite Lamps Ltd. vs Secretary, Ministry of Industries, reported in 61 DLR 641.

12. We have examined the Writ Petition, the affidavits-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 9 and 11 respectively and the connected materials on record. We have also studied the Notification (Annexure-A to the Writ Petition) and the Bank's Guidelines dated 22-9-2010 (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition) to the best of our ability.

13. The facts of the case that the ABC Attire Limited-the petitioner obtained loan from the Bank and failed to repay the loan , the Bank then filed Title Suit No.69 of 2001 for recovery of the huge amount of loan amounting to Tk. 4,59,99,042 as stood on 31-12-2000 against the petitioner and others, ex-parte judgment and decree in the suit for the aforesaid amount in favour of the Bank with interest till realization, non-payment of the said decretal dues by the Judgment-debtor-petitioner and others, filing of Title Execution Case No.160 of 2003, attempts to auction sale of the mortgage property by the Bank in compliance with the provisions of sections 33(1) and 33(4) of the Ain in the execution case without success, issuance of certificate under section 33(5) of the Ain in favour of the Bank are all admitted.

14. From the materials on record it transpires that certificate under section 33(5)) of the Ain was issued by the learned Judge of the Adalat in favour of the Bank on 24-2-2008 in Artha Jari Case No. 160 of 2003 (Annexure-D-(2) to the Writ Petition) and the Circular No.41 continently the Guidelines (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition) was issued on 22- 9-2010. Thus it is evident that the Guidelines was issued by Sonali Bank long after issuance of the certificate in favour of the Bank.

15. Section 33 (5) of the Ain reads as under:-

৩৩। নিলাম বিক্রয়।

(১)	.............................................

(২)

(৩) ...............................................

(৪) ................................................

(৫) কোন সম্পত্তি উপ-ধারা (১),(২),(৩) ও (৪) এর বিধান অনুসারে বিক্রয় করা সমম্ভব না হইলে, উক্ত সম্পত্তি, ডিক্রীকৃত দাবী পরিপূর্ণভাবে পরিশোধিত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত দখল ও ভোগের অধিকারসহ ডিক্রীদারের অনুকূলে ন্যস্ত করা হইবে, এবং ডিক্রীদার উপ-ধারা  (১),(২),(৩) ও (৪) এর বিধান অনুসারে উক্ত সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় করিয়া অপরিশোধিত ডিক্রীর দাবী আদায় করিতে পারিবে, এবং আদালত ঐ মর্মে একটি সাটিফিকেট ইস্যূ করিবে।

.................................................................

16. Therefore, it is evident that in view of the above clear provision of the Ain, the Bank was empowered to possess/enjoy and sell the mortgaged property by virtue of the certificate issued by the Adalat. Therefore, after issuance of certificate the Bank was/is at liberty to sell the mortgage property in auction for which certificate was issued in its favour. The Guidelines was issued on 27 September, 2010 long after the issuance of the certificate by the Court of competent jurisdiction i.e. the Adalat, so, the Bank was not bound to consider the applications filed by the petitioner in the light of the Guidelines dated 22 September, 2010. Moreover, as the certificate has been issued under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, and the Ain was enacted by the Parliament, the provisions of the Ain shall prevail over the Notification issued by the Government or the Circular with the Guidelines issued by the Bank.

17. Furthermore, on scrutiny of the Notification dated 7.3.2005 (Annexure - A to the Writ Petition) it transpires that it merely contains some recommendations and no legal right has been created to any one by this recommendations.

18. This view of ours is also supported by the case reported in 61 DLR 641, wherein this Division in considering the cases of Professor Abdur Rahim Khan vs Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries, reported in 7 BLT (AD) 313, Greenways Tannery vs Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka (Writ Petition No. 6270 of 2003), Mirzaboo Steels Ltd vs Bangladesh reported in 59 DLR 141, Edruk Ltd vs Secretary, Ministry of Industries (Writ Petition No. 7300 of 2003) held as under :-

"From the discussions made in the forgoing paragraphs and the decisions referred to as above, it is clear that by now it is a well-established principle of law that policy guideline, recommendations, etc. not being law cannot be enforced through Court.

Since, the recommendations cannot be legally enforced by the Court and it is not legally binding upon the Bank, no direction can be given for withdrawing a suit for non-implementation of those recommendations. The Bank will proceed with the suit in accordance with law. "

<u>19. The certificate has been issued by the Adalat under section 33(5) of the Ain, and, as such, there is no scope to follow the provision of paragraph (ট) of the Guidelines by the Bank so far as it relates to sell of the mortgage property but the provisions of section 33(5) of the Ain is to be followed. In the instant case the Bank sold the mortgaged property in compliance with the provision of section 33(5) of the Ain. Moreover, the Circular containing the Guidelines (the Guidelines) has also no legal binding force and it is also subject to certain terms and conditions.</u>

20. This view of ours is also supported by the decision reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 103 wherein it has been decided as follows :- "We however, find that the rules have only given the guideline as to how the settlement is to be made but how these rules can be invoked for claiming a legal right inhering in the petitioner which has no statutory force is not understood. The argument of the learned Counsel that the petitioner's right was to apply for settlement and it is the statutory duty of the respondents to deal with this matter in accordance with rule and memorandums is not tenable. It is well settle that in order to entitle a person to ask for the performance of any public duty by mandamus it is necessary to show that he has a legal right for claiming such performance apart from the fact that he is interested in the performance of such duty."

21. Therefore, there is also no scope to give any direction upon the Bank for implementation of the Circular i.e. the Guidelines which is subject to certain terms and conditions.

22. Further, from the Writ Petition, it appears that the petitioner did not deny the fact about obtaining the loan, failing to repay the loan, etc. The petitioner did not claim that he has paid the decretal dues in favour of the Bank after the decree or during the pendency of the execution case. Therefore, the certificate was issued by the learned Judge of the Adalat lawfully and the property has been sold in favour of respondent No. 11 by the Bank in accordance with law. The sale has become absolute after the transfer of the property in favour of the auction-purchaser by execution and registration of saf-kabala deed dated 28-10-2010 which is followed by delivery of possession of the property.

23. In view of the discussions made hereinbefore, we find that there is no scope to direct the Bank to dispose of the applications filed by the petitioner in compliance with the Guidelines dated 22-9-2010 and there is also no scope for declaration that the saf-kabala deed NO.9193/2010 dated 28-10-2010 to be unlawful.

24. In view of the discussions made above, we find no merit in the submissions of Mr. Arif, the learned Advocate for the petitioner rather, we find and force in the submissions of Ms. Hoseneara Begum and Mr. Huq the learned Advocates for the respondent Nos. 9 and 11.

<u>25. Before parting with the Judgment, we would like to note that on examination of the record, it transpires that the suit was decreed for an amount of Tk. 4,59,97,000 as stood on 31-12-2000 and with interest till realization along with cost of the suit. Admittedly, out of the said decretal amount Tk.70 lakh was recovered by the Bank by auction sale of the mortgaged property and huge decretal dues is still recoverable by the Bank for which admittedly another execution case is pending. Therefore, the Bank and the Judgment-debtors are at liberty settle the matter, excluding the auction sold property, if they are willing to do so in terms of the Guidelines for the balance decretal amount due to the Bank from the judgment-debtor-petitioner and others as amicable settlement is permissible at any stage during the execution case be the parties under the Ain.</u>

26. In view of the above, the rule and the supplementary rule fails.

27. In the result, the rule as well as the supplementary rule is discharged without any order as to costs along with the observations made in the body of the judgment.

The order of stay granted earlier by the Court stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment to respondent No. 10 at once.

End.

Rafique-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate with Aminul Hoque and Ms. Dilara Khandaker, Advocates ------ For Appellants 
AKM Nazrul Islam Rokonuddin Mahmood. Abdur Razzaque Senior Advocates with Ehsan A. Siddiq, SA Nabi and Mir Ahmed Bin Quasem, Advocates ------ For the Respondents.
