Social Islamic Bank Limited and others ------ Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Major (Retd) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque  ------ Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Rezaul Hasan J: This Appeal under Order XLIII Rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). has been preferred by the Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL) and five others being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned Order No. 08 dated 26-10-2011 passed by the 5th Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 422 of 2011 allowing the application filed by the plaintiff- respondent under Order XXXIX, Rule 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and passing a temporary order of injunction in mandatory form directing the defendant Nos. 1-6 to serve the notice of the Board Meeting upon the plaintiff and to allow the plaintiff to act as a Director of the defendant No.1 Bank.

2. This appeal was admitted on 14-11-2011 and after hearing an application for stay, filed by the appellant, this Court has passed an order staying the impugned order for a period of 4(four) weeks and has also fixed this matter for hearing.

3. Facts leading to file this appeal, in brief, are that on 05-10-2011 the Plaintiff-Respondent has filed, on 15-07-1995, a Title Suit No. 422 of 2011 against the appellants stating,' inter alia, that the Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL), which is defendant No.1, has been registered as a public company limited by shares as per provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 and that the plaintiff is a sponsor director of the SIBL, holding 55,83,766 shares. The defendant No.1 (SIBL)is a banking company, defendant No.2 is the Chairman of the said Bank and the defendants No.2-6 are directors of the Bank. The defendant No.7-9, namely the Governor of Bangladesh Bank, the General Manager (BRPD). Bangladesh Bank and the Register, Joint Stock Companies and Firms are the pro-forma defendants. Plaintiff's further case is that since registration of the Bank he has been regularly attending the board meetings of the Bank and has been performing functions as member of different sub-committees and was the chairman of the audit committee in 2009- 2010; that by a notice dated 26-09-2011 an emergency meeting of the board of directors of SIBL was called on 28-09-2011; that there was no agenda in the said meeting to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors of SIBL, rather agenda NoA2 of the meeting was regarding discussion of the legal opinion of Barrister Mr. Rafiqul Haque and to take corrective measures for protecting interest of the Bank and of the shareholders; that at the time of discussion on agenda No. 42 defendant No.2, all on a sudden, made a comment that in the matter of renunciation of right shares in favour of IFIL (Islamic Finance and Investment Limited) the plaintiff might have some interest and he had invited opinion of director Sultan Mahmud Chowdhury, who has opined that the plaintiff had connivance in the matter of renunciation of shares in favour of IFIL and Mr. Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury had proposed to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors. Accordingly, the defendants Nos.2-6, pursuant to a pre-plan, had removed the plaintiff from the board of directors of Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL) in the 258th meeting of the board of directors, which is totally illegal. The plaintiff further states that, as per provisions of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994, in order to remove a director from his office an extra ordinary resolution will have to be adopted and that the board of directors has no power or authority to remove another director and that all these acts and deeds were done at the behest of defendant No.2 to take entire control of the SIBL in the hands of defendant Nos.2-6. He also states that the board had no power even to remove him with reference to section 108(2) of the Companies Act read with article 65.3 (Clause 1C of the undertaking) or Article 82.9 of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the Bank. He then states that the plaintiff had never interfered in the administration or management of the business of banking, nor he had taken any loan from the Bank, nor did any act contrary to sariah and, as such, there was no scope to declare that his office has fallen vacant. But the plaintiff has been removed from the board of directors of SIBL. His further case is that, after his removal from the board of SIBL the board has issued a notice dated 28-9-2011 convening its 259th meeting on the following day, that is on 29-9-2011, but no notice of the 259th board meeting was served upon the plaintiff. Hence, he asserts, that the said notice dated 28-9-2011 convening 259th board meeting is absolutely illegal, irregular, unlawful and ineffective. Accordingly, he has prayed for declaring that his removal in the 258th board meeting dated 28-9-2011 was done in violation of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994 and that the decision of his removal from the office of director was illegal, ultravires and not binding on him and to declare further that he is still continuing as a lawful director of the SIBL. He has also asked for further declaration to the effect that the notice dated 28-9-2011 for co-option of a new director in the board meeting dated 29-9-2011 is illegal and ultravires.

4. In the pending suit, the plaintiff has also filed an application, on 17-10-2011, under Order XXXIX Rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), stating almost similar facts and praying for a mandatory injunction to the effect that-

(ক) অত্র মোকদ্দমা নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত ১-৬ নং বিবাদী যাতে বাদীকে পরিচালনা সভার নোটিশ প্রদান সহ পরিচালনা পর্যদের সভায় যোগদানের এবং পরিচালক হিসাব দায়িত্ব পালনের সুযোগ প্রদান করা হইতে বঞ্চিত করিতে না পারে সেই মর্মে বিবাদীগণকে বারিত করিয়া এক অস্থায়ী আদেশাত্মক নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দিতে,

(খ) ইত্যবসরে অত্র অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্ত শুনানী ও নিষ্পত্তির পূর্ব পর্যন্ত ১-৬নং বিবাদী যাতে বাদীকে পরিচালনা সভায় নোটিশ প্রদান সহ পরিচালনা পর্ষদের সভায় যোগদানের এর্ব পরিচালক হিসাবে দায়িত্ব পালনের সুযোগ পালনের সুযোগ বঞ্চিত করিতে না পারে সেই মর্মে বিবাদীগণকে বারিত করিয়া এক অর্ন্তবর্তীকালীন আদেশাত্মক অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দিতে।”

5. The defendants (appellants before us) have entered appearance in the suit and had filed a joint written objection, on 26-10-2011, against the plain- tiff's petition for injunction controverting all material allegations made in that petition and further stating that, it was found that the petitioner and his family members were entitled to right shares worth of Tk. 3.45 crores. However, the petitioner entered into an agreement with IFIL, for getting investment facility of Tk. 10.80 crores to purchase right shares in the name of IFIL by way of renunciation by the other shareholders of the Bank. IFIL not being a shareholder of the said Bank, right shares were not offered to it. Thereafter, it was found that several foreign shareholders of the Bank renounced their offer of right share worth Tk. 10.00 crores in favour of IFIL. Therefore, it is crystal clear that the petitioner persuaded the foreign shareholders not to purchase the right shares offered to them and to renounce it in favour of IFIL as per his instruction. As per the terms and condition of the investment facility extended by IFIL, after realization of the invested amount from the sale proceeds of the said shares, the petitioner and IFIL will be entitled to the rest of the shares or the profit at the ratio of 80.20. Thereafter, it is apparent that the petitioner, with a view to make personal profit, persuaded the foreign shareholders to renounce their shares in favour of IFIL. It has further been stated in the written objection that the petitioner as a Director of the said Bank held a fiduciary relation to the said Bank and its shareholders and depositors. The petitioner, by abusing his office of Director, involved in illegal and unethical practice purely for his personal gain which is contrary/derogatory to the interest of the said Bank and its shareholders and depositors and thus the office of the petitioner as Director of the said Bank is vacated. Therefore, the Board of Directors of the said Bank in its 258th emergency meeting resolved to simply remove the petitioner from the office of Director since his office of Director has already been vacated pursuant to section 108(2) of the Companies Act, 1994 read with clause 65(3) and 82.09 of the Articles of Association of the said Bank.

6. After hearing both the parties the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, by order dated 26-10-2011, has allowed petition for injunction in mandatory form holding that the plaintiff shall have right to attend all the meetings and the defendants should issue all notices on him as usually treating him as a director of the Bank. Being aggrieved by this order dated 26-10-2011 the appellants has preferred the instant appeal before this court.

7. The learned Senior Advocate Mr. Rafique-ul-Haq alongwith Mr. Aminul Hoque and Ms. Dilara Khandaker, Advocates appearing for the appellants, having placed the memorandum of appeal and other documents on record before us, has taken us through the case and submits that there are consistent decisions of almost all the jurisdictions that the Court should not interfere with the internal management of a company by issuing an order of injunction. He also strenuously argued that, in passing the impugned order, the trial Court has restored directorship to the plaintiff that has ceased at least one month before the date of passing the impugned order and this order of the trial Court restoring status-quo anti is absolutely illegal. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has referred to the cases of Nurul Islam vs Khatibuddin Ahmed: 56 DLR 545; Abul Hayat Sunu vs M A Reja: 47 DLR 170; Abdul Jalil vs Abu Bakr Siddique: 35 DLR (AD) 43 and Mr. Mainul Hosein vs Mr. Anwar Hossain: 4 BLT (AD) 76. He next submits that, although in the resolution adopted in the 258th board meeting, dated 28-9-2011, the word removal has been used it was indeed an act of recording 'vacation of office' of the plaintiff as would be apparent from the fact of referring to section 108 of sub-section (2) of the Companies Act, 1994 and article 65.3 paragraph 1 (c) of the undertaking and Article 82.09 of the Articles of Association (AoA) in the said resolution. He also submits that, as the board of directors has power to record vacation of office as per Article 65.3 (paragraph 1(C) of the undertaking) and 82.09, so mere error in using the proper term would not pollute the Board's power to record a decision regarding the vacation of office. In support of his contention the learned advocate has referred to a decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 1: Col. Md. Hashmat Ali (Retd.) vs Government of Bangladesh. The learned advocate, then drawing our attention to paragraph 1 (c) of the undertaking forming part of Article 65.3 of the AoA, submits that the Board, which is better posted with the relevant facts, is the sole authority to decide as to whether a director has acted in breach of the undertaking and that the power exercised by the board, apparently to record the vacation of office, is quite within the ambit of the board's power conferred on it by the AoA of the SIBL. He continues maintaining that, as recorded in the concerned minutes of agenda No. 42 of the 258thboard meeting, apparently the board has taken a decision for violation of the undertaking and simply recorded the vacation of his office as per provisions of article 82.09 of the AoA of the SIBL. As such, it is a clear case of vacation of office recorded in the said resolution and since there is source of power vested in the directors, so mere mentioning of the word 'removal' could not make the resolution illegal, he asserts. He also submits, referring to the renunciation form, that the form of renunciation contains a date being 6-5-2011 at the top right hand comer and shows that the signature of the renouncee was verified on 4-5-2011 and that the price of the right shares (at face value) was deposited in the Bank on 5-5-2011, as such, on the face of these documents a case of anti-dated fraudulent transaction, at the behest of the plaintiff, has been revealed and that justifies the action taken. He finally submits that, in passing the impugned order the trial Court has given the full relief pending disposal of the suit and this is contrary to the law declared in the case of Government vs Md. Matiur Rahman: 3 LG (AD) (2006) 25. Accordingly, the learned advocate concludes that, the impugned order has been passed without appreciating the facts and law involved in this case and in violation of the principles guiding discretion in the matter of granting temporary injunction. Hence, the impugned order is liable to be set-aside and the appeal be allowed.

8. Mr. AKM Nazrul Islam, Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood and Mr. Abdur Razzaqu, Senior Advocates along with Mr. Ehsan A Siddiq, SA Nabi and Mr. Mir Ahmed Bin Quasem, advocates appeared for the plaintiff-respondent. They have referred to the documents annexed to the petition for injunction filed by the respondent, the petition for vacating the stay, the additional paper book filed by the respondent and to other documents and materials on record.

9. Mr. Abdur Razzaque has made the following submissions, namely-(1) filing of the suit against the company should not necessarily mean interference with the internal management of a company. Referring to the decision reported in 4 BLT (AD) 76, cited on behalf of the appellant, he submits that what was decided in that case is that it is advisable that the Court should not interfere by granting injunction wherein the internal management and functioning of the company may be affected. In that decision the apex Court has very calculatively used the word 'advisable' and this clearly indicates that this Court can pass an order of injunction in an appropriate case filed against the company. (2) He then submits that there are other cases, yet to be distinguished, in which the individual right of a director is involved and in such a case the director aggrieved can maintain a suit and an order passed in such a case would not amount to interference in the internal management of a company. In support of his contention the learned advocate has cited (1987) 69 Company Cases (AP) 301: Avanthi Explosives P Ltd vs. Principal Subordinate Judge Tirupathi; AIR (38) 1951 (Mad) 542: Rathnavalusami vs. Manickavelu and (1969) 35 Company Case 249: Panipat Woolen & General Mills Co. Ltd vs. RL Kaushik. (3) The learned advocate thereafter, to rebut the submission that a temporary mandatory injunction to restore status-quo anti can not be passed, has referred to AIR 1995 (Guzrat) 92: Jibanbhabi vs. Bhavanjee and AIR 1990 (SC) 867: Dorab vs. Coomi Sorab and submits that in an appropriate situation, like the one before this court, the Court can not sit and watch the proceedings as a silent spectator and show its helplessness and that merely because the status of a party is in dispute the Court is not restrained from granting relief at the interlocutory stage. He accordingly supports the impugned order and submits that there was no illegality committed by the trial Court in passing the impugned order in the form of temporary mandatory injunction. (4) He next submits that in the minutes to the agenda No. 24, referring to board memo No. 514 of 2011 dated 9-8-2011, it has been clearly recorded by the company secretary that "the Company Secretary also informed the Board that the Bank accepted the renunciation as the renouncee (IFIL) and others deposited the required money observing the formalities as per right shares of her documents". This being the admitted possession, the submission of the appellant that the plain- tiff was involved in any fraudulent transaction in the matter of renunciation of shares in favour of IFIL has no legs to stand and such a submission is repelled by the admitted position as recorded above. (5) The learned advocate then, drawing our attention to the form of renunciation, submits that it is true that, at the top right hand comer date has been mentioned as 6-5-2011. But the signature was verified on 4-5-2011 by the official of SIBL and the signatures dated 5-5-2011 showing receipt of money is also signature and seal of the SIBL officer. As such, he continues, the Bank itself is trying to attribute fraud on its own conduct and this submission advanced on behalf of the appellant stands rebutted by the admission recorded in the minutes quoted above. Hence, he concludes, that the submissions of the appellant has no substance and the impugned order does not call for interference by this court.

10. The learned senior advocate Mr. AKM Nazrul Islam mainly submits that the act of renunciation is absolutely legal and according to the Securities & Exchange Commission (Rights Issue) Rules, 2006 and that the board cannot exercise its power arbitrarily without affording the plaintiff- director an opportunity to explain his position. He further submits that when there is a wrong there must be some remedy and the trial Court has simply remidied the wrong done to plaintiff, therefore, it has committed no illegality in passing the impugned order. The learned advocate has also referred to a decision reported in 31 DLR (1995) 5: Shamsul Huda vs Jalaluddin Ahmed wherein a' Bench of this Division has held, to record an execption to the law laid down in Foss vs Harbottle, that "for the protection of right of individual members of a company can sue. The Court below wrongly decided that the plaintiff has no cause of action, just because he was not suing in the name of the company in accordance with the law laid down in Foss vs Harbottle". We shall advert to this decision at the appropriate place.

11. The learned Senior Advocate Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood, drawing our attention to the resolution and the notice of the 258th Board meeting, mainly submits that there was no agenda in the notice to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors. He then submits that, it was a proposal for removal of the plaintiff from the board of directors and this is clearly evident from the minutes itself and it has been recorded in the minutes that some directors have taken decision to remove the plaintiff. So this is a clear case of 'removal' of the plaintiff on the proposal and decision of the members of the SIBL board of directors and the verbal submission of the learned advocate for the appellant that it was a case of using wrong term cannot be accepted in the absence of any materials on record to substantiate such verbal submission. Rather, apparently, this decision of removal from the board, taken in the 258th (emergency) meeting of the board, held on 28-9-2011, has been taken in clear violation of section 106 of the of the Companies Act, 1994 that lays down a special procedure for removal of a director requiring an extraordinary resolution to be adopted, by two-third majority of the members present, in a general meeting summoned for that purpose. Board of directors has no power to remove the plaintiff director, more so without any agenda or any notice expressing any intention to adopt such a resolution. As such, he submits, that the impugned resolution removing the plaintiff is prima facie ultravires, a nullity and void as initio. Hence the trial Court has committed no illegality in passing the impugned order. He then submits that, by a letter dated 03-10-2011 issued by the General Manager BRPD of Bangladesh Bank the appellants were asked to show cause, within five days, under what authority they had removed the plaintiff from the office of the director. He finally submits that, it was the exclusive authority of Bangladesh Bank to remove a director, as authorised by section 46 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. Next, drawing our attention to section 2 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 (BCA) the learned Advocate further submits that, the BCA being a special law it will prevail over the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994, and that, specific provisions having been made in the BCA for removal of a Bank director by Bangladesh Bank and Bangladesh Bank having not taken any step against the plaintiff-respondent, the appellants had no authority to take any decision to remove the plaintiff-respondent. On all these grounds, he concludes, the impugned order was quite proper, hence the same do not warrant any interference by this Court and the stay granted by this Court is liable to be vacated along with appropriate direction to restore the status-quo that was prevailing on the date of passing of the order impugned in this appeal.

12. We have heard the learned advocates, perused the memorandum of appeal, the petition for stay filed by the appellants, the injunction petition, the petition for vacating the stay, the additional paper book filed by the respondent and other materials on record.

13. We have stated, herein above, the facts leading to preferring this appeal.

14. Now looking at the minutes of the 258th emergency board meeting, held on 28-9-2011, as pointed out by the senior counsel Mr. Mahmood, we find that the plaintiff-respondent was removed on the basis of a proposal of the director Mr. Alhaj Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury to remove the plaintiff-respondent from the board of directors, recording some allegations against the plaintiff, and all other directors accepted the proposal for removal. The relevant motion, as recorded in the minutes reads as follows: "Alhaj Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury, honourable Director proposed 12 remove Major (Retd.) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque, honourable Director from the Board of Directors and Alhaj Nasiruddin, honourable Director and Mr. Md. Shah Alam, honourable Director seconded the proposal, removal decision may be taken as empowered in pursuance to Companies Act, 1994, Section # 108(2) read with Article No.# 65(3)-1C and Article No. # 82.9 of Articles of Association of the Bank. All other directors accepted the proposal for removal." Accordingly, the following resolution was adopted in that meeting, namely- "(a) Major (Retd.) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque, honourable Director is hereby removed in pursuance to Companies Act, 1994, section # 108(2) read with Articles No. # 65(3)-1C and Article No. # 82.9 of Articles of Association of the Bank with immediate effect from the position of Director of Social Islami Bank Limited for his unethical and oath-violating activities by renunciation and sale of Foreigner's Shares in collaboration with the Islamic Finance and Investment Limited (IFIL) which is contrary/derogatory to the objectives or interest of the Bank and Shariah".

15. Prima facie, the concerned minutes shows that a motion was moved by a director to remove the plaintiff from the office of director, which was accepted as such by all the directors and plaintiff was removed from his office with immediate effect, vide the resolution quoted above, although the defendant-appellants can adduce evidence, at the time of trial, to prove that in substance the decision taken was one for recording vacation of office as per section 108(2) read with the Artices 65(3) and 82.9 of the AoA of the SIBL, as recorded in the concerned resolution. However, at this stage this Court will simply consider as to whether the plaintiff- respondent has been able to make out an arguable case.

16. Since, prima facie this appears to be a case of removal of a director, so the board of directors, in order to implement its decision to remove the plaintiff-respondent, could have further resolved to convene a general or extraordinary general meeting to consider and adopt an extraordinary resolution for removal of the plaintiff as per provision of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. Similar provision for removal of a director has also been made in Article 92 of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the SIBL that provides that, the company may, by an extra ordinary resolution, remove any director before the expiration of his period of office. This article has been incorporated in terms of the provisions of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. But in this particular case apparently the respondents did not follow the procedure laid down in article 92 of the AoA of the SIBL or in section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. However, whether this is a mere case of using wrong terminology, as was argued by the learned senior advocate appearing for the appellant, has to be proved by the defendant- appellant at the time of trial.

17. Besides, the office of a director of the SIBL is subject to retirement by rotation. This being the fact we are also of the view that, in this case, the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of granting injunction and that the plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss in the absence of an appropriate order of injunction. We also consider the decision reported in AIR 1995 (Guj) 93: Jivanbhai vs Bhavanjee is of immense persuasive value and has declared the correct position of law. It has been held in that case that "it is true that when there is contest or controversy between the parties about the status, the Court normally refrains from granting the final relief at an interlocutory stage, but Court is certainly entitled to scan the so-called defence about the denial of status of tenancy raised by the other side. Otherwise, Court would be encouraging the dishonest defence and allowing the party to live at the mercy of the opponent till his rights are finalized. It is very easy for the opponent in any case to deny the status of one party who goes to Court after doing illegal acts and then to contend that no final relief be granted at an interlocutory stage. The Court in such situation cannot sit and watch the proceedings as a silent spectator and show its helplessness". We respectfully endorse this view. Simultaneously, we have also considered the decision reported in 3 LG (2006) AD 25: Government vs Md. Matiur Rahman, wherein the apex court: in a writ matter, has held that, "ad-interim order amounting to full relief should not be granted." The law thus declared by the apex Court is, indeed, a settled position of law guiding the practice and procedure in writ matters. But, the case before us is a civil matter and the question of granting or refusing petition for injunction is guided by different considerations, namely- (I) whether the petitioner has been able to make out a prima facie case, (II) in which side the balance of convenience and inconvenience is titled and (III) whether the petitioner would suffer irreparable loss in the case of not granting an order of injunction. There are other principles that has shaped the practice and procedure in this respect, but obviously it would amount to asking us a wrong question, in a civil matter, as to whether the Court below has given full relief by the impugned order passed under Order XXXIX, rule 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the CPE. Hence, we find that the decision reported in 3 LG (2006) (AD) 25 is liable to be distinguished and is not applicable to this case.

18. Thereafter, adverting to the contentions that the plaintiff-respondent has committed some illegalities or resorted to some fraudulent practices, as has been recorded in the minutes of the 258th (emergency) Board meeting pirating to agenda No. 42 and as regards the form of renunciation, we consider this as a. matter concerning the merit of the case to be decided by the trial Court upon considering the evidence that may be adduced by the contending parties. Similarly, the correspondence by and between SIBL and Bangladesh Bank are also to be looked, if the pleadings permits, at the time of trial.

19. It is also advisable, as has been held in the case reported in 4 BLT (AD) 76: Mr. Moinul Hossein vs Mr. Anwar Hossain, that the Court should not interfere by granting injunction where the internal management and functioning of the company may be affected: This decision of the apex Court has not only laid down the consistent views expressed by the courts under various jurisdiction, more so this decision is binding on this Division as per Article III of the Constitution. Learned senior advocate Mr. Huq has relied on this decision when he was very impressively assailing the legality and propriety of the impugned decision. But, the facts of this case [4 BLT (AD) 76] is liable to be distinguished from the facts of the case before us, while we find nothing apparent from the record before us as to how the impugned decision would affect the internal management or functioning of the SIBL, and this again remains to be the onus of the defendant-appellant to prove their case at the time of trial. Besides, we have looked into the statement of the company secretary recorded in Board Memo No. 514 of 2010, dated 9-8-2011, quoted herein before, only to decide about the prima-facie case. We shall, however, make it clear that this statement is indeed a report made by the company secretary for appraisal of the Board. We have not treated this as admission made by the company (SIBL) or by the defendants-appellants, who are always entitled to ascertain the correctness of such a report. Nor we have regarded this report to operate as an estoppel against the defendant-appellants.in stating their case.

20. We have rather considered the views expressed in the cases, cited by the learned counsel for the respondent Mr. Abdur Razzaque, as more relevant to the situation of the case before us. We, therefore respectfully endorse the view that, "the rule against interference by Court with internal management of the companies is not applicable to cases of infringement of individual membership rights as distinguished from corporate membership right" as has been held in the case of Avant he Explosives P. Ltd., reported in (1987) 69 Company Cases 301. Accordingly, we are of the view that the suit brought by the plaintiff to have it declared that his removal from the office of the director of SIBL is illegal, ultravires, malafide and that the notice to co-opt another director in his place is one pertaining to the individual right of the plaintiff-director and this has no nexus with the internal management or functioning of the company. Here, we also accept the ratio of the case reported in AIR (38) 1951 Madras 542, cited on behalf of the respondent. Besides, the principle laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR 5 (paragraph. 11) also lends support to our this view.

21. Having considered the record on its face, we are also of the opinion that the ratio of the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 1 is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of this case, at least at this stage.

<u>22. However, tuning our attention to the sub- mission, made on behalf of the respondent, that section 46 or section 17 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 (BCA) supersedes the provisions of section 106 or of section 108 of the Companies Act, 1991, we are of the view that this interpretation and the submission, if adopted, would lead to absurdity and frustrate the object of the Companies Act, 1994. The powers vested in Bangladesh Bank under section 46 of the BCA is a power vested in the regulator to enable it to perform its duties, while the provisions of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994 vesting power in the members of the company to remove a director is not inconsistent with power vested in Bangladesh Bank under section 46 of the BCA. Moreover, the provisions of sections 106 and 108 of the Companies Act, 1994 is protected by section 2 of the BCA.</u>

23. We have also taken notice of the Right Share Offer Documents (RSOD) of some other Banks and Fincial Institutions, contained in the Additional Paper Book submitted by the respondent. We are of the view that, despite showing uniform practices being followed by them in the matter of offering right shares, we have treated these RODS of other Banks and Financial Institutions as extraneous for our consideration. In our opinion, the Court should decide the legality and propriety of the acts complained of strictly with reference to the laws applicable to the given facts of this case, not with reference to any practice or precedent followed or created by other Banks, whether uniformly or not.

24. Before parting of, we must record that the plaintiff-respondent has filed one injunction petition and another petition for vacating stay and submitted that, taking advantage of the stay order passed by this court, the Bank was proceeding with undue haste to curtail valuable rights of the plaintiff respondent while the appeal was pending. We have kept these two petitions with the record for consideration at the time of hearing of the appeal and the learned lawyers of both sides have agreed that this Court can pass consequential order in accordance with the fate of the appeal.

25. In the light of our deliberation recorded herein before; we find no merit in the appeal. The appeal is liable to be dismissed with appropriate direction.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. The order No.8 dated 26-10-2011 passed by the 5th Court of Joint District Judge in Title Suit No. 422 of 2011 is hereby affirmed. The appellants are directed to intimate the decision of this Court to its two other sister. concerns, namely-SIBL Investment Ltd and SIBL Securities. Ltd. in order to restore status-quo that was prevailing on the date of passing the impugned order dated 26-10-2011 by the Court below, within 3(three) workings days of receiving copy of this judgment. Since, this case merits urgent disposal because of the limited period of the office, we further direct that the trial Court should put this case at the top of its daily cause list and shall dispose of the same within sixty working days upon considering the evidence that may be adduced by the parties and independently of the views expressed by us for the disposal of this appeal.

No order as to cost.

Send down the Lower Court Records.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29-9-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.6286 of 2010).
full_judgment:
Md. Muzammel Hossain, J: This petition for leave to appeal under Article 103 of the Constitution of Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and order dated 29-9-2010 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.6286 of 2010 discharging the Rule.

<u>2. The present petitioner preferred Writ Petition No.6286 of 2010 before the High Court Division challenging the Constitutional validity of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2009 (Act No.8 of 2009) and the legality of the initiation and continuation of Metro Special Case No.126 of 2010 corresponding to ACC GR Case No,83 of 2009 arising out of Cantonment Police Station Case No.08 dated 26-10-2009 under Sections 2 and 4(2) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2009, now pending before the Court of Metropolitan Senior Special Judge, Dhaka.</u>

3. The petitioner in the writ petition stated, inter-alia, that he is a citizen of Bangladesh, the elder son of the former President Shaheed Ziaur Rahman and the former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia and he is a Director of Rahman Navigation Co. Ltd. and the Senior Joint Secretary of Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP); that he having been arrested in connection with Gulshan Police Station Case No.34(03) 2007 was taken into custody and because of his serious illness the Government released him on parole and he has been under treatment in London; that the Assistant Director, Special Enquiry and Investigation, Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), Head Office, Dhaka lodged a First Information Report (FIR) on 26-10-2009 with Cantonment Police Station under Sections 2 and 4(2) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2009 (hereinafter referred to as the "Ain of 2009") implicating the petitioner as accused No.2 while one Gias Uddin-al-Mamun was named as accused No.1 alleging, inter alia, that various incidents of offence alleged to have been committed by the petitioner and the accused no.1 under the Ain of 2009 during the period from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007. We have noticed that the details of the allegations of the offence of money laundering have been elaborately set out in the FIR, being Cantonment Police Station Case No.08 dated 26-10-2009 under Sections 2 and 4(2) of the Ain of 2009, which was subsequently registered as ACC GR Case No.83 of 2009 in the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka.

4. The Assistant Director, Special Enquiry and Investigation, ACC, Dhaka after completion of investigation submitted charge sheet No.48 dated 05-7-2010 under Sections 2(ট)(আ)(ই) and 4(2) of the Ain of 2009 against the petitioner and another Gias Uddin-al-Mamun as per sanction of the Anti Corruption Commission vide memo dated 05-7-2010 and the case was transferred to the Court of Metropolitan Senior Special Judge, Dhaka and registered as Metro Special Case No.126 of 2010.

<u>5. It appears from the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6286 of 2010 that Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that he would not press the Rule so far it relates to the vires of the Ain of 2009. Therefore, the petitioner challenged the legality of the Metro Special Case No. 126 of 2010 in Writ Petition No.6286 of 2010 mainly on the ground that the proceedings under the provisions of the Ain of 2009 is barred under Articles 35(1) and 44 of the Constitution since the alleged offences were committed admittedly before the enactment of the said Ain. After hearing, the High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 29-9-2010 discharged the Rule, holding inter alia:</u>

<u>i) The writ petition is not maintainable.</u>

<u>ii) The Proceedings under the Ain of 2009 was not barred under Article 35(1) of the Constitution since money laundering was an offence even under the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2002 (hereinafter referred to as the "Ain of 2002") although its definition has been elaborated under the subsequent Ain of 2009.</u>

6. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the petitioner preferred the instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before this Court.

7. This Petition involves the question as to whether an offence alleged to have been committed prior to the enactment of the Ain of 2009 can proceed under the said Ain.

8. Mr. Ahsanul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner assails the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division mainly on the ground that admittedly the alleged offences had been committed during the period from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 but the FIR was lodged as late as on 26-10-2009 under the pro- visions of the Ain of 2009 which saved only the proceedings pending under the provisions of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ordinance 2008 (the "Ordinance of 2008") and the said Ordinance saved only the proceedings pending under the provisions of the Ain of 2002. But, Mr. Karim submits that since no proceeding was pending either under the Ain of2002 till it was repealed on 15-4-2008 by the Ordinance of 2008, the offences, even if committed are not saved either by the Ordinance of 2008 or by the Ain of 2009, as such, the learned Advocate contends that a proceeding under the ambit of a subsequent Ain in respect of an offence allegedly committed long before the enactment of the said Ain is ultra vires the Sub Article (1) of Article 35 of the Constitution, as such void.

9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General appearing for the respondent No.1 Government of Bangladesh submits that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order since the allegation raised against the petitioner discloses an offence of money laundering under the Ain of 2009; that the provisions of the Ain of 2002 was saved by the Ordinance of 2008 with some modifications of the provisions of the Ain of 2002 and the provisions of Ordinance of 2008 was saved by the Ain of 2009 and there is a continuity of law relating to the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain and as such the case should be disposed of under the Ain of 2009; that the Ain of 2002 and the Ordinance of 2008 were saved by the Ain of 2009 and the provisions of Article 35(1) of the Constitution is not a bar of initiation of a proceeding against the petitioner under the Ain of 2009, since the definition of money laundering under the Ain of 2002 remains more or less the same under the Ain of 2009 and as such the instant leave petition is liable to be dismissed.

10. Mr. Anisul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.3-ACC submits that the allegation raised against the petitioner discloses an offence of money laundering in respect of transactions made between the period of 01-1-2003 and 31-5-2007 under the provision of Sections 2(ট)(অ)(ই) and 4(2) of the Ain of 2009 and that the Ain of 2009 as well as the Ordinance of 2008 authorizes the ACC to investigate the offence, committed under the Ain of 2009 and since there is a continuity of legislation from the Ain of 2002 to Ain of 2009, the provision of Ain of 2002,Ordinance of 2008 and Ain of 2009 have created no bar in proceeding against the petitioner.

11. The learned Attorney General and Mr. Anisul Haque, the learned Advocate have argued in unison that the writ petition has been filed on misconception of law for quashment of a criminal proceeding under the guise of writ petition and as such the writ petition is not maintainable in law.

12. In the instant case, the alleged offences of money laundering were committed from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 during which the Ain of 2002, was in operation. If the allegations come within the definition of money laundering it was an offence under the said Ain, no matter it was disclosed or not at that time. This Ain of 2002 was repealed by Section 31 of the Ordinance of 2008 on and from 13-4-2008. This provision of the Ordinance saved the pending cases and proceedings under the Ain of 2002 as if the said Ain had not been repealed. Similarly, this Ordinance was also repealed by Section 31 of the Ain of 2009 on and from 24-2-2009. The said provision likewise saved the pending cases and proceedings under the said Ordinance as if those were filed under the Ain of 2009. But nothing has been said about those offences which were committed earlier but either were not disclosed or even if dis- closed no FIR was lodged during the operation of the concerned legal provision. Does it then mean that those offences cease to be an offence? No it cannot be, even if the said provision is repealed in view of the provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 which is discussed herein below.

<u>13. It appears that after filing of the charge sheet the next date was fixed on 10-8-2010 for taking cognizance but before taking cognizance the petitioner moved the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the initiation and continuation of the aforesaid Metro Special Case and also challenging the vires of the Ain of 2009. The High Court Division observed that the learned Advocate for the petitioner had not pressed the Rule in respect of vires of the Ain of 2009 and that he had only pressed the other part of the Rule challenging the legality of the Metro Special Case No.126 of 2010 under the Ain of 2009.</u>

<u>14. In delivering the judgment arid order, the High Court Division dealt with the question in this manner:</u>

<u>"In this case, the acts for which prosecution has been started were done during the period when Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2002 was in operation. The description of 'money laundering' was given in the Act of 2002. The said description was in general terms, but the description of 'money laundering' in the Ordinance of 2008 and the Act of 2009 has made clear the description given in the Act of 2002. If the descriptions in these legislations are carefully analyzed it will be found that the criminal quality of 'money laundering' as assigned in the Act of 2002 remains unaltered in the description of 'money laundering' in the Ordinance of 2008 and in the Act of 2009. What is now 'money laundering' under the Act of 2009 was also 'money laundering' under the Act of 2002. Hence, no objection taken by the petitioner under Article 35(1) of our Constitution can be sustained.</u>

<u>We have already held that 'money laundering' was an offence under Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2002 and that the punishment provided for by Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2009 is not greater than that of Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2002. Therefore, there is no chance of prejudice to the petitioner."</u>

<u>15. The question is whether an offence committed within the validity period of the Ain of 2002 be prosecuted under the provisions of the Ain of 2009 when the Ain of 2002 had already been repealed by the Ordinance of 2008 on 15-4-2008 with a provision of savings clause of pending cases and proceedings which will be disposed of in such a manner as if the said A in had not been repealed and subsequently the said Ordinance was also repealed by the Ainof 2009 with another savings clause in Section 31 (2) of the Ain whereby pending cases and proceedings have been saved as if those were filed or initiated under the provisions of the Ain of 2009. There is no doubt that the alleged offence was committed when the Ain of 2002 was in force. But subsequently the FIR was lodged on 26-10-2009 under the Ain of 2009. Having considered the FIR, Charge Sheet and other materials on record we have found that the allegation lodged against the petitioner discloses a prima facie case under Section 2(ঠ)(অ)(আ) and 13 of the Ain of 2002.</u>

16. In the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that the Ain of 2009 was given retrospective effect from 15-4-2008. In this context it is pertinent to refer to the relevant provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act which reads as under:

"6. Where this Act, or any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act, repeals any enactment hitherto made or hereafter to be made, then unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not-

(a) 	.

(b) affect the previous operation of any enactment so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or

(c) affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under any enactment so repealed; or

(d) affect any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against any enactment so repealed; or

(e) affect any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such right, privilege, obligation? liability, penalty, forfeiture or punishment as aforesaid and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment may be imposed as if the repealing Act or Regulation had not been passed."

17. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act,1897 deals with the effect of repeal of any Act of Parliament by passing a repealing Act providing certain consequences stated in Sub-Section (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of Section 6 of the Act.

18. The sole object of a repealing and amending Act is to get rid of certain provisions of obsolete matter and replacing the same by subsequent amendment of an Act, thereby abrogating the earlier provisions of the law, since right of repeal being inherent in legislature alone. Generally in the repealing Act a special saving clause has been inserted in order to deal with the effect of repeal thereby making exception to the general rule that the normal effect of repeal is to obliterate the repealed Act from the statute book as if it had never been passed.

<u>19. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides an exception to the rule that the normal effect of repealing Act is to obliterate the repealed Act from the statute book unless a different intention appears in the repealing Act.</u>

20. While commenting on the applicability of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act in the case of Md. Nazimuddinvs State reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB) 70 in para 60 Ruhul Islam, J observed as under:

"Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is applicable to a simple case of repeal, as well as to a case of repeal of a statute followed by a fresh enactment on the same subject. Section 6 would be applicable unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the section, and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new law.

In the enquiry to find out the intention of the legislature, one of the cardinal principles of interpretation of the statutes to be followed is that the intention which appears to be most in accordance with convenience, reason, justice and legal principles, should, in cases of doubt, be presumed to be the true one. Another principle is that when the repeal is followed by a fresh legislation on the same subject and a contrary intention does not appear therein, the repeal does not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the enactment so repealed."

21. In the case of TS Baliah Vs Income-tax Officer, Madras reported in AIR 1969 SC 701 the Supreme Court of India held that in view of the pro- visions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act prosecution under Section 52 of the Income Tax Act 1922 in respect of proceedings pending at the commencement of the Income Tax Act 1961 against the appellant Baliah was legally instituted under the Act of 1922 even after it's repeal by the repealing Act of 1961. While delivering judgment of the Supreme Court of India Ramaswami, J observed as follows:

"The principle of this section is that unless a different intention appears in the repealing Act, any legal proceeding can be instituted and continued in respect of any matter pending under the repealed Act as if that Act was in force at the time of repeal. In other words whenever there is a repeal of an enactment the consequences laid down in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless, as the section itself says a different intention appears in the repealing statute. In the case of a simple repeal there is scarcely any room for expression of a contrary opinion. But when the repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject the Court would undoubtedly have to look to the provisions of the new Act, but only for the purpose of determining whether they indicate a different intention. The question is not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Section 6 of the General Clauses therefore will be applicable unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the section. Such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new statute and the mere absence of a saving clause is by itself not material. in other words, the provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act will apply to a case of repeal even if there is a simultaneous re-enactment unless a contrary intention can be gathered from the new statute."

22. In the case of Sarju vs The State reported in AIR 1964 Allahabad 6, the Allahabad High Court was required to decide whether the whole proceedings under Section 19(f) of the Arms Act 1878 instituted on 02-5-1962 and on trial the conviction of the applicant on 25-8-1962 are void and cannot be cured in view of the repeal of the Act of 1878 by the Arms Act of 1959, which came into effect from 01-10- 1962. In answering to the question the Allahabad High Court held that:

"Where the accused had already incurred a penalty or punishment in respect of an offence punishable under Section 19(f) of the Arms Act,1878, before the new Act came into force, i.e. before 01-10-1962, the repeal of the old Act cannot affect such penalty or punishment as per provisions of S.6( c), (d) of the General Clauses Act. The punishment awarded to the accused cannot therefore become ineffective by the repeal of the old Act under which it was imposed."

23. In the case of Akhtar Hossain Khan vs State reported in 29 DLR (SC) 101 where FIR was lodged at the Police Station of Mehdiganj in respect of occurrence took place on 04-8-1972, charge sheet was submitted on 20-7-1974 and cognizance was taken on 31-8-1974 under PO 50 of 1972 after it was repealed on 09-2-1974 by Section 36 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. The question is whether the GR Case No.255 of 1973 arising out of the occurrence took place on 04-8-1973 can be tried under the PO 50 of 1972 after the repeal of the same on 09-2-1974 by the Special Powers Act, 1974 in view of the Section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act. The Supreme Court affirming the decision of the High Court Division held that the investigation started under a repealed law would not be affected by the subsequent repeal of the said law unless a contrary intention appeared from the repealing statutes. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J in delivering the judgment of the court observed as under:

"The provisions of clauses (c) and (e) of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act are clear enough to show that any investigation or legal proceedings started under the repealed statute will not be affected by the subsequent repeal of the said statute. It is thus difficult to accept the contention that the legislature did not intend to keep alive any other proceedings under PO 50 except pending cases as mentioned in Section 36(2)(b) of the Act. Simply because Section 36(2)(b) is silent on other cases it does not follow that the parliament intended to destroy them. There is nothing in the language in clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 36 of the Act from which it cannot be concluded that only the cases pending before the Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal in its restricted meaning have been saved. If, however, that restricted view is taken then the offence under PO 50 committed immediately before its repeal will go unpunished which, we think, could not be the intention of the legislature. It is true that specific mention of the pending cases was only made in the repealing Act but it does not appear from the repealing Act that the cases pending for investigation which are covered by section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act would be deemed to have been destroyed. There is nothing to show from the provisions of the repealing Act that any intention-contrary to the saving provisions of section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act has been expressed in the Act with a view to show that the legislature intended to destroy the offences committed under PO 50 up to the date of its repeal but did not come before the court through submission of charge sheet under Article 4(i) of PO 50."

<u>24. The Supreme Court further held that the provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act must come into operation in case of repeal of an enactment and in that view of the matter the proceedings in respect of offences of PO 50 pending investigation with the police must be covered by the provisions of section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act (29 DLR SC 101). However, in the case reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB) while discussing about repeal of statute followed by fresh legislation, Ruhul Islam, J (as he then was) observed as under:</u>

<u>"When a repeal of a statute or a statutory provision is followed by a fresh legislation on the same subject, and a contrary intention does not appear therein, the repeal does not affect any right, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under repealed enactment. According to this view there is no reason for giving any different effect to these two methods which achieve the same result. There is hardly any controversy that the above principle of raw is not applicable to both the cases where a statute has been repealed; and where the statute has been amended or repealed and after repealing a new provision on the same subject has been re-enacted. When repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject the court has to look to the provision of the new law to examine whether the new law indicates a different intention. The enquiry would be not to find out whether the new law expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Another test is, to find out whether the new provision manifests an intention incompatible with the provisions of the section, and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the provisions of the new law. There is no doubt that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is fully applicable to the amendment in the Act as indicated above."</u>

25. On perusal of the FIR, Investigation Report and other materials on record it appears that a primafacie case of money laundering has already been made out against the petitioner under Section 2(ট)(আ)(অ)of the Ain of 2002. From the discussions and findings made above it is clear that the occurrence of the alleged offence took place from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 when the Ain of 2002 was in force. But the case was instituted long after the repeal of the said Ain and after the enactment of the Ain of 2009. The savings clause contained in Section 31(2) of the Ain of 2009 has no manner of application in saving the instant case which was not in existence on the date of enactment of the Ain of 2009. Sub-Sections (b), (c), (d) and (e) of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is applicable in such a case of repeal of statute followed by a fresh enactment on the same subject "unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the Section and such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new law."

<u>26. In the instant case no where from the repealing Ordinance of 2008 or the subsequent Ain of 2009, one can find any indication stating the intention that Repealing Act showing any different intention that such repeal has destroyed the liability or penalty incurred or investigation initiated under the repealed Ain of 2002. Section 31(2) of the repealing Ain of 2009 provides that inspite of such repeal any case or proceeding pending under the repealed Ordinance of 2008 shall be disposed of in such a manner as if it has been filed or accepted under the Ain of 2009. The repealing Ordinance or Ain has not destroyed the offence committed under the Ain of 2002. But a prima-facie case as has been disclosed under the Ain of 2002 is found to have been saved by the provisions of Section 6(b), (c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act,1897.</u>

27. In the instant case the alleged offence was disclosed under the provisions of Section 2(ট)(আ)(ই) of the Ain of 2002 but there was no pending case or proceeding under the Ain of 2002 when the said Ain of 2002 or the Ordinance of 2008 was repealed. Rather the FIR was lodged under Sections 2 and 4(2) of the Ain of 2009 on 26-10-2009 long after the repeal of the Ain of 2002 by the Ordinance of 2008 and also after the enactment of the Ain of 2009 on 24-2-2009. It appears that according to the FIR occurrence took place from 01-1-2003 to 31-5- 2007 when the Ain of 2002 was in operation. The Ain of 2009 was given retrospective effect from 15- 4-2008 when the Ain of 2002 was repealed by the promulgation of the Ordinance of 2008. The facts and circumstances of the instant case is very unique in its nature wherein an offence committed under the repealed Ain of 2002 and the FIR was lodged much long after the repeal of the said Ain when the Ain of 2009 came into effect with the intervening Ordinance of 2008 which had already been repealed before the lodging of the FIR. It is well established that a criminal offence never abates or destroyed even after the repeal of the law under which the offence is alleged to have been committed. From the aforesaid discussions it is obvious that the Ordinance of 2008 or the Ain of 2009 has not saved the offence alleged to have been committed from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 under the Ain of 2002 till the date of its repeal. According to Halsbury's Laws of England Vo1.36, para-714 the general principle that an enactment which is repealed is to be treated as if it had never existed is subject to any saving which may be made expressly or by implication by the repealing enactment.

<u>28. When a law is repealed by a fresh legislation on the same subject we should not find out whether the new law expressly saves the rights and liabilities accrued or incurred under the repealed law rather we should find out whether the repealing law indicates a clear intention to destroy them. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is applicable to a repeal of a law without any fresh enactment on the same subject. It is also equally applicable to a case of repeal followed by fresh legislation in the same subject unless a different intention appears in the repealing law with that of the provisions of the Section and such different intention has to be ascertained from consideration of all the relevant provisions of the repealing law.</u>

<u>29. There is no merit in the submission that a prima-facie case disclosed from the FIR, charge sheet and other materials on record under the provisions of the repealed Ain of 2002 cannot be proceeded with since there would be an anomalous situation in continuing with the proceedings under the repealed Ain. The consequence of repeal of an Act is that the repeal of an Act does not affect the "passed and closed transactions" under the repealed Act which means the rights, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred will be effective as if the relevant law had not been repealed by the repealing Act. As we have already discussed above that inspite of repeal of the Ain of 2002 under which the offence was alleged to have been committed from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007, Section 6(b), (c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act enables the prosecution to continue with the legal proceeding or to institute any legal proceeding or to take recourse to any remedy which may have been effective before the repeal of the Act for getting remedy in respect of rights, privilege, liability, penalty or punishment as the case may be. We have noticed that in the case of Md. Nazimuddin vs State reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB) it has been held that while a statute is repealed by a fresh legislation on the same subject, and a contrary intention does not appear therein, the repeal does not affect any right, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under repealed enactment. Their Lordships further observed that in such a case the court has to examine the provisions of the new law to examine whether the new law indicates a different intention and the enquiry would be not to find out whether the new law expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. According to their Lordships another test is, to find out whether the new provision manifests an intention incompatible with the provisions of the section, and such incompatibility will have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the provisions of the new law.</u>

30. In that view of the matter the proceeding may continue under the provisions of the Ain of 2002 as if the Ain of 2002 had not been repealed by the subsequent legislation. In this context we may safely rely on the decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 101 and we cite with approval the decisions reported in 30 DLR 49 (FB), 21 BLD 30 and also the decisions of the Apex Courts of the sub-continent as discussed above.

31. The next question is as to which procedure has to be followed for prosecuting the petitioner. The answer is that Ain of 2002 has been inserted in the schedule to the Anti Corruption Commission Act 2004 (the "ACC Act, 2004") and as such the procedure in respect of inquiry, investigation, conducting prosecution and holding of trial shall be governed under the provisions of the ACC Act, 2004. Since the Ain of 2002 has been incorporated in the schedule to the ACC Act, 2004 by an amendment made by the ACC (Amendment) Ordinance of 2007 and thereby the offence of money laundering disclosed under the Ain of 2002 has been made triable under the provisions of the special procedures enumerated in Section 28 of the ACC Act of 2004. According to Section 28(1) the offences under the Act or the offences mentioned in the schedule to the Act shall be exclusively triable by the Special Judge who has been appointed under the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act,1958. But the offence as well as its punishment would be dealt with under the provisions of the Ain of 2002.

<u>32. Function of the Anti-Corruption Commission has been described in Section 17 of the ACC Act, 2004 which amongst others provides that the ACC shall enquire into and conduct investigation of offences mentioned in the schedule and file cases on the basis of inquiry or investigation and conduct prosecution of the case before the Court of Special Judge.</u>

33. We do not find any difficulty in reading the offences under the Money Laundering Ain, 2002 in the schedule when the entire Ain of 2002 has been incorporated in the schedule to the Act of 2004 which means inquiry, investigation, lodging of complaint and holding of trial of cases in respect of offences under the Ain of 2002 shall proceed under the provisions of the ACC Act, 2004.

34. On perusal of Clause (aa) in the schedule to the Criminal Law Amendment Act,1958 it appears that offences punishable under the Ain of 2002 was inserted by Section 7 of the Anti Corruption Commission (Amendment) Ordinance,2007 (Ordinance No.7 of 2007) with effect from 18-4-2007.

35. By effecting amendments to the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and also the schedule to the ACC Act, 2004 by inserting offences under the Ain of 2002 in both the schedules, the ACC has been emboldened with the exclusive power and jurisdiction to enquire into and conduct investigation of offences of money laundering, prosecution of cases before the Court of Special Judge.

<u>36. We have already noticed that Ain of 2009 though not included in the schedule to the ACC Act, 2004, yet Section 9 of the Ain of 2009 provides that the offences committed under the said Ain shall be deemed to be scheduled offences under the ACC Act, 2004.</u>

37. As we have already noticed earlier that legislature has consciously included the Ain of 2002 in the schedule to the ACC Act, 2004 and also included the offences under the Ain of 2002 in the schedule to the Criminal Law Amendment Act,1958 whereby any enquiry, investigation, lodging of complaint, conducting of prosecution before the Special Judge and the holding of trial exclusively by the Special Judge have been mandatorily required under the provisions of ACC Act, 2004 and the same provision is equally applicable in the case of offences under the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2009.

<u>38. The Ain of 2002 has not been deleted from the schedule to the ACC Act, 2004 to be substituted by the Ain of 2009. Rather a special provision has been made in Section 9 of the Ain of 2009 which provides that the offences under the Ain of 2009 shall be treated as offences mentioned in the schedule to the ACC Act,2004 and all procedures in respect of investigation, trial and all other related matters shall be proceeded with and continued under the provisions of the ACC Act, 2004 and the offences under the Ain of 2009 shall be triable by the Special Judge appointed under Section 3 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act,1958.</u>

<u>39. It is well established that legislature has full power to make a law with retrospective effect so as to destroy a right or a remedy all together but this must be expressly laid down or by necessary implication in the repealing legislation. In the case of Mofizur Rahman Khan vs Government of Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 321 it has been held that parliament being the supreme legislative authority subject to the constitutional limitations under Article 65 has the plenary power to pass any law on any subject both prospectively and retrospectively. But the parliament cannot pass a law to create a new offence which is not in existence at the time of commission of the act charged as an offence nor can it increase penal liability with retrospective effect. In the instant case the offence of money laundering under the Ain 2002 was alleged to have been committed from 01-1-2003 to 31-5-2007 and the procedure in respect of lodging complaint, holding investigation, trial and other related matters shall be initiated or continued under the ACC Act of 2004 and the ACC Rules,2007. By incorporating the Ain of 2002 in the schedule to the ACC Act of 2004 the offence of money laundering was brought within the purview of the ACC Act of 2004 and no new offence was created nor any penalty was increased retrospectively rather the offence of money laundering under the Ain of 2002 was made triable under the ACC Act of 2004 and the ACC Rules, 2007. It has not in any way created a new offence or increased penalliability retrospectively. Article 35(1) of the Constitution envisages the prohibition on conviction or sentence under an "ex post facto law" not trial of the offence alleged to have been committed or the procedure to be followed in the investigation, inquiry in respect of an offence alleged to have been committed. In the case reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90 while delivering judgment the Appellate Division observed that a person accused of the commission of an offence has no fundamental right to a trial by a particular Court or by a particular procedure except insofar as any Constitutional objection by way of discrimination or violation of any other fundamental right may be involved. In other words, the prohibition under this clause does not extend to merely procedural laws and procedural law would not contravene Article 35(1) merely because retrospective effect is given to it. The Appellate Division has considered the expression "ex post facto law" as interpreted in the case of Calder vs Bull reported in 3 US 384 where in the destination between 'ex post facto law' and  laws having to respective operation was explained by Mr. Justice Chase.</u>

40. In the case of Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh vs State of Vindhya Pradesh reported in AIR 1953 SC 394 the Supreme Court of India observed as follows:

"what is prohibited under Article 20(1) is only conviction or sentence under an ex post facto law and not trial thereof. Such trial under a procedure different from what obtained at the time of commission of the offence or by a Court different from that which had competence at the time cannot 'ipso facto' be held to be unconstitutional. A person accused of the commission of an offence has no fundamental right to trial by a particular court or by a particular procedure, except insofar as any constitutional objection by way of discrimination or the violation of any other fundamental right may be involved."

41. In the case reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90 the Appellate Division having meticulously considered the decisions of the cases reported in AIR 1953 SC 394, AIR 1979 (SC) 602, 19 DLR (SC) 242, PLD 1965 (SC) 681, 48 DLR (AD) 6 and 49 DLR (AD) 115 held that procedural law is always retrospective unless a different intention is expressly made in the statute itself and no one has a right far less a fundamental right, to trial by particular court or a particular procedure.

42. In view of the above discussions and findings, and also the provisions of Article 35(1) of the Constitution we are of the view that in the instant writ petition the prayer challenging the legality of Metro Special Case No. 126 of 2010 is misconceived and writ-petition is not maintainable.

43. As to the maintainability of the writ petition, the petitioners contention that for quashment of a criminal proceedings, writ petition is maintainable and in support of that the petitioner has cited the case of Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh vs Iqbal Hasan Mahmood alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku reported in 60 DLR (AD) 147 wherein the Appellate Division held that availability of alternative remedy by way of appeal or revision will not stand on the way when the question of law and interpretation of statute is involved. The facts and circumstances of the cases reported in 60 DLR (AD) 147, 49 DLR (AD) 111, 40 DLR (AD) 206 and 15 MLR (AD) 141 and the questions of law involved in those cases are totally distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant case before us and as such those decisions have no manner of application in the instant case before us.

<u>44. From the facts and circumstances of the instant case we are of the opinion that the principle of 'ex post facto' laws as embodied in Article 35(1) of the Constitution is not applicable in the instant case since the alleged offences were committed during the operation of the Ain of 2002, the punishment for the said offence as provided under Chapter IV of the said Ain be applicable. Therefore, there is no bar to hold trial of the petitioner under provisions of the ACC Act, 2004 for the commission of the offence alleged to have been committed under the Ain of 2002 and the question of prejudice does not arise at all. The case be treated as one instituted under the Ain of 2002.</u>

<u>45. From the foregoing discussions to sum up our findings it is held that firstly, the writ petition is misconceived one and not maintainable since vires of no law has been challenged. Secondly, the provision of Sub Article (1) of Article 35 of the Constitution will not be attracted since the offence as well as its punishment, if any, would be dealt with under the Ain of 2002. Thirdly, from a clear reading of the FIR, Investigation Report and other materials on record, a prima-facie case under Sections 2(ট) (আ) (ই) and Section 13 of the Ain of 2002 has been disclosed and the prosecution may proceed in accordance with law, if so advised. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is modified in the light of the findings and observations made above.</u>

Accordingly, the leave petition is disposed of with the above observations and modifications.

End.
