case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated February 26, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 206 of 1996).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is a defendants appeal by leave against the judgment dated February 26, 1997 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No.206 of 1996 sending back the suit on remand to the trial Court upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated April 27, 1996 of the Court of Sub- ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Narayanganj in Title Suit No. 67 of 1995 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title in respect of 2.95 acres of land and khas possession in respect of 4 decimals of land as mentioned in schedule 'ga' to the plaint which are claimed to be part of the accretal land measuring 1.51 acres.

2. It is the case of the plaintiffs that land measuring 2.95 acres is the accretal land to the CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 and that as the said land accreted to the aforesaid plots which were owned and possessed by plaintiffs, as such, they are legally owners of the accreted land. It may be mentioned quantity of the land of the aforesaid CS plot before accretion was 2.39 acres and the plaintiffs claiming 2.95 acres of land which said to have accreted to the aforesaid land i.e. land measuring 2.39 acres.

3. The plaintiffs are claiming the land of the CS plots by inheritance and by purchase. It is the case of the plaintiffs that since 1935 they are possessing and enjoying the accreted land as their vendors possessed and enjoyed the accreted land. It is also the case of the plaintiffs that they are in possession and enjoyment of the accreted land measuring 2.95 acres more or less for 60 years. The plaintiffs said to have filed Title Suit No. 27 of 1995 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Narayanganj and while the said suit was pending the defendant dispossessed the plaintiffs from 4 decimals of land accreted to the CS plot Nos. 670 and 671, by storing bricks and also by cutting earth from CS Plot No. 671, that the defendants have dispossessed the plaintiffs from the land of 'ga' schedule i.e. the land measuring 4 decimals of land accreted to the CS plot Nos. 670, 671 and 675. It has been averred by the plaintiffs that on February 12, 1995 they went to Tahshil Office for payment of rent in respect of the land described in schedule 'Kha' i.e. accreted land and then came to know that the said accreted land has been recorded in the name of the Government in the khas khatian. It has been contended since their land described in the schedule 'Kha' has been recorded in the name of the Government and that as they have been dispossessed from the land of schedule 'ga' they were constrained to file the suit seeking declaration of title in respect of the land described in schedule 'Kha' and for a declaration that the proceedings of Settlement Case No. 264 of 1988-89 and Settlement Case No. 221 of 1988-89 were illegal and that also for a decree for khas possession in respect of the land described in schedule 'ga'.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos.1 and 2, Government of Bangladesh and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Narayanganj, by filing one set of written statement and by the defendant Nos. 6-8 i.e. the appellants, by filing separate set of written statement. The defendants denied the averments made in the plaint. It is the case of the defendants that the land described' in schedule 'Kha' i.e. accreted land, did not accrete till the publication of the SA record on 1-8-1963, that land described in schedule 'kha' accreted to the CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 after the publication of the SA record i.e. coming into operation of part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It is the case of the defendant Nos. 1-2 that in respect of the accreted land to the aforesaid CS plots "চর্চা ম্যাপ" was prepared by the Collector of the Narayanganj Collectorate and the accreted lands to the CS plots were recorded in "চর্চা ম্যাপ". Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 asserted that it is not correct to say that the land described in schedule 'kha' accreted in 1935 or that before 1-8-1963 and that at the time of preparation of SA record and at the time of publication thereof on 1-8-1963 there was no existence of the accreted land as described in schedule 'kha', that the accreted land in respect whereof "চর্চা ম্যাপ" was prepared and listed in plots were given settlement to the defendant Nos. 6-8 in Settlement Case Nos. 265 of 1988-89 and 229 of 1988-89 for the use of industrial purpose, that the land of CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675,676 and 250 have been acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 27 of 1978-79 for utilisation by the defendant Nos. 6-8.

5. It was the case of the defendant Nos. 6-8 that the land described in schedule 'kha' was the Government's khas land and the said land has been settled with the defendants by starting Settlement Case Nos. 265 and 229 of 1988-89 and the land so taken lease is possessed by them. It is also the case of the defendants that at the time of SA survey which started in 1956 and continued upto some part of 1963 there was no existence of the land described in schedule 'kha' or, in other words, there was no accretion of land as described in schedule 'kha' to the CS plots land whereof has been acquired by the Government in LA Case Nos. 27 of 1978-79, that land described in schedule 'kha' accreted to the CS plots after publication of the SA record on 1-8-1963 i.e. subsequent to the coming into operation of the part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

6. It may be mentioned the plaintiffs are claiming the land in suit by purchase and as heirs of the purchasers and the purchases were made between 1932 and 1968. It was the case of the plaintiffs that land described in schedule 'Kha' accreted in 1935 to the CS Plots. If that assertion of the plaintiffs is accepted then it would have been quite natural to have the mention of the accreted land in the kabalas of the years between 1943 and 1968 and there would have been mention of said fact upon referring to the plot(s) to which there was accretion of land and the quantity thereof, but conspicuously in the deeds of the years 1943-1968 there is no mention of the plot of the accreted land nor quantity of land accreted to particular CS plot and also there is no mention of quantity as stated hereinbefore. It was the definite case of the defendants that there was no existence of accreted land till 1963 i.e. at the time when the SA record was made final. Had there been any accretion of land to the CS plot during SA survey the same would have surely been recorded in the SA record which was published on 1-8-1963. In the aforesaid state of the matter it has been observed by the trial Court that there was no reason to believe that the accreted land was in existence in 1963. It may be mentioned that during the period between 1935-1947 no rent was paid by the plaintiffs in respect of the land said to have accreted to the CS plots.

7. The plaintiffs tried to make out a case upon referring to the recital in the deed as to transfer of the land of CS plot with accreted land and asserted that there had been existence of accretal land prior to the coming into operation of part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or, in other words, prior to the publication of the SA record which was finally published on 1-8-1963. The case so tried to make out by the plaintiffs about the existence of accretal land prior to preparation of SA record and at the time of preparation and publication of SA record hardly inspires one to accept the same as correct since had the accretal land been in existence at the time of preparation of the SA records the same surely would have been recorded in the SA Records and that there would have been no occasion for the Government to prepare the "চর্চা ম্যাপ" with "m" plot in respect of the land accreted to the CS plots mentioned hereinbefore. The land of the "চর্চা ম্যাপ" with "চর্চা" plot has been recorded in the name of the Government in khas khatian.

8. The trial Court while dismissing the suit has observed

“স্বীকৃত মতেই নালিশী জমি এস,এ, রেকর্ড হয় নাই। এস, এ, রেকর্ড চূড়ান্ত হয়েছে ইং ১৯৬৩ সালে। বিবাদী পক্ষ সাক্ষী দিয়ে এবং কাগজ পত্র দালিখ করে প্রমাণ করেছেন নালিশী সম্পত্তি শীতলক্ষা নদী থেকে জাগার পর চর্চা ম্যাপ হয়েছে এবং নালিশী সম্পত্তি সরকারের ১নং খাস খতিয়ানে আর,এস, রেকর্ড হয়েছে। .......১নং বাদী জেরাতে নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে ৬-৮নং বিবাদীর দখল স্বীকার করেছেন। বাদী পক্ষের ২নং সাক্ষী নালিশী জমির পরিমাণ বলতে পারেন নাই। এবং সি, এস, দাগের পয়স্তি জমির পরিমাণও বলতে পারেন নাই। উক্ত সাক্ষী জেরাতে আরো উল্লেখ করেছেন, লপ্ত পয়স্তি জমি কে কতটুকু দখল করেন তাহা তিনি বলতে পারেন না। নালিশী জমি সরকারের জমি কিনা তাহা তিনি বলতে পারেন না। ফলে বলা যায় নালিশী জমি সম্পর্কে বাদী পক্ষের ২নং সাক্ষীর কোন ব্যক্তিগত জ্ঞান নাই। বাদী পক্ষের ৩নং সাক্ষী নালিশী জমিতে বাদীগণের দখলের কথা বললেও জেরাতে উল্লেখ করেছেন, নালিশী জমিতে ৬-৮ নং বিবাদী পাকঘর ও টিউবওয়েল বসাইয়াছে। নালিশী জমিতে গজারী কাঠ, শাল বাল্লী, ইট বালু আছে বলে তিনি বলেছেন। অর্থা বাদী পক্ষের ৩নং সাক্ষী নালিশী জমিতে ৬-৭ নং বিবাদীর দখল স্বীকার করেছেন।”

9. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, has held that there is no reason to disbelieve the “চর্চা ম্যাপ" and the RS record prepared in respect of the alluvial land. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence also held that Government by starting Settlement Case No. 265 of 1988-89 has settled the land accreted to the CS Plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 to the defendant Nos. 6-8 and since settlement they are in continuous possession and thereupon held that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the accreted land. The trial Court further held that since the land was settled by initiating the Settlement Case Nos. 265 and 229 of 1988-89 by the Government, as such, it cannot be said that the Settlement cases so started in respect of the accreted land and on the basis thereof settlement was made to the defendant Nos. 6-8 was illegal. The trial Court refused the prayer for khas possession of 4 decimals of land as described in schedule 'ga' on the finding that the land in respect whereof khas possession has been sought is unspecified and undemarcated, that from the papers filed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 it is seen that the land of CS plots as mentioned hereinbefore have been acquired in LA Case Nos. 27 of 1978-79 and the plaintiffs have received compensation and that no material was brought on record to show that the land so acquired have been released by the Government. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the land of 'kha' schedule and that the land of the said schedule is of the Government and that the defendant Nos. 6-8 have taken settlement from the Government the land described in schedule 'kha'.

10. The trial Court on consideration of the entire materials on record arriving at the finding that plaintiffs have no title and possession in the land in suit and that accreted land settled with the defendant Nos. 6-8 was the khas land of the Government. Since the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest as well as possession in the land in suit, the suit as framed is not maintainable as per provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

11. As against the decree of the Court of 1st instance the plaintiffs went on appeal before the High Court Division. The High Court Division without considering the materials on record as well as without entering into the merit of the appeal and deciding the appeal on merit allowed the appeal and sent back the suit to the trial Court "for proper adjudication afresh" upon observing "So all the issues are to be considered after the parties get an opportunity to adduce evidence in respect of their respective claim". In making the order of remand the High Court Division also observed "Learned Subordinate Judge, we find, was not aware of the legal position as settled by the Appellate Division in 31 DLR (AD) 195 and that Part V of SA & T Act came into force in the suit Mouza on 1-8-63".

12. As against the judgment of the High Court Division the defendants (defendant Nos. 6-8) moved this Division for leave to appeal.

<u>13. Leave was granted to consider the contentions whether the High Court Division was wrong in setting aside the finding of the trial Court without adverting to the reasoning assigned by it and upon a completely erroneous view that the trial Court was not aware of the legal position as settled by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, whether the High Court Division without applying its judicial mind to the finding of the trial Court and to the oral and documentary evidence on record wrongly set aside the judgment of the trial Court, whether the High Court Division proceeded on the wrong premise that in deciding the suit the trial Court not been aware of the law enunciated in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, since had the trial Court not been aware of the law settled by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, the said Court would not have put emphasis on the question as to whether there has been accretion of the land as claimed by the plaintiffs prior to 1-8-1963 or after 1-8-1963 i.e. after coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, whether payment of rent in respect of the accreted land would have been the best evidence to establish that the land so accreted was recorded in SA khatian and that plaintiffs paid rent in respect of the accreted land, but evidence is nil as to payment of rent at any point of time i.e. the period starting from 1935 as claimed by the plaintiffs. It may be mentioned the plaintiffs have asserted that accretion took place in 1935. Even if it is taken that accretion was not complete in 1935, as the High Court Division considered, but started in 1935 and gradually there has been accretion till the time of their purchase, prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in the year 1944, but the said fact i.e. accretion started in 1935 and that at the time of the purchase made in 1944 there was existence of the accreted land has not been established by the plaintiffs by leading any tangible evidence and that the fact of payment of rent for the accreted land till the time of acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government to the landlord has not been established by adducing any evidence. The undisputed position is that the accreted land has not been recorded in SA khatian. Had the accreted land been in existence since 1935 and at the time of preparation of the SA record and had the plaintiffs any claim in the accreted land they would have certainly got the accreted land recorded in their name in SA khatian. This vital fact shows that at the time of preparation of the SA record the accreted land was not in existence or, in other words, there has been accretion of the land as claimed by the plaintiffs subsequent to the coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in that state of the matter the Government got the accreted land surveyed and prepared the চর্চা ম্যাপ" with the চর্চা" plot. The learned Counsel further submitted that the trial Court. was not in error in holding in the background of the materials on record that the plaintiffs failed to prove that there has been accretion of the land claimed by them to the CS plot Nos. 670, 671, 674, 675, 676 and 250 as well as the corresponding RS plot Nos. 605, 608, 613, 613, 612 and 302 before coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. As stated hereinbefore Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into operation in the Dhaka District on 1-8-1963 vide notification No. SA 116/63/609 dated 18th July, 1963 published in the Dhaka Gazette (ordinary) dated 1st August, 1963 (part 1, page 1169). In the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195 it has been observed, "The date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in any area must necessarily be a date later than that of the publication of the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act in that area ..... only such accretions, as took place after Part V of the Act had come into force in the area where the accreted lands are situated, have been brought under the purview of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 87 of the Act. It is natural that sub-section (3) will have operation only in respect of such accretions as have been contemplated in sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 87 of the Act.</u>

14. We have noticed that all accretions, which took place before the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act, have been statutorily recognised to be the lands appertaining to the tenancies of the riparian owners and the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of section 3(4) or items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act have clearly conferred the right of tenancy upon the riparian owner in respect of such accreted lands".

15. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the said Court in its judgment in more than one place had put stress on the question relating to time of accretion of the land described in schedule 'kha' in the background of the contention of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and 6-8, and on consideration of the materials on record held that the land in suit i.e. accreted land as claimed by the plaintiffs were not in existence at the time of preparation of the SA record and that on 1-8-1963 when Part V of the Act came into operation in Dhaka District. This clearly shows that the trial Court was quite aware of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195 that in case of accretion of land prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act the tenant to whose land there has been accretion would be the tenant or, in other words, would be the owner of that accreted land, but if there is accretion of land to the tenancy of a person subsequent to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act the land so accreted would remain to the Government. As stated hereinbefore the plaintiffs did not establish by leading any evidence that there has been accretion of the land as claimed by them to their tenancy prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act i.e. prior to 1-8- 1963, and that as the claimant of the land paid rent either to the landlord prior to the acquisition of rent receiving interest or to the Government any time prior to the coming into operation of Part V of the Act i.e. on 1-8-1963.

<u>16. It has been submitted that the High Court Division proceeded on the wrong premise that the trial Court was unaware of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court we are of the view the submission or the contention so made by the learned Counsel of the appellant appears to be of merit. As stated hereinbefore the trial Court while dismissing the suit considered the question of accretion' of the land claimed by the plaintiffs prior to 1-8-1963 and that the fact of accretion of the land prior to 1-8-1963 having not been established the trial Court dismissed the suit amongst others, on this ground also. The plaintiffs filed the suit seeking declaration that the settlement made by the Government to the defendant Nos. 6-8 of the land claimed by them as accreted land was illegal and the proceeding of the LA case was not legal and prayed for recovery of khas possession of 4 decimals of land described in schedule 'ga' to the plaint. It is the plaintiffs' case that they have been dispossessed by the defendants from 4 decimals of land described in schedule 'ga'. This means the plaintiffs are in possession of the rest of the land in suit i.e. 2.91 acres of land. The total land in suit is 2.95 acres. The suit as framed was declaratory suit simpliciter in respect of the land described in schedule 'kha' to the plaint measuring 2.95 acres i.e. the accreted land. The trial Court on consideration of the oral evidence as well as the documentary evidence arrived at the definite finding that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the land described in schedule 'kha' and that failed to establish that they have been dispossessed from the land described in schedule 'ga'. Since the plaintiffs are not in possession of the land in suit and also failed to prove their case of dispossession from the land of 'ga' schedule they are not entitled to the relief as prayed for. The trial Court has held that the land in suit belonged to the Government and the Government settled the same to the defendant Nos. 6-8. The finding of the trial Court as to that the land in suit belonged to the Government has been made upon arriving at the finding that at the time of final publication of SA khatian in 1963 the accreted land was not in existence or, in other words, there has been accretion of the land claimed by the plaintiffs after coming into operation of Part V of the Act and, as such, the same belonged to the Government. The aforesaid finding of the trial Court clearly demonstrates that the said Court was quite aware of the law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. This being the position the High Court Division was in error in holding that the trial Court was unaware of law laid down by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. From the judgment of the trial Court it is seen that the said Court on detailed discussions and considerations of the evidence, both oral and documentary, arrived at the finding that there has been accretion to the CS plots after coming into operation of Part V of the Act.</u>

17. The learned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that a tenant cannot claim accreted land in excess of the land of his original tenancy as per provision in the proviso to the first paragraph of Regulation 4 of the Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation XI of 1825. The proviso to the aforesaid first paragraph of Regulation 4 runs as:

"Provided that the increment of land thus obtained shall not entitle the person in possession of the estate or tenure to which the land may be annexed to a right of property or permanent interest therein beyond that possessed by him in the estate or tenure to which the land may be annexed, and shall not in any case be understood to exempt the holder of it from the payment to the Government of any assessment for the public revenue to which it may be liable under the provisions of Regulation II, 1819, or of any other Regulation in force".

18. It is seen from the materials on record, at least in two cases, i.e. CS plot Nos. 676 and 250, land accreted and claimed as accreted land is more than the land for which there has been tenancy. The contention so made is not so much relevant for the disposal of the appeal since the point involved in the appeal whether the High Court Division without adverting to the reasoning’s given and findings arrived at by the trial Court in disposing of the suit and the trial Court also having had considered the provision of law as regard accretion after coming into operation of part V of the Act in the particular locality the High Court Division without disposing of the appeal on merit was correct in sending the suit back on remand.

<u>19. It may be mentioned the High Court Division did not at all advert to the finding and decision made by the trial Court while making the observation that the said Court was unaware of the law laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195.</u>

<u>20. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the defendants by adducing reliable evidence proved their possession in the entire land in suit. The fact of defendants being in possession of the land in suit has also been admitted by the plaintiffs' witnesses. In that state of the matter the claim of the plaintiffs that they are in possession of the land in suit except 4(four) decimals is anything but not the fact. Had the plaintiffs would have started to claim and to possess the land gradually accreted to the CS plots they would have certainly been in possession, but they failed to prove their claim of possession in the accreted land i.e. land in suit. The Government settled the accreted land with the defendant Nos. 6-8 by starting Settlement Case Nos. 265 and 229 of 1988-89 and made over possession to the said settlement holders on 30-5-1989. As against the settlement so made and possession made over to the defendant Nos. 6-8 by the Government the plaintiffs did not take any step. The defendants have proved the fact of settling the land in suit with them and handing over possession of the land so settled with them by oral and documentary evidence. As stated hereinbefore that the appellate Court did not at all consider legality of the judgment appealed before it. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division has sent back the case on remand to afford an opportunity to the parties to, adduce evidence in respect of their respective claim. It is difficult to understand what further fact to be established by the parties adducing fresh evidence while parties have lead evidence to establish their case regarding period of accretion of the land in suit and there is no insufficiency of evidence for arriving at the finding and decision as regard the period of accretion of the land in suit. The plaintiffs filed the suit seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore and led evidence in support thereof. The defendants in rebuttal of the claim of the plaintiffs and in proof of their case led evidence. The Trial Court on detailed discussions of the evidence and upon consideration of the law involved in the case made decision as regard the case of the parties on merit. It is difficult for us to understand what remains for the parties to establish since no new fact was placed before the High Court Division which needs adjudication by the trial Court upon affording the parties opportunity to adduce evidence in support of the fact so placed before the appellate Court. The plaintiff did also not raise question of law mixed with fact before the appellate Court and the question so raised could only be adjudicated upon taking fresh evidence. The law is settled now that an order of remand is not well founded in law if the same is premium for the laches and negligence of one of the parties to the suit or to enable a party to fill up a lacuna in his case which in spite of the opportunity to fill up the said gap, the party did not care to take step in that regard.</u>

<u>21. On reading the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division did not at all apply its mind to the reasonings and findings of the trial Court while disposing of the suit and that also was not correct in arriving at the finding that the trial Court was unaware of the law laid down by this Division in the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. Since the trial Court addressed itself to all the points involved in the suit and that in addressing itself to the points involved in the suit the trial Court was not in error we are of the view the High Court Division was not correct in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.</u>

22. In that state of the matter we find merit in the appeal.

23. Accordingly the appeal is allowed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 3-9-2001 (decree signed on 10-9-2001) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Natore in Title Appeal No. 234 of 1998 reversing the judgment and decree dated 3-11-1998 (decree signed on 5-11-1998) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Natore Sadar, Natore in Title Suit No. 163 of 1996.

2. The brief fact relevant for disposal of the Rule is that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 herein as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.163 of 1996 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Natore Sadar, Natore for declaration that the kabala in question is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The gist of the plaintiffs case is that the plaintiffs have been possessing in the suit land by making a dwelling hut as well as by cultivating; that the defendants filed a criminal case being CR No. 4639 of 1996 against the plaintiffs and subsequently, the notice of the said criminal case was served upon the plaintiffs on 22-8-96 in which the plaintiffs became dumb to know that they sold out the suit land to the defendants on 19-2-75. In such background the plaintiffs made an inquiry and found that the father of the defendants named Shahar Ali in connivance with the employees of the Sub-Registrar Office created the alleged forged kabala dated 19-2-75 by false personification. Hence the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the said suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to the plaintiffs inejmali; that 1.20 acre of land of 2 plots belonged to the predecessor of the defendants named Shahar Ali, who died leaving behind his wife, 2 sons and 6 daughters; that the father of the defendants purchased 15-1/2 decimals of land from the plaintiffs in the name of the defendant No.1 The defendants on the basis of a registered kabala accrued their rights, title, interest and possession over the suit land; that the plaintiffs without complying with the decision of the salish brought the suit on false allegation and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. At the trial the plaintiffs examined as many as 3 witnesses and defendants examined 2 DWs and exhibited a series of documents in support of their respective cases. The Senior Assistant Judge, Natore Sadar, Natore on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 3-11-98 (decree signed on 5-11-98) mainly on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation.

5. On appeal, the judgment and decree dated 3-11-98 (decree signed on 5-11-98» was reversed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Natore vide judgment and decree dated 3-9-2001 (decree signed on 10-9-2001).

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 234 of 1998 the defendant-respondent- petitioners have come before this Court in an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the impugned judgment and decree is not a proper judgment of reversal and not based on valid and cogent grounds. He next submits that the learned trial Judge on assessment on the entire materials on record rightly arrived at a finding that the instant suit was barred by limitation, inasmuch as admittedly the kabala in question was executed and registered on 19-2-75 and the instant suit was has been brought on 3-10-96 praying the kabala in question is forged, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed further submits that the appellate Court below as a last Court of fact has failed to consider that the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence, that the father of the defendant petitioners in connivance with the employees of the Sub-Registrar Office managed to obtain the forged kabala dated 19-2-75. Mr Zulfiqur further submits that the trial Court rightly held that the plaintiffs failed to prove the date of knowledge about the impugned deed by producing the original copy of the notice of CR Case No. 463/P of 1996, but brushing aside this material aspect of the case the appellate Court below reversed the finding of the trial Court and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.

8. Mr Zulfiqur, finally most emphatically submits that the plaintiffs are party in the impugned kabala dated 19-2-75 and thus, without any cancellation prayer of the kabala in question the suit is not maintainable. The learned Advocate in support of his last contention has relied on a decision reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39.

9. On the other hand, Mr Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, supports the impugned judgment and decree dated 3-9-2001 which was, according to him, just, correct and proper. The learned Advocate in the course of argument, after placing the plaint, submits that the specific case of the plaintiffs as stated in paragraph No. 1 of the plaint that they received notice of CR Case No. 463-P/96 under sections 144/145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed by the defendant-petitioner against the plaintiffs on 22-8-96 and then they came to know about the impugned sale deed which was admitted by PW- 1 and DW-1 in their respective testimony and, as such, the question of limitation does not arise at all, but the trial Court below without appreciating the case from a correct angle most illegally held that the suit was barred by limitation.

10. Mr Saba, the learned Advocate further, after placing the judgment of the trial Court below, submits that the learned Judge in his judgment did not at all consider/discuss the evidence of PWs and, as such, the judgment of the trial Court below is not a proper judgment. He further submits that the judgment of the trial Court below is not based on correct evaluation, facts and materials of the case nor on proper appreciation of the evidence on record and, as such, the appellate Court as a final Court of fact rightly reversed the same which should not be disturbed. Mr Saha in support of his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 10 = 50 DLR (AD) 50, 54 DLR (AD) 26, 1987 BLD (AD) 103, 42 DLR 499, 44 DLR 79 & 5 DLR 17.

11. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the revisional application, the judgments of two Courts below and other materials on record. It is the specific case of the plaintiff-opposite parties that on 22-8-96 after receiving the notice of CR Case No. 463-P/96 under sections 144/145, CrPC the plaintiffs came to know about the impugned sale deed dated 19-2-75 and whereupon, the opposite parties as plaintiffs preferred the instant suit on 1-10-96 for declaration that the kabala in question is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

12. At the trial in order to prove the date of knowledge about the deed in question dated 19-2-75, the plaintiffs filed a photo copy of the notice of GR Case No. 463-P/96 under sections 144/145, CrPC before the trial Court. The Trial Court held that as there was no seal and signature of the Court in the photo copy of the notice, the same cannot be relied upon. The trial Court also held that the plaintiffs did not take any step to call for the record of the criminal case and they could not file any certified copy of the notice of CR Case No. 463-P/96 and it is apparent that the impugned sale deed was registered on 19-2-75 and the suit was filed on 1-10-96 and the plaintiffs have been failed to prove the date of know- ledge by adducing sufficient oral and documentary evidence and hence on both the counts the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation.

13. The Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Natore on assessment of the entire evidence on record arrived at a finding that the suit was not barred by limitation as the plaintiffs filed certified copy of the notice of CR Case No. 463-P/96 before the appellate Court below proving that the plaintiff-appellants received the same on 22-8-96.

14. It is found that plaintiff No. 1 Md Moslem Miah as PW 1 testified that on 8th Bhadra, 1403 BS corresponding to 22-8-96 he received the notice of the criminal case and then he came to know about the impugned sale deed. The plaintiffs filed the present suit on 1-10-96. Therefore, in any view of the matter the appellate Court below rightly arrived at a finding that the suit is not barred by limitation.

15. Mr Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate relying on the decision reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 10 = 50 DLR (AD) 50 , submits that in a case of fraud, the question of limitation will run from the date of 'knowledge and not from the date of execution of the disputed document.

16. In the instant case, it appears that the deed in question was registered on 19-2-75 and the plaintiffs after receiving the notice of criminal case on 22-8-96 came to know about the impugned kabala dated 19-2-75, thereafter filed the suit on 1-10-96. It transpires from the record that defendant-petitioners applied for mutation after filing the criminal case in 1996, after a long lapse of 2l years. This inordinate delay of 21 years for applying for mutation creates serious doubt upon the genuineness of the impugned sale deed dated 19-2-75.

17. It is found that the trial Court observed that the plaintiffs did not implead the father of the defendants in the suit and, as such the suit was bad for defect of parties. The appellate Court below, in its turn, arrived at a finding that the suit was not bad for defect of parties as DW-1, admitted in his cross-examination that his father died long 14/15 years ago and thus, a dead man cannot be impleaded in a suit. The finding of the appellate Court's below is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record.

18. The trial Court also held that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that the impugned deed dated 19-2-75 is a product of forgery. The appellate Court below reversed the said finding of the trial Court holding that the deed in question was registered on 19-2-75 but after filing the criminal case by the defendants in the year 1996 the defendants approached for mutating their names and such inordinate delay of 21 years raises a serious doubt upon the genuineness of the impugned sale deed.

19. In the impugned deed, it is found that both the plaintiffs put their left thumb impression (LTI) but it appears that in the plaint as well as in the deposition, PW-1 put his signature. Apart from that, in the plaint, it has been stated that: “১নং বাদী বরাবরই সহিত করিতে এবং পড়িতে পারে In their written statement the defendants did not deny this material averment of the plaint. According to Order VIII, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or stated not to be admitted by the defendant shall be taken to be admitted. So, the LTI of the plaintiff No. 1 in the impugned sale deed is not free from doubt.

20. The defendant-petitioners claimed that after the impugned sale deed is registered on 19-2- 75 they are possessing the suit land. The trial Court below did not, at all, discuss this vital point regarding possession. On the contrary, the appellate Court below, after elaborately discussing the evidence of PWs and 2 DWs, arrived at a positive finding that the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their possession in the suit land. Moreso, the defendants did not cross-examine PW 3, Afaz Uddin, who stated that the defendants have no possession in the suit land.

21. Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners has argued that the onus of proof is upon the plaintiffs.

22. In the case of Ishaque vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury reported in 54 DLR (AD) 26, it has been held as follows:

"It has been well settled that when both the parties have led evidence question of onus is out of place and matter is to be decided on the evidence led by the parties."

23. In the case of Chinibash vs Md Nurul Hossain Molla reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103, it has been held as follows:

"When both parties adduced evidence in order to set up their respective cases the question of onus loses significance."

24. In the case of Amirun Nessa vs G Kashem reported in 42 DLR 499, it was observed as follows:

"Where initial onus is discharged by the plaintiffs by giving a slight evidence the burden shifts to the defendants to prove the contrary."

25. On a perusal of the evidence on record, it appears that the defendants did not bring the scribe and the attesting witnesses of the impugned sale deed to prove the same is genuine one it also appears that the defendants did not or could not adduce any evidence to prove the talk of sale, payment of the consideration money and the hand over of possession of the suit land. According to section 101 of the Evidence Act the defendants are under obligation to prove that the impugned sale deed is a genuine one, specially when the plaintiffs have denied the execution of the deed.

26. In the case of Anwar Hossain vs Abul Hossain Mollah reported in 44 DLR 79, where it has been held:

"The defendants want the Court to believe sale deed as Exhibit 2, is a bonafide document for valuable consideration but no evidence in this regard having been adduced the said Exhibit cannot be allowed to stand.”

27. Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, could not point out any misreading or non reading of the evidence by the appellate Court below. Thus, I do not find any substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners.

28. Here it may be further mentioned that the case relied on by the petitioners as reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case as the facts of the instant case are quite distinguishable from the facts of that case.

<u>29. However, Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed at the end of the day submits that the suit may be sent back to the trial Court on remand for fresh decision on taking evidence for the ends of justice. I find no merit in this contention since both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record to decide the case on merit.</u>

30. Considering all the above facts, circumstances and the principles of law enunciated in the cited decisions, I do not find any ground to differ with the view taken by the appellate Court below which, in fact, is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record.

31. Accordingly, the Rule fails.

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 3-9-2001 (decree signed on 10-9-2001) passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Natore in Title Appeal No. 234 of 1998 is hereby maintained.

Let a copy of this judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Raisuddin Ahmed with Md Arshadur Rouf (present at the hearings but not present at the time of Judgment) Advocates------- For the Petitioner. 
Abdur Razzaque Khan with Md Nesar Ahmed Advocates------- For Respondent No.6.
parties:
Elite Lamps Ltd   ------- Petitioner
Vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Industries and others   -------  Respondents.
full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the respondents should not be directed to implement the recommendation made by the Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell in its report dated 25-8-1992 (Annexure- 'E'-3 to the writ petition) and rehabilitate the petitioner's sick industry and to implement the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee of Bangladesh Jatiya Sangshad over the petitioner's Sick Industry for the above purpose and to withdraw the suit being Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 30 of 1991 now pending in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka.

2. The case of the petitioner, in short, is as under:

The petitioner, Flite Lamps Limited, represented by its Managing Director, Md Ishaque is a public limited company. The object of the petitioner company includes manufacturing of electric GLS Bulbs, other bulbs, etc for local consumption. The petitioner company which is classified as a "Small Industry" was established during 1986-87 under IDA Credit No. BD-1065 with equity investment by the sponsor and a loan of Taka 29,00,000 from Sonali Bank, Dhaka (briefly, the Bank). The Government of Bangladesh made promises to the public in its first industrial policy in 1982 with higher emphasis on setting up of new industries for (a) local production, (b) reducing imports, (c) create opportunities for employment. The Board of Investment also made promises to the public to assist the industry but such promises have never been materialised causing large scale chaos and anarchy in the industrial sector. The Bank also published a Booklet on Industrial Investment in 1984 wherein it invited proposals from entrepreneurs for setting up new industries. It offered project loan on easy terms of 80:20 debt-equity basis in an effort to supplement the Government policy of rapid industrialisation in different sectors. Other nationalised banks and a few private banks also made similar proposal for investment in setting up of new industries but the banks had failed to act upon its promises. The petitioner made repeated proposals during the years 1986-92 to the Bank for appropriate working capital but the working capital as sanctioned by the Bank was inadequate to its actual requirements. Consequently, the petitioner company went on production in weak condition during 1986-90. Finally, the petitioner stopped all production works and terminated all workers and employees and such closure was due to lack of appropriate working capital. Many other small industries were also closed down for similar reasons. On that, the petitioner made applications to the Ministry of Industries and Ministry of Finance for suitable remedies but with no result. The management of the closed small industries formed a group namely, Bangladesh Sick Industries Association. Thereafter, the petitioner and that Association approached before the Prime Minister of Bangladesh in the matter and the Prime Minister assured them of a suitable remedy. Then, the Ministry of Industries constituted a Committee in the name of "Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell" by Gazette Notification dated 15-6-1991 to look into the problems of sick industries and ultimately the said cell constituted a sub-committee by its letter dated 2-8-1992. This sub-committee submitted its final report to the Cell and it was approved by the Cell in its meeting dated 25-8-92. The Ministry of Industries by Gazette Notification dated 22-10-88 gave direction to the financial institutions for providing appropriate working capital to the concerned industrial projects but the Bank and other financial institutions deliberately neglected implementation of such directives causing large-scale closure of many industrial establishments. Bangladesh Bank by its Circular No. 25 dated 25-11-1988 had also directed the financial institutions including the Bank about sanction and disbursement' of working capital to industrial projects but without any result. Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell was constituted by the Government to identify the -sick industries and the said Cell identified the petitioner as a 'Sick Unit' in 1992 and advised respondent No. 6 (Sonali Bank, Head Office) for interest remission and suitable working capital for rehabilitation of the petitioner's industrial project by letter dated 30-9- 1992. Whereupon, respondent No.6 allowed interest remission but did not provide working capital. Consequently, the petitioner failed to recover from its sick position to a healthy unit of industry and sustained heavy loss. Meanwhile, the Bank as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Case No. 30 of 1991 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. I. Dhaka (in short, the Adalat) for recovery of its outstanding dues of Taka 75,56,66l.28 against the petitioner. The petitioner filed written statement to contest the suit. The petitioner also filed an application for rejection of the plaint which was rejected by the Adalat. So, the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 1494 of 1995 whereupon a Rule was issued by this Division. However, finally the said Rule was discharged on 2- 11-2003. Ministry of Industries prepared its report dated 25-8-1992 on sick industries for implementation by the financial institutions. Ministry of Indus- tries again constituted a পুর্নগঠিত রিভিউ কমিটি” by Gazette Notification dated 6th March 1997. There-after, Ministry of Industries through advertisement in the national media invited applications from the affected sick industries. The petitioner and other affected persons (industrial projects) applied but the Ministry of Industries did not act upon any such applications. The Ministry of Finance constituted as many as 4 committees within a span of five years between 28-1-1992 and 17-1-1998 and gave recommendations for remission of interest only. Ministry of Finance also issued notifications dated 28-10- 1992, 29-12-1994, 4-2-1997 and 4-10-1998 to solve the problems of sick industries. However, the Ministry of Industries (respondent No.1) failed to implement the recommendations made by the Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell in its report dated 25- 8-1992. Therefore, the petitioner served a notice demanding justice to respondent No. 1 but in spite of that the respondent No. 1 did not make any response. Hence, this writ petition.

3. Respondent No. 6, Sonali Bank, opposes the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material averments made in the writ petition contending, inter alia, that on an application of the petitioner dated 1-11-1986 for setting up of electric bulb industry the Bank under 3rd IDA Credit Scheme sanctioned a sum of Taka 29,00,000 as loan by letter No.BBA/ADB-3rd/IDA/ELL/10645 dated 26-7-1987. Out of total loan limit the project loan was Taka 24,00,000 and working capital was Taka 5,00,000 only but the petitioner due to non-com- pletion of the project did not avail of the working capital loan. Thereafter, the petitioner applied for loan in current account and the Bank from its own source sanctioned Taka 5,00,000 only on hypothecation basis in lieu of working capital, vide sanction letter dated 17-3-1987. Again, the petitioner applied for LC limit for import of raw material for production and accordingly, the Bank sanctioned LC Limit for Taka 10,85,250 by letter dated 12-8-87 but the petitioner did not avail of the limit in full and it only availed of the facilities for Taka 5,97,000 by apprising letter of credit. As against the letter of credit terms, when the raw materials had arrived the petitioner also failed to release the imported raw materials. So, at the request of the petitioner, the Bank by creating AAM facilities released the goods. The period of repayment of loan expired on 31-12- 1987 but the petitioner did not adjust the same. Thereafter, the Bank on prayer of the petitioner again sancetioned cash credit loan of Taka 20,00,000 on pledge basis and sanctioned cash credit loan of Taka 5,00,000 on hypothecation basis. Thus, total cash credit limit stood at Taka 25,00,000 vide letter No. BBAIADB/3rd lDA/ELL/12086 dated 26-12- 1987. Thereafter, on an application of the petitioner cash credit limit was further enhanced by the Bank by its letter dated 4-5-1988 to Taka 20,00,000. Subsequently, the Bank by letter dated 3-10-1988 re-allocated the cash credit limit as pledge for Taka 10,00,000 and as hypothecation for Taka 10,00,000. The Bank as per request of the petitioner ultimately sanctioned cash credit limit from Taka 20,00,000 to Taka 35,00,000 vide letter dated 16-5-1990. Although the petitioner took the above credit facilities but it did not properly utilise the said money and stopped the production of the project with malafide intention beyond the existing norms and terms of the Bank as well as the industrial policy of the country. The petitioner did not repay the Bank's money as per terms of the sanctioned letters. Therefore, the liabilities of the petitioner to the Bank stood of Taka 75,50,661.28 as on 31-12-1999. In these circumstances, the Bank was compelled to file Dewani Suit No. 30 of 1991 against the petitioner before the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka on 19-2-1991 for recovery of the above loan amount.

4. The petitioner's factory was closed due to its own fault although the Bank gave a lot of credit facilities. However, the Board of Directors of the Bank in its meeting dated 6-7-1993 made the following recommendations for the petitioner.

“১. বিভিন্ন ঋনাদিও খেলাপী পরবর্তী ১০০ % সাধারন সুদ/দন্ড সুদ বাবদ ২৬,৮১,৬৮৫ টাকা মওকুফ।

২. প্রকল্প ঋনের মওকুফ পরবর্র্তী বকেয়া ৩৫,০৮,৬০৮ টাকা সুদসহ ৬(ছয়) মাস পর তথা ডিসেম্বর ৯৩ হতে পরবর্তী ৯ (নয়) বৎসরে (৩১ ডিসেম্বর ২০০২ পর্যন্ত) ত্রৈমাসিক কিস্তিতে আদায়ের লক্ষ্যে পুনঃ তফসিলীকরন।

৩.  বিদ্যমান ক্যাশ ক্রেডিট ঋনাদির মওকুফ অবশিষ্ট বকেয়া ২৬,৬২,৪৭৭ টাকা সুদসহ ৬(ছয়) মাস পর তথা ডিসেম্বর ৯৩ হতে পরবর্তী ৯ (নয়) বৎসরে (৩১ ডিসেম্বর ২০০২ পর্যন্ত) ত্রৈমাসিক কিস্তিতে আদায়ের লক্ষ্যে পুনঃ তফসিলীকরন।

৪. ব্যাংক হতে ঋনগ্রহীতার বিরুদ্ধে ১৯ ফেব্রুয়ারি ১৯৯১ তারিখে দায়েরকৃত মামলা প্রত্যাহার/স্থগিতকরণ।

৫. প্রকল্পের প্লেজ গুদামে রক্ষিত মালামাল ঋন গ্রহীতা ও  শাখার যৌথ তত্ত্বাবধানে বিক্রি করতঃ গুদাম খালিকরণ এবং প্রাপ্ত অর্থ ক্যাশ ক্রেডিট বক্র হিসাবে স্থানান্তর।

৬. প্রকল্পের কাঁচামাল আমদানীর জন্য ২০% মার্জিনে ৬০,০০,০০০ লক্ষ টাকার এলসি লিমিট মঞ্জুরী।

৭. প্রকল্পের অনুকলে ১(এক) বৎসর মেয়াদ ১২৩.০০ লক্ষ টাকা চলতি মূলধন (প্লেজ ৮৩.০০+ হাইপোঃ ৪০.০০ লক্ষ) টাকা মঞ্জুরী ( দৈনিক উৎপাদন ক্ষমতা ১২৪০০ পিস বিবেচনা করে)।

৮. প্রকল্পের যন্ত্রপাতি মেরামত/সার্ভিসিং করার জন্য হাইপোপিকেশন সীমা হতে ৪.০০ লক্ষ টাকা বিতরনের অনুমোদন। যা পরবর্তীতে ঋনগ্রহীতা স্টকদ্বারা পরিপূর্ণ করবেন।”

5. The aforesaid Board decision was communicated to the writ petitioner by the Bank letter dated 20-7-1993 but petitioner neither came forward to accept the proposal nor executed any agreement with the Bank rather, the petitioner instituted a suit for damages against the Bank in Title Suit No. 122 of 1994 in the Court of the First Sub-ordinate Judge, Gazipur but the same was dismissed on the ground of maintainability. The petitioner then filed Writ Petition No. 296 of 1994 in which the Rule was discharged. The petitioner again filed Writ Petition No. 1494 of 1995 challenging the maintainability of the Artha Rin Suit pending before the Artha Rin Adalat but finally the Rule of the said Writ Petition was also discharged on 2-11-2003. Hence, the instant misconceived and not maintainable Writ Petition and the Rule should be discharged.

6. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply dated 13th November, 2007 mostly reiterating the same facts as in the Writ Petition and annexing the photostat copies of the same documents.

7. Respondent No. 6 also filed an affidavit-in- reply against the affidavit-in-reply of the writ petitioner annexing some documents.

8. Mr Raisuddin Ahmed and Mr Md Arshadur Rouf, the learned Advocates, appeared for the petitioner. Mr Md Arshadur Rouf in the course of argument has taken us through the writ petition and affidavit-in-reply and then submits that the Government has to implement the recommendations made by the Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell in its report dated 25-5-92 and the Government is legally bound to implement the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on this matter. He also submits that the Bank did not provide adequate working capital to the petitioner as a result of which the petitioner became a sick industry for the fault of the Bank. So, according to him, the Bank is to implement the recommendation of the Sick Industires Rehabilitation Cell and the recommendations made by the Parliamentary Committee and the Rule is liable to be made absolute.

9. Mr Abdur Razzaque Khan, the learned Advocate appearing along with Mr Md Nesar Ahmed for respondent No. 6, has taken us through the affidavit-in-opposition and affidavit-in-reply and then contends that the Bank gave enough money and opportunity to the petitioner to run the industry properly but the petitioner deliberately did not utilise the loan properly as per sanction letter. He next contends that it was the fault of the petitioner as a result of which the industry became sick industry. He further contends that admittedly 100% interest remission was given to the petitioner and the petitioner was communicated to avail the opportunity given by the Board of Directors for re-scheduling the loan by executing proper agreements but the petitioner did not come forward to enter into any agreement as proposed by the Bank. He also contends that the instant writ petition is not maintainable, inasmuch as the recommendations made by Sick Industry Rehabilitation Cell dated 25-8-92 and/or of the Parliamentary Committee has no legal binding force of a law and so, it cannot be implemented through court whatsoever. He also con- tends that the petitioner prayed for withdrawal of the Artha Rin Suit for the purpose of implementation of those recommendations but the Artha Rin Suit cannot be withdrawn since the recommendations are not binding upon the Bank.

10. In view of the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the parties the most vital question to be decided in the Rule is, whether the court can direct implementation of the recommendations as stated earlier.

11. Perused the writ petition, affidavits-in- opposition, affidavits-in-reply submitted by the petitioner and respondent No. 6. Considered the materials on record and the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the contending parties.

12. We have already seen that in this Writ Petition the petitioner sought for a direction for implementations of the recommendations made by the Sick Industries Rehabilitation Cell and the Parliamentary Committee.

13. We have examined the recommendation dated 25-2-1992 (Annexure-E3 to the writ petition) along with connected decision of our Apex Court as best as we could. It appears to us that this recommendation is not a legal instrument creating any legal right for the petitioner so as to implement it through a Court. Similarly, we have examined the recommendation of Parliamentary Committee (Annexure-Q to the writ petition). It appears to us that this recommendation is neither a legal instrument having force of law nor a law creating any legal right to the petitioner.

14. This view has been well settled in the following cases:

(i) Professor Abdur Rahim Khan vs Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries reported in 7 BLT (AD) 313 wherein our Apex Court decided as follows:

"It is true that the High Court Division suffered from a misconception of fact that there was already an agreement contract between the parties and a dispute has arisen over the terms and conditions thereof which was the subject matter of the writ petition. In fact, the petitioners came to the writ petition for a direction upon the respondents to finalise the agreement only on the basis of the recommendation of the Cabinet Committee as approved by the Prime Minister vide aforesaid Memo dated 8-5-94. The High Court Division's misconception was there but the misconceived nature of the petitioner's writ petition was equally showing. Unfortunately. the High Court Division failed to take notice of the same and proceeded upon a wrong ground of fact. The recommendation of a Cabinet Committee cannot be enforced through a writ for the simple reason that it is not law. It is as simple as that. The Writ Petition was misconceived at the inception."

(ii) Ms Greenways Tannery represented by its Proprietor Sirajuddowla vs Secretary Ministry of Industries, Government of Bangladesh. This Writ Petition No. 6270 of 2003 was filed for implementation of the recommendations made by Sick Industry Rehabilitation Cell in its report 25-8-92 (i.e. like the present writ petition) and the Rule of this writ petition was discharged by judgment dated 18-5- 2004 by this Division mentioning that Judgment and decision of Writ Petition No. 3992 of 1999 passed on that date shall govern the Judgment of this Writ Petition.

(iii) Greenways Tannery vs Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka. This earlier mentioned Writ Petition No. 3292 of 1999 was filed challenging the institution and proceeding of Artha Rin suit on the ground that recommendations were not implemented by the Government and suit cannot be proceeded without implantations thereof. In this Writ Petition this Division by judgment dated 18-5- 2004 decided as under:

............................................................................................................................

In the notification issued by the Government for implementation of the recommendation made by the Government there is no legal obligation on the part of the loan granting bank not to initiate the legal proceeding or to institute a suit for realisation of the outstanding dues and the recommendation and the policy as formulated in the notification dated 6-3-97 for settlement of the dues out of court for the purpose of rehabilitation of the sick industries are not binding upon the respondent bank and the respondent will proceed for realisation of the dues under the law, namely. the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990. "

(iv) Mirzaboo Steels Ltd vs Bangladesh reported in 59 DLR 141. This Writ Petition No. 1527 of 2001 was filed for implementation of the recommendation of the Sick Industry Rehabilitation Cell dated 29-9-92. This Rule was discharged by this Division by judgment dated 13-12-2006 with the following observations:

"However, it is now a settled principle of law that Article 102 of the Constitution can be invoked only where the petitioner's right has undisputedly accrued under the Constitution or under any other legal instrument and such right has not been given effect to. In other words, the petitioner is being deprived of the benefit to such right. The aforesaid letter dated 29-9- 1992, Annexure 'B' to the writ petition is not a legal instrument creating legal right for the petitioner for waiver of 100% interest and other benefits as has been observed above. It only lays down the policy of the government making recommendation for waiver of such interest without creating any legal right... ..........

15. In view of the observations made above as to enforceability of the notification, we are of the opinion that the notification dated 29-9-92, Annexure B to the writ petition, has no force of law and accordingly, has no binding effect upon the respondent Bank. Moreover, the legislature having had incorporated the same concept of amicable settlement in the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 the respective petitioner company cannot be said to have been left without any forum to place its grievance in accordance with law. Hence, the proceeding of the Mortgage Suit being No. 71 of 1995 cannot be adjourned in view of Annexure-E and shall proceed in accordance with law. Considering the observations and the findings made hereinabove by this court we are of the view that this Rule bears no merit for consideration. Accordingly, it is liable to be discharged.

(v) Edruk Ltd vs Secretary, Ministry of Industires. This Writ Petition No. 7300 of 2003 was also filed for direction for implementation of the recommendations made by the Sick Industry Rehabilitation Cell in its report dated 25- 9-92 (similar to the present one) in which we were parties. This Rule was also discharged by our Judgment dated 1-10-2007 deciding that the recommendation bears no binding force to the Court in any way.

16. From the discussion made in the foregoing paragraphs and the decisions referred to as above, it is clear that by now it is a well established principle of law that policy guide line, recommendations, etc not being law cannot be enforced through Court.

<u>17. Since, the recommendations cannot be legally enforced by the Court and it is not legally binding upon the Bank, no direction can be given for withdrawing a suit for non-implementation of those recommendations. The Bank will proceed with the suit in accordance with law.</u>

<u>18. The question as to whether the petitioner became a sick industry due to its own fault or for the fault of the Bank being a disputed question of fact it cannot be decided in summary Writ jurisdiction.</u>

19. Lastly, we feel it necessary to add a few words about the conduct of the writ petitioner. The petitioner earlier filed a suit being No. 122 of 1994 against the Bank which was dismissed. Then the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 296 of 1994 challenging the order of the Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 30 of 1991 and the Rule issued in that Writ Petition was discharged. Then the petitioner again filed a Writ Petition No. 1494 of 1995 challenging the maintainability of the same suit and the Rule issued in that writ petition was also discharged. The matter did not end there. The petitioner further stands in the way of the Artha Rin Case No. 30 of 1991 by filing this third writ petition which is also without any merit.

20. The petitioner also left no stone unturned to delay the disposal of this writ petition which would be apparent from our order dated 18-11-2007. All these are cunning devices adopted by the petitioner only with the intent to delay the disposal of the original suit being Artha Rin Case No. 30 of 1991 filed in the year 1991 for realisation of the Bank loan against the petitioner. The petitioner by this way successfully delayed disposal of the suit for about 16 years till now. The conduct of the petitioner is disgraceful.

21. In the given facts and circumstances of the case and the uniform decisions of the highest Court as cited above, we have no hesitation to hold that the instant Writ Petition is incompetent, ill advised, vexatious and filed by the defendant-petitioner with sole motive to hang the realisation of the Bank's money by dragging the matter for an indefinite period.

22. The order of stay has already been vacated earlier discussing the conduct of the petitioner by order dated 18-11-2007.

23. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

24. The Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka is directed to dispose of the Artha Rin Case No. 30 of 1991 expeditiously preferably within 4 (four) months from date.

Communicate the Judgment to the Adalat at once.

End.

2. In the aforesaid Writ petitions, Rules were issued in identical terms calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the aforesaid decision and order dated 3-3-2004 passed by the Chairman, 3rd Labour Court, Dhaka respondent No.1, in the IRO cases, shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. For the sake of brevity and convenience we would like to discuss, in brief, the respective petitioner's cases separately. In Writ Petition No. 1405 of 2004 arising out of IRO Case No. 23 of 2001 the 1st party petitioner Hasmat Ali along with other colleagues initially was appointed Aircraft Mechanic on causal basis for 90 days against permanent posts in the Engineering Division of Bangladesh Biman Corporation, Zia International Airport, Dhaka, with effect from 14th July, 1996 which was extended for another 90 days on 14-10-1996 and then the petitioner was again appointed in the same post and the same place out of practical necessity and in the interest of Biman in terms of Administrative Order No. 12/86 and thereafter he was appointed for another 90 days on 18-1-1997 and then he was also appointed continuously on 13-3- 2001 till 22-3-2004 when the service was discontinued after the decision of the 3rd Labour Court, Dhaka passed on 3-3-2004. It is stated that on 18- 12-2000 there was an internal transfer whereby the first party petitioner was transferred to Line Maintenance until 13-3-2001 when he was again transferred to Base Maintenance wherein he was working till date. The first party was paid wages @ Taka 65.00 per day for the first term of 90 days and Taka 65.00 again per day for the second term of 90 days as a causal worker on casual basis and payments were made by the Engineering Department. The first party-petitioner worked for 270 days in the first 3 terms and after a short gap he was working continuously since 13-6-2001 till date. Thus he was entitled to be made permanent as he has put in a period of service of 8 years. Though the first party- petitioner was engaged in causal service against vacant permanent posts and has been working continuously for many years and thereby the first party- petitioner is entitled to a permanent post. In this circumstance the opposite party No. 1 in order to regularise those posts made advertisement in National Dailies. The petitioner passed SSC Examination in Science Group in the 2nd Division and HSC examination in Science Group in the 2nd Division and, as such, there is no scope to hold that the petitioner had no requisite qualification to get appointment to the post of Aircraft Mechanic. In this way the first party-petitioner was deprived of his right of being appointed to the permanent post. The petitioner made several representations to the Higher Authorities of Bangladesh  Biman Corporation without any success. It is further stated that the petitioner was appointed for 90 days on 14-7-1996 and thereafter his tenure was extended for another two terms and after a gap of 3 days he has been working continuously since 13-3-2001 till date. First party was initially appointed as a skilled worker having completed or deemed to have completed his period of probation after the expiry of 6 months.

Sub-sections (I) and (2) of section 4 of the Employment of Labour (SO) Act, 1965 read as follows:

"Classification of workers and period of probation-( I) A worker employed in any shop or commercial or industrial establishment shall be classified in any of the following cases according to the nature and condition of work and in the manner provided in this Act-

(a) apprentices.

(b) badlis.

(c) casual.
